samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
# The Sound of the Crossing

On the last morning of the ferry, the town came down to the river before sunrise.

Some people arrived in coats over their pajamas. Others carried paper cups of coffee or cameras with long lenses. A few brought folding chairs, though there was nowhere to set them except the muddy strip beside the road. By five o’clock, a line had formed beneath the yellow lamp at the landing.

I was there with a recorder borrowed from the library, trying to capture the sound of the engine.

The librarian, who had lent me the machine, said I should record everything. “You never know what people will miss,” she told me.

I thought people would miss the ferry’s horn: two low notes that came across the water every morning and told half the town it was late for work. I thought they would miss the engine’s uneven growl and the heavy knock of the ramp when it met the bank. Those were the sounds I had come to collect.

But when I listened to my first recording, the ferry was barely audible. Close to the microphone, someone was shaking sugar into a coffee cup. A man behind me cleared his throat. Two children argued over which of them had seen the boat first. Somewhere in the dark, my mother laughed.

I stopped the recording before I had meant to. I didn’t want her voice on it.

The ferry had crossed the Graywater River for ninety-three years. It was not the first boat to work that route, but it was the one everyone remembered: a squat green vessel called the *Ada Bell*, with a wheelhouse that leaned slightly to port and benches polished smooth by wet coats and waiting hands.

The new bridge stood a mile upstream. Its opening had been delayed twice, once by high water and once by an error in the steel measurements. For two years we had watched it grow above the reeds. On clear days its white cables made a fine pattern against the hills. Trucks would soon be able to cross the river at any hour, and an ambulance would no longer have to wait for the boat.

Almost everyone agreed that the bridge was needed. Almost everyone had come to say goodbye anyway.

My mother had worked on the ferry since I was eleven. At first she sold tickets and directed cars into rows. Later she learned to operate the ramp, inspect the engine, and steer. By the time I left for college, she was captain on the early shift. When I was young, she came home smelling of diesel and river water, with a white mark on her forehead where the edge of her cap had kept off the sun.

I had moved back to town three months earlier, after twelve years away. My mother called it a visit, although I had brought all my books.

“Get the bell,” she said now, stepping off the ferry to find me.

She wore her old blue jacket. The last time I had seen it, it hung on a hook behind her kitchen door. I had assumed she’d retired it years ago.

“What bell?”

“The brass one by the ticket window. People ring it when they’ve paid on foot.”

“I know the bell.”

“Then get it.”

She went back up the ramp before I could answer. Even off duty, she spoke as though a boat were about to leave without me.

At the library, I had volunteered to make a short audio record of the crossing. It had seemed like a task with clear edges. Record the ferry, ask a few people what they remembered, return the machine. I had not expected to spend the morning taking orders from my mother, or to have strangers lean toward the microphone and tell me about their divorces, weddings, first jobs, and dead dogs.

A woman named Elsie said she met her husband on the ferry during a storm. He had offered her his dry seat, though she was already soaked. For fifty-one years, she told me, he claimed he’d fallen in love when she refused it.

A delivery driver remembered the time the engine failed halfway across and the boat drifted downstream. He had been frightened until my mother opened the wheelhouse window and told him to stop honking. There was nothing ahead for him to warn.

The children who had argued in the dark came over with their father. They had ridden the ferry that morning for the first time. When I asked what they thought of it, the younger one said the water looked colder than it did from shore. Her brother said he liked the gate.

Neither mentioned the horn.

At six, the first full load pulled away. Cars occupied every space on the deck. Along the rail stood people who had left their vehicles so they could feel the boat move. From shore, I held the recorder toward them. The engine rumbled, the horn sounded, and the brass bell rang as someone arrived too late to board.

Through my headphones, I heard a man beside me say, quietly, “There she goes.”

He was looking at the ferry, not at anyone aboard. I turned, but he had already walked away.

For a long time I had believed that leaving made events easier to see. In other cities I could tell the story of the place I came from: the river, the boat, the houses that faced the road rather than the water. I could describe how the fog rose in autumn and how the school bus sometimes waited behind a line of tractors headed for the landing.

What I couldn’t explain was my mother.

While I was growing up, the ferry ran on a schedule that governed our house. She left early, came home tired, slept when other mothers attended concerts or games. She remembered to arrange rides for me, remembered to leave money for lunch, remembered everything practical. If I wanted to talk to her, I often sat at the kitchen table after she came home and waited for her to finish her dinner.

When I moved away, we got along better by telephone. She asked about my work at the museum, and I told her about exhibitions and difficult visitors. I asked about the river. She told me when it flooded and when the ferry needed repairs. We said goodnight before either of us could become impatient.

I returned because the museum eliminated my job. I told her I was taking time to decide what came next. For the first few weeks, I stayed in her spare room and tried to make as little noise as possible.

At the landing, it became clear that she knew far more people than I did. They called to her from the queue and asked for photographs. A woman from the bakery handed her a bag of warm rolls. My mother put one in her pocket and passed the rest to the crew.

I followed her aboard for the second crossing. She stood near the wheelhouse, answering questions about the bridge as if she had designed it herself.

“Yes, there’s a footpath. Yes, it’ll be lit at night. No, I don’t know whether they’ll allow fishing from it.”

“What will you do?” someone asked.

“Sleep until seven,” she said.

People laughed. Then another passenger asked, and she gave the same answer.

I stood by the ticket window and recorded the bell. It made a brighter sound than I remembered, a short clear strike followed by a faint vibration. Between payments, I tried to catch it without people talking. Each time I thought I had managed it, a car door shut or a voice entered the recording.

My mother came over and saw me waiting.

“You’re making that harder than it is,” she said.

“I’m trying to get the bell by itself.”

“Why?”

“So they’ll have a clean recording.”

She looked at the line of passengers, at the man holding out a five-dollar bill, and at the bell mounted beside the window.

“It’s never rung by itself,” she said.

Then she went back to work.

By midmorning the landing had the air of a fair. Someone put out a box of doughnuts. The local paper interviewed the oldest passenger they could find, a woman of ninety-six who informed the reporter that she had crossed on the ferry less than a week earlier and saw no reason to make a fuss about it today. People signed the back of an old timetable that would be framed at the library.

I recorded the ramp lowering, the scrape of tires on metal, a gull crying above the wheelhouse. I recorded Elsie telling her husband to button his coat. I recorded a long interval in which very little happened: footsteps, water against the hull, someone turning the pages of a newspaper. Listening to it afterward, I knew exactly where I had stood.

The last scheduled crossing was at noon. The crew would take the *Ada Bell* back to its mooring afterward, but no passengers would be aboard. The bridge would open the following morning.

At eleven thirty, my mother sent a deckhand to find me. She was in the wheelhouse with the door open, drinking coffee from a chipped thermos cup. I had not been up there since I was sixteen. Back then I used to visit after school, partly to see her and partly because from the wheelhouse I could watch every car that came aboard.

She nodded toward the river. “You should record from here.”

“I have plenty.”

“Come on the last trip.”

I sat on the stool behind her. The windows had been cleaned, though a thin line of grime remained along the bottom of each frame. A worn photograph of the crew was tucked beside the radio. In it, my mother was younger than I had ever thought of her being, grinning with one hand on another woman’s shoulder.

“Who’s that?” I asked.

“Marion. She taught me to steer.”

I knew Marion’s name. She had died when I was in high school. I had never seen the photograph.

My mother held out the thermos. I shook my head. She poured the rest of the coffee into the cup and left it on the shelf.

For a while we watched the crew load the deck. A man drove aboard with flowers on the passenger seat. Two cyclists waited beside a pickup. Near the ticket window, the children from earlier pointed to the bell but did not touch it.

“I heard you got the museum job because you knew how to talk to people,” my mother said.

“I lost it despite that.”

“I know.”

I adjusted the recorder in my lap. There had been many moments since I came home when one of us might have begun this conversation. I had let each pass.

“I’ve been applying for other jobs,” I said. “There aren’t many nearby.”

“You don’t have to stay nearby.”

“I know.”

She checked the side mirror while a deckhand guided a car into the last space. Then she said, “You don’t have to leave, either.”

Outside, the deckhand raised his hand. My mother acknowledged him and reached for the controls.

The engine changed pitch beneath us. The ramp lifted slowly, shedding a narrow stream of water. I turned on the recorder. On the shore, the crowd pressed against the fence, and the yellow landing lamp burned in daylight. My mother sounded the horn.

As the ferry drew away, I expected her to say something else. She didn’t. She watched the water and steered toward the opposite bank.

I had brought home twelve years of questions about why she had worked so much, and whether she had wanted to. Sitting beside her, I could see the faint scar on her knuckle from the winter she caught it in a hatch. I remembered her at our kitchen table with a plate of reheated food, asking me to tell her about my day. I wished I had asked more about hers.

The boat reached the middle of the river. Below us, people moved to the rail. One of the cyclists took off his helmet and let the wind flatten his hair. The child who liked the gate waved at someone on shore.

“I’m glad you came back for this,” my mother said.

“So am I.”

“It wasn’t why you came back.”

“No.”

She rested a hand beside the throttle. “I’m glad anyway.”

On the far bank, another crowd was waiting. Someone had hung a banner between two posts, its letters too small to read from the water. My mother eased the ferry toward the landing. I had watched her do this hundreds of times, usually from behind a car windshield, with my thoughts already on the road ahead. Now I watched her judge the current and the distance, making tiny corrections until the boat came level with the dock.

The ramp went down with the heavy knock I had wanted to record.

Passengers began to leave. A few stopped to shake my mother’s hand. One man thanked her for getting his wife to the hospital years ago, on a night when the river was high. My mother told him she remembered. When the deck was empty, the crew closed the gate.

I stopped the recorder and looked at its screen. The file was forty-three minutes long. I thought of the librarian, who would have to listen to all of it, and of the many hours I had recorded that morning. I had the horn, the engine, the ramp, and the bell. I had the voices of people whose names I knew and people I would never see again.

My mother took the photograph from beside the radio and slipped it into her jacket pocket. Before we left the wheelhouse, she ran a finger along the edge of the shelf where it had stood.

That afternoon, we drove home by the new bridge. It was not yet open to traffic, so we stopped at the fence and got out. Workers were carrying away the last barriers. From there we could see the river bend toward town, though the old landing was hidden by trees.

My mother studied the footpath. It was wide enough for two people to walk side by side. Along the outside rail, there were small openings where a person could stop and look down at the water without blocking the way.

“Good view,” she said.

I told her I would bring the recorder back when the bridge opened. The librarian had asked for the sound of the first traffic, and I had agreed.

My mother turned toward the car. “Ask her for an extra set of headphones.”

The next morning we walked across together. Cars passed behind a low barrier, making a steady rush across the bridge deck. We stopped at one of the openings and looked down. The river moved between the piers, dark in the deeper channel and pale over the stones near shore.

I put on the headphones and played a piece of the final crossing. My mother leaned close enough to hear. First came the engine, then the voices on deck. A few seconds later, faint but distinct, the brass bell rang.

# The Map of Ordinary Things

When Mara returned to Bellweather, she found a paper map of the town pinned to the inside of her father’s workshop door. He had marked it in blue pencil. A circle around the post office was labeled *good clock, five minutes fast*. Beside the footbridge, he had written *loose plank, left side*. A small star sat over the bakery, though the bakery had closed eleven years earlier. There was no key, no date, and no indication of what the marks meant together. She studied it while rain clicked against the windows and decided that her father had probably been keeping notes for himself.

She had come to empty the workshop. Her father had been dead for six weeks, the landlord wanted the space back by spring, and there was no one else to sort the cabinets. Her brother lived overseas and had offered to hire a removal company. Mara had said she would do it. At the time, she had imagined three or four days of work.

The workshop had once been a cartographer’s office, though her father’s paying work had gradually become more varied. He repaired survey drawings for the council, made signs for walking trails, and produced careful diagrams for people who needed to explain a boundary dispute. On one wall hung the tools of his earlier trade: a brass ruler, a compass with a worn wooden handle, several pens with metal nibs. The broad desk beneath them was covered in envelopes. Most contained receipts or photographs of roads taken from the same position years apart.

Mara spent her first morning filling a box with things she understood. She kept the compass because he had taught her to draw circles with it. She put the invoices in a folder for the accountant. The rest defeated her. There were notebooks recording the dates when particular trees had flowered, slips of paper naming houses by the families who had once lived in them, and a square biscuit tin full of bus tickets. He had kept a record of the town, but she could not tell which parts were important.

At lunch she took a sandwich outside. The workshop stood near the harbor, on a street of small businesses that had changed since she left. The chandlery was a café now. A shop that had sold curtains was empty, its windows white with old dust. Across the road, a man in a green coat tried to fold an umbrella against the wind. Mara recognized him only when he looked up.

“Your dad used to tell me when the tide would come over that wall,” he said. His name was Mr. Vale. He had taught music at her secondary school and now walked with a stick. “He was usually right.”

“Was that something he measured?”

Mr. Vale considered this. “I expect he did. But he’d also seen it happen before.”

After he went on, Mara looked at the harbor wall. It seemed high enough. The water below it was a gray, restless strip, moving between the tied boats and the stone steps. Her father had spent years walking this street; she had spent years away from it. What Mr. Vale called experience might be written down somewhere in the workshop, if she could learn how to read it.

That afternoon she returned to the map on the door. There were forty-seven marks. A red cross identified *June’s bench*, though Mara knew June had died when she was a child. A penciled arrow pointed toward an alley behind the old cinema: *cut through when market road floods*. Near the primary school were the words *Mrs. Iqbal opens gate early for rain*. Some notes described conveniences, others hazards. Several named people.

At four, a woman knocked and entered without waiting. She carried a damp cardboard box, held away from her coat.

“I’m sorry,” she said when she saw Mara. “I forgot.”

She introduced herself as Leena, a librarian from the branch near the square. Mara remembered her vaguely as the girl who had won every school reading competition. The box contained maps her father had promised to flatten and repair. Leena said there was no rush; she could take them back. Mara offered to look at them before she left.

“Your father was helping us with a local history display,” Leena explained. “People brought things in. His rule was that we had to ask what each map left out.”

Inside the box was a railway plan from 1892, a children’s drawing of the town, and a tourist map printed just before the old pier was demolished. The tourist map showed a bright yellow sun over Bellweather, although the harbor had never been especially sunny. The children’s map gave most of its space to a pond where Mara had caught tadpoles. On the railway plan, that pond did not exist. A map, she thought, could be precise and still have very little to say about a place.

Leena noticed the sheet on the door while they talked. She read a few labels and smiled at one: *best blackberries after first frost*. Then she found another, written along the lower edge in smaller letters: *water reached here, 14 October*. She asked Mara if she could photograph the map. The library had begun collecting accounts of recent floods, and the date might help them check a timeline.

Mara had seen photographs of the flooding. Bellweather appeared regularly in the regional news when a storm drove the tide into its streets. Her father had mentioned water in his emails, usually to say that it had missed the workshop. Standing in the room where he had made his marks, she realized how little she knew about what had happened on the days it had not missed other people.

She helped Leena carry the box back to the library. The route took them past the post office, whose clock was indeed fast, and over the footbridge. Mara tested the plank marked on her father’s map. It shifted under her shoe. On the far side, Leena pointed to a line of shops that had all replaced their lower shelves with metal racks.

“There was water in there twice last winter,” she said. “The owners compare notes, but half of them are new. They don’t know which warnings to trust.”

At the library, a noticeboard displayed storm advice from the council: emergency numbers, sandbag collection points, instructions about insurance. The information was useful, printed clearly in large type. Underneath it, someone had pinned a handwritten note about the door at the community hall sticking when the floor got damp. Beside that was a phone number for a woman who could lend a van. The board had filled with the sort of detail no official leaflet could anticipate.

Mara went back to the workshop and stayed until dark. She found three notebooks devoted to floods. Her father had written down tides, wind direction, and rainfall, but also where people had moved their cars and which businesses had a dry room upstairs. Sometimes he corrected an earlier entry. In one place he had written *Ask Saira—my account may be wrong*. Mara knew his tidy handwriting so well that the sentence sounded almost spoken.

Over the next week, she began asking people about the marks on the door map. The bench named for June had been put there by her children, and its position was useful: it stood on a patch of ground that remained dry when the lower path disappeared. Mrs. Iqbal no longer worked at the school, but she had opened the side gate early during heavy rain so children could enter without crossing the road by the drains. The bakery star meant that its former owner had once let anyone wait inside during a sudden storm. A few notes were out of date. The footbridge plank had finally been repaired the previous summer; the one Mara had tested was meant to move.

There were disagreements, too. Mr. Vale thought the alley behind the cinema flooded before the market road did. The owner of the café said it depended on which drain was blocked. An older fisherman insisted that a painted line on the harbor wall was a better warning than any forecast, while the harbor office said it should not be treated as one. Mara wrote down each account and where it came from. Her father’s map was becoming more useful as she discovered its mistakes.

By March, the landlord had found someone to rent the workshop. Mara had sorted the invoices and packed the tools. She had also scanned most of the notebooks and taken their originals to the library, where Leena could keep them available for anyone who wanted to check the entries. Mara expected that to be the end of her task. Instead, Leena asked whether she would help make a new map for the summer display.

“It doesn’t have to be your father’s project,” Leena said. “You know how to handle the drawings, and you’ve met everyone who’s been correcting them.”

Mara was not a cartographer. She designed instruction sheets for a company that made kitchen appliances, a job she liked because it required her to think about what a person might need at the exact moment they needed it. She could see why Leena had asked. Still, she spent a day considering whether she was trying to continue something that had belonged to her father. Then she went to the library with a notebook and asked how much wall space they had.

They called the display “Bellweather, As Told Here.” It included her father’s map in a protective frame, with a transcription beside it so visitors could read his cramped labels. A larger map showed current routes, public buildings, and places people had identified as useful during bad weather. Leena kept practical safety advice separate and gave it prominent space. Nobody wanted a memory about a painted wall mistaken for an official flood warning.

On a table beneath the maps, they left cards asking visitors to add a detail or correct one. The first additions were modest. A child drew the drinking fountain in the playground. Someone reported that the back entrance to the pharmacy had a step, important to know if you used a wheelchair. Mr. Vale wrote that the post office clock was now three minutes fast. Then came longer accounts: a woman described the afternoon her neighbors carried her furniture upstairs; a shop owner explained why he had stopped opening his cellar after rain. A teenager drew the route he took home when the seafront road closed, with a warning that the shortcut through the car park was dark.

Mara spent two Saturdays at the display answering questions and sharpening pencils. She was surprised by how many people wanted to argue with the map. They pointed to roads that had changed names, paths that existed only on paper, and a public toilet marked open on a council plan though it had been locked for months. Some were annoyed by what was missing. Mara listened, made notes, and asked for details. It felt like working at her father’s desk, except that the room was full of people who could tell her when she got something wrong.

One afternoon, a boy stood in front of the framed door map for a long time. He looked about ten. Mara asked if he was searching for somewhere.

“My nan’s house,” he said. “It’s not on this.”

She told him the streets were there, and he showed her which one. His nan had moved away the year before, but he could still remember the view from her front window: the bus stop, two chimneys, a tree that dropped sticky seeds on the pavement. Mara gave him a blank card. He drew the house with its green door and wrote *Nan always knew when the bus was coming because she could hear it turn the corner*. He placed it on the table near the other additions. For the rest of the afternoon, people stopped to look at it.

The display closed at the end of April. Leena filed the cards, and Mara took photographs for the library’s archive. Some details would be useful in a storm; others preserved a way of finding a house that belonged to one family. She liked that the collection made room for both, as long as readers could tell what each note was for.

On her last evening before returning to the city, Mara took the long way to the harbor. The tide was low. Seaweed lay across the steps, and gulls worked at something among the moorings. She stopped beside June’s bench. From there she could see the workshop windows, empty now, with a fresh notice taped inside. Someone would soon fill the room with different tools.

Mara sat down and opened her notebook. She had meant to record one final observation for the library, perhaps the state of the path or the time on the post office clock. For several minutes she watched people cross the square instead. Leena passed with a bag of groceries and raised a hand. A man guided his bicycle around a puddle. Two children ran toward the footbridge and slowed to walk over it, their shoes thudding on the planks.

At last Mara wrote: *From June’s bench you can see who is coming along the harbor road before they see you.* She put the date beneath it. Then she added, *Bench dry today. Path muddy by steps.*

The first sentence might matter to someone looking for a friend. The second might spare somebody wet shoes. Mara could imagine her father reading both, deciding whether he had seen the same thing, and leaving space for a correction. She closed the notebook, waited while the children reached the far bank, and went home.

# The Path Behind the Bakery

The first complaint arrived on a Tuesday, written in blue pen on the back of a grocery receipt.

**Your map shows a path that isn’t there anymore.**

Underneath, in smaller letters: **It is still there. You just can’t get through.**

Mara pinned the receipt beside her monitor, where it joined a bus timetable with an incorrect stop, a photograph of a missing street sign, and a note from a man who insisted that Willow Lane had always been Willow Street. The city’s online map could be updated in minutes. Persuading the physical city to agree with it was another matter.

Mara worked in Municipal Information, a department whose name suggested more certainty than anyone inside it possessed. She maintained the public walking map: crossings, steps, footbridges, ramps, alleys, and the narrow passages that made a neighborhood navigable on foot. Her colleagues dealt with water bills and parking permits. She dealt with questions like whether a path existed if everyone used it but nobody knew who owned it.

The receipt concerned a shortcut behind Bell’s Bakery. On the map, a thin green line connected Orchard Street to the path along the canal. Mara had walked it herself in spring, before the weather grew hot. It was not scenic. You passed the bakery’s bins, a brick wall furred with moss, and the back of a plumbing supplier’s yard. But it saved seven minutes on the way to the clinic, and it was nearly level. The official route went down a flight of steps by the old mill and climbed another on the far side.

She went to look at lunchtime.

Someone had installed a chain-link fence across the passage. It was new enough that the concrete around its posts remained pale. Through the mesh Mara could see the canal path, close enough to make the obstruction irritating. A laminated sign said **PRIVATE PROPERTY—NO ACCESS**. Below it, someone had taped a handwritten amendment: **We know.**

A woman in a flour-dusted apron came out of the bakery’s rear door carrying a crate of empty bottles.

“It’s yours?” Mara asked, pointing at the fence.

“No,” the woman said. “If it were mine, I’d have chosen a prettier one.”

She introduced herself as Halima Bell. The bakery had belonged to her father-in-law, then her husband, and now mostly to her, she said, though her husband still got up at four to make the dough.

“The plumbing people put it in,” Halima said. “Or their landlord did. Everybody thinks I did because my bins are here.”

“Do you know when?”

“Friday. They came before breakfast. By nine, six people had come through the shop to ask why I’d closed the path. One of them had bought a pastry first, to be polite.”

Mara explained her job and showed Halima the line on her phone. Halima looked at it with the particular impatience people reserve for an error that has been presented as evidence.

“That line’s right,” she said. “It’s the fence that’s wrong.”

Back at the office, Mara opened the oldest map she could find. The passage appeared on a survey from 1936 as an unshaded strip between two parcels. It was absent from a map made twenty years later, then reappeared on a pedestrian plan from the seventies. The property database placed the fence near a boundary but not clearly on either side of it. Records made by different departments disagreed in ways that suggested each had assumed another department knew the answer.

Her supervisor, David, leaned over her desk.

“If it’s closed, mark it closed.”

“I will.”

“Then why are you pulling paper files?”

“Because people need it.”

David glanced at the receipt. “That’s not quite the same question.”

He was right, which was annoying. Mara marked the route temporarily unavailable and added a warning to the map. The software offered a menu of reasons. She selected *access obstructed*, though it sounded like a condition that might clear itself after a fallen branch was removed. Then she went home on the bus, watching people thread through the city by routes no planning committee had designed.

Over the next week, messages came in. A nurse who used the passage before the early shift at the clinic. A parent whose child liked to watch canal boats on the way to school. A man who said he had walked that way for forty years and had never thought to ask permission. They offered different accounts of the fence: a safety measure, a land grab, a misunderstanding, an inevitable sign of the times. Two correspondents disagreed about whether the path had been open during the winter of 1991.

Mara printed the messages, not because paper would make them more authoritative, but because she wanted to spread them across her desk. The map reduced the passage to a line. On paper, the line acquired mornings, habits, and people who would miss appointments if they had to take the long way around.

One message gave her pause. It came from a woman named Ruth Soto.

**Your detour is no good to me.**

Mara called her.

“The steps?” she asked.

“The steps,” Ruth said. “And the bit across the car park. There’s a ramp there on your map, but there’s a delivery van on it most afternoons.”

Mara opened the route on her screen. The detour appeared as a continuous blue line. Nothing in the data mentioned the van.

“I can report the blocked ramp,” she said.

“You should. But the van won’t be there when they come to look.”

Ruth did not sound angry. She sounded as though she had learned to describe obstacles without expecting surprise. She used a mobility scooter, she said, and lived three blocks from the bakery. The canal path led to the clinic and to a little public garden where she met a friend on Thursdays.

“What are you doing now?” Mara asked.

“Going on Wednesdays instead. My friend comes to me.”

Mara could not work out whether this counted as a solution.

On Friday morning, she walked the detour with a clipboard. The mill steps were steeper than she remembered. The car-park ramp was clear, but a deep crack ran across its base. A cyclist swerved around her and called an apology without slowing down. By the time she reached the garden, she had taken eleven extra minutes and crossed two roads. She wrote all of it down.

The landlord’s name was printed on the notice beneath the plumbing supplier’s window. Mara called him that afternoon. He told her the fence was necessary because someone had been leaving rubbish behind the yard and because his insurer had raised concerns. He said the passage was private property. When Mara mentioned the old maps, he asked if the city intended to pay for the rubbish removal.

“No,” she said.

“Then you see my difficulty.”

She did. She also saw that he had avoided saying whose property the passage was. She gave him her number and asked for a copy of the survey on which the fence placement was based. He said he would ask his agent.

For three days, nobody called.

Mara spent those days learning more about the passage than she wanted to know. The city’s legal team found a reference to a pedestrian easement in a deed from 1948, but the deed described the route using the corners of two buildings. One had been demolished. The other had been extended. The surveyor assigned to the case was away until Monday. David suggested that Mara stop treating the matter as a map correction and send it upstairs.

“It is a map correction,” she said.

“It’s a property dispute wearing a map correction’s coat.”

“I can still fix the detour.”

“That you can do.”

So she did. She added a notice about the steps and removed the car-park ramp from the recommended accessible route pending an inspection. The map could now tell Ruth more honestly that it had no suitable alternative. It felt like a poor improvement, but it was an improvement.

On Sunday, heavy rain reached the city. Water pushed leaves against the drains and made the canal look higher than its banks. By noon the passage behind the bakery had become a shallow pool. Halima sent Mara a photograph. Water stood against the fence, carrying paper cups, twigs, and a bright orange traffic cone. The yards on both sides were wet. The bakery’s back step was almost submerged.

Mara forwarded the photograph to the drainage team. A crew came out and found that a small channel beneath the passage had filled with debris. The fence had caught rubbish that the water would otherwise have carried farther along—where, the crew pointed out, it might have blocked a different grate. They cleared the channel and left the fence in place.

The rain gave everyone a new argument, though it did not settle the old one. The landlord said the flooding proved the area needed to be secured. Halima said people who walked there had always noticed when the drain was blocked and told her. A man from the drainage team said both claims could be true.

On Monday, the surveyor returned. By Wednesday, she had compared the 1948 deed, three surveys, and a set of building permits. The city’s lawyer wrote a preliminary opinion: the easement probably survived, but its precise width was unclear. “Probably” was enough to begin a conversation and not enough to cut a lock.

The city invited the landlord, the plumbing supplier, Halima, and several residents to a meeting. Mara attended to explain the map. She arrived with a projector and expected to say very little.

Instead, the map occupied most of the first hour. A council officer displayed Mara’s current version: the former shortcut marked as closed, the mill steps indicated, the accessible route broken where no safe connection existed. The landlord stared at the screen.

“Your map sent people behind my tenant’s building,” he said.

“Yes,” Mara said. “It showed a route the public had been using.”

“You made it look official.”

“It was on a city pedestrian plan before it was digital. We’re trying to establish why.”

Halima folded her arms. “It didn’t need a map to send people there. I can see them from my kitchen.”

Ruth Soto had come with her friend from the garden. She held a printed photograph of the fence on her lap.

“I’d like to know whether I can get through,” Ruth said. “If the answer is no, tell me that. But don’t point me to steps.”

The room quieted. The council officer wrote something down.

Nothing was resolved that evening. The landlord agreed to meet the surveyor at the site. Halima offered to move her bins farther from the passage, though nobody had asked her to. The plumbing supplier’s manager said the rubbish had been worst on weekends, when his yard was closed. A resident suggested a gate. Someone else asked who would lock it.

They met again two weeks later. This time the city brought a proposed plan: remove part of the fence, install a wider gate that would remain open, improve the drainage channel, and place a low barrier to keep vehicles out of the passage. The route’s public status would still have to be formally confirmed. The landlord wanted a written arrangement for maintenance before he would agree to the work. The city said it could provide one, after three departments approved it.

Mara learned the names of the three departments. She learned which of them answered emails promptly. She learned that *temporary* could describe either six days or six years, depending on who had written it. Each Friday she checked the passage and updated the note on the map. For a while, there was little to update.

In early autumn, a contractor took down the section of fence across the route. The new gate stood open while work continued on the drain. A temporary sign at each end warned people to take care around the uneven surface. The path was not yet a good route for Ruth’s scooter; gravel had been disturbed near the yard, and a lip remained at the canal end. Mara left the accessible route unconnected on the map.

Ruth called her the next day.

“I hear it’s open,” she said.

“For most people. I wouldn’t recommend it for the scooter yet.”

“Good,” Ruth said.

Mara thought she had misheard.

“Good that you told me,” Ruth clarified. “My neighbor says I can get through, but he hops over things without noticing.”

The contractor smoothed the gravel and lowered the lip the following week. Mara walked the route with Ruth on a clear Thursday morning. They moved slowly, stopping once where the passage narrowed beside the bakery wall. Ruth tried the turn, backed up, and approached it again. She cleared it with room to spare.

On the canal path, her friend was waiting by the garden gate. Ruth lifted a hand in greeting. Mara took a photograph of the completed surface and left them together.

Back at her desk, she changed the map. The green line returned, though it was not exactly where she had drawn it before. The survey had moved it a little to the east, and the new gate gave it a small, awkward bend. She added the surface and width measurements, marked the canal-end transition as step-free, and removed the warning about the closure.

For a few seconds she looked at the finished screen. Anyone opening it would see a simple connection between Orchard Street and the canal. They would not see the receipt, the disputed deeds, the rainwater against the fence, or Ruth testing the turn beside the bakery. Mara was pleased that they would be able to find their way through without knowing any of that. She saved the update, pinned a fresh walking map beside her monitor, and began reading a message about Willow Lane.

# The Last Bus to Bell Street

The bus reached Bell Street at 11:47 every night, unless there was snow, a parade, an accident on the bridge, or the sort of rain that made the traffic lights blink yellow for no apparent reason. By then its windows were usually dark mirrors. Mara could see her own face in the glass, laid over the sleeping storefronts and the thin bands of light under apartment doors.

Bell Street was the end of the line. She waited there for seven minutes, then crossed to the other side of the road and began the return trip. In fourteen years of driving the 6, she had spent enough time at that stop to learn which upstairs neighbors watched television late, which windows held plants through the winter, and when the bakery replaced its sign. She knew less about the people inside those rooms than she knew about the man who boarded each Thursday carrying an empty birdcage.

On her last night, the cage was occupied.

“New bird?” she asked as he climbed aboard.

“Same bird,” he said. “First time she’s agreed to travel.”

He held up the cage. A small gray parrot regarded Mara with one polished eye.

“Where’s she going?”

“Home. She’s been at my sister’s.” He lowered his voice. “I told my sister I missed her.”

“The bird?”

“That’s what I let her think.”

He tapped his card and sat behind the front wheel well. The parrot made a noise like someone trying to start a lawn mower. Mara pulled away from the curb.

The 6 had once gone all the way to the brickworks, when there was still a brickworks. It had once turned at the hospital, before the hospital moved uphill. Next Monday, the route would be folded into two others. The new buses would come more often during the day and not at all after ten. That was the part Mara’s passengers talked about. Everyone understood that a faster trip downtown was useful. They also understood what time the kitchens closed, and what time the second shift ended at the care home.

The transit authority had offered Mara a place on the new route. She had chosen the 23 instead: mornings, a shorter loop, two elementary schools and a supermarket. People congratulated her on the sensible hours. She agreed that they were sensible. She had also grown used to finishing work when most people were asleep, and she wasn’t sure what she would do with an evening.

At the next stop, a woman in green kitchen trousers boarded with a paper bag held carefully upright.

“Last one,” the woman said.

“Last one.”

“That’s a shame.”

Mara waited while she found her fare card. She had never learned the woman’s name. For years they had discussed the weather, a loose tile at the bus stop, the price of oranges, and once the woman’s mother, who had turned ninety and wanted to climb a ladder to clean the gutters. Tonight the woman took a seat halfway back, the bag settled on her knees.

At the station, six passengers came aboard together. The train from the airport had been late. They stood under the shelter looking at their phones and then at the destination sign, uncertain that a bus could be going where they needed to go at this hour. One asked if Mara stopped near Hanover Court. Another needed North Mill Lane. A young man with a silver suitcase named a hotel Mara had never heard of.

“It might be new,” he said.

“Most things are new to someone,” Mara said, and gave him directions from the closest stop.

The last person onto the bus was an older woman pulling a grocery trolley. Its wheels squeaked at different pitches. Mara lowered the bus and watched her cross the gap from curb to floor. The woman thanked her without looking up. Mara knew her as Mrs. Vale, although she had never been told whether that was her name. Once, years ago, a neighbor had called it across the street.

The bus climbed out of the station and passed the dark windows of the post office. At the first red light, Mara heard a tapping near the front of the bus. She checked the mirror. The parrot’s owner was holding one finger against the cage bars. The bird had its head tilted toward him.

They continued through the old shopping district. A few years earlier, the council had put lantern-shaped lights above the street. Most of the shops closed at six, leaving them to illuminate a long row of metal shutters. Tonight a florist was still working inside her shop. Through the window Mara could see buckets of flowers and someone moving between them, lifting stems into bunches. She had passed this shop thousands of times and never been inside.

Mrs. Vale rang the bell for Ash Lane. Mara drew in close to the curb. The grocery trolley caught briefly on the door frame, then rolled free.

“Thank you,” Mrs. Vale said.

“You’re welcome.”

Mrs. Vale looked at the route sign above the windshield. “I suppose I’ll have to find another way on Monday.”

“There’s the 12. It goes down Market Road.”

“I know.”

Market Road was four blocks away. Mrs. Vale took hold of her trolley and set off along Ash Lane. Mara watched until she reached the streetlamp at the corner, then closed the doors.

At the end of her first year on the route, Mara had tried to memorize the regular passengers. It had seemed like part of doing the job well. The effort soon defeated her. People changed jobs, changed coats, went away for months and appeared again. They brought children who grew too tall for free fares. They came aboard carrying flowers or bags from pharmacies, spoke eagerly into phones, or stared at the floor. She learned to recognize some faces without expecting to see them. When a familiar passenger returned after a long absence, she was usually glad.

Near the river, the bus passed the temporary barrier that had replaced the iron railing. A delivery truck had broken through the railing in spring; no one had been hurt, but part of the pavement remained fenced off. The truck was gone long before the repairs were scheduled. Mara had watched weeds grow up between the concrete blocks.

The river itself was high and fast after three days of rain. From the driver’s seat she could see a strip of moving black beneath the bridge lamps. She remembered crossing it with her father when she was little. He had made her count the lamps so she would stop worrying about the traffic below the bus windows. There were eleven. She still counted them sometimes.

A bell sounded. The woman in kitchen trousers came forward with the paper bag.

“Want a roll?” she asked. “They make too many on Fridays.”

“It’s Saturday.”

“We made them yesterday.” She reached into the bag and lifted out a round roll wrapped in a napkin. “Still good.”

Mara took it. It was warm, perhaps from the woman’s hands. “Thank you.”

The woman got off at the care home, went around to the side entrance, and unlocked it. Before the bus moved, she turned and raised a hand. Mara raised hers in return.

By the time they reached the warehouses, the passengers from the station had all gone. The young man with the suitcase had asked twice about his hotel and then recognized its sign from half a block away. Mara waited while he pulled his suitcase over the uneven pavement.

The parrot and its owner remained. So did a student asleep against the window, his headphones hanging around his neck. Mara knew his stop. He had missed it twice in the past month, waking at Bell Street and getting a ride back. At his corner she pulled over and waited. The bus idled. He slept.

“Is this his?” the parrot’s owner asked.

“Yes.”

He leaned across the aisle and touched the student’s shoulder. The student woke with a start, took in the bus stop, and scrambled up.

“Sorry,” he said to both of them.

“No hurry,” Mara told him.

He stepped off, turned around as if checking that he had everything, and found his wallet in his pocket. Then he went toward the apartments above the hardware store.

At Bell Street, Mara set the brake and opened the doors. The parrot’s owner did not move. He lived two stops back, but he often rode to the end if he wanted to finish a conversation. Tonight he was bent over the cage, making a series of soft clicking sounds.

“Seven minutes,” Mara said.

“I know.”

She turned off the interior lights nearest the driver’s seat. Outside, the bakery sign glowed red. The original sign had shown a loaf of bread; the new one had only the name. Mara could remember arriving one night to find the bread gone. She had missed the workers who changed it.

“Are you moving to the 12?” the man asked.

“The 23.”

“Morning route.”

“Yes.”

“You’ll see children, then.”

“I expect so.”

He considered this. “My sister used to drive a school bus. She could tell when a child had lost a tooth before they said anything.”

“How?”

“I never asked.”

The parrot scraped its beak against a perch. Mara unwrapped the roll and took a bite. It had rosemary in it and a few crystals of salt. Across the road, a man came out of the bakery carrying a crate of empty trays. He loaded it into a van, shut the doors, and went back inside.

“What’s her name?” Mara asked, nodding toward the cage.

“Edith.”

“After someone?”

“My sister’s landlord. We named her when we thought she was a boy.” He smiled down at the bird. “By the time we knew better, she knew her name.”

The seven minutes passed. The man carried Edith off the bus, and Mara crossed Bell Street to start back toward the station.

The return trip was quieter. A cleaner boarded outside an office block, then two friends at the cinema, still arguing about the ending of a film. Near the river, a man waved for the bus from the wrong side of the road. Mara pointed across the street to the stop for his direction. He waved again, more vigorously. At the next light she watched him cross safely behind her and disappear toward the shelter.

When Mara first began driving nights, she had thought of every trip as a list of places she had to reach on time. She still checked the clock, but she now thought just as often about the minutes between stops. On some nights those minutes were enough for a passenger to dry off after the rain or finish a call before going home. On others, they were simply the time it took a bus to get from Ash Lane to the bridge.

At the station, the cleaner got off. The two friends remained, their argument unfinished. One said the ending had been obvious; the other said being obvious did not make it bad. Mara was tempted to ask the name of the film, but the doors opened for four new passengers, and she needed to hear where they were going.

She finished her shift at 1:18, thirteen minutes late. The dispatcher asked whether there had been a problem.

“Nothing much,” Mara said. “A slow boarding at the station.”

She parked in the depot and walked through the bus, checking beneath the seats. She found a receipt, a single glove, and a child’s blue hair clip. All three went into the lost-property box. The bus had picked up that kind of small inventory every night. Someone would be looking for the glove by morning. She hoped the hair clip belonged to someone who had others.

In the drivers’ room, a paper notice on the wall thanked everyone who had worked the 6. Beneath it was a map of Monday’s routes. Mara stood in front of the map while she ate the rest of her roll. The 12 would run down Market Road, as she had told Mrs. Vale. She traced its line with one finger to see where it turned after that. Then she found the 23 and followed the neat loop she would learn next week.

On Monday morning, Mara arrived at the depot early. The yard looked different in daylight: smaller, with oil stains showing clearly beneath the parked buses. Someone was washing a windshield with a long brush. Inside, another driver was filling a travel mug at the sink.

Her new bus smelled faintly of cleaning fluid. Mara adjusted the seat, checked the mirrors, and pulled up the route on the console. At 6:42 she drove out onto the street.

The first passengers were a man going to the supermarket and a woman carrying a stack of folders tied with string. At the school stop, three children boarded together. One had a yellow plaster on his chin. Another counted out his fare in coins while the others waited beside him. Mara gave him time to find the last one at the bottom of his pocket.

As she closed the doors, she noticed the florist from the old shopping district crossing ahead of the bus. Mara recognized her from the late-night window, though she looked different in her coat, with no flowers around her. She was walking quickly toward the bakery.

The light turned green. Mara checked both mirrors and drove on.

# The Hours We Misplaced

The office was between a shoe repair shop and a place that sold lampshades. Its sign read **MUNICIPAL TIME RECOVERY**, though most people assumed it meant parking tickets. The windows were frosted, the door stuck in damp weather, and inside, behind a counter with a brass bell, Leena kept three clocks. They never agreed.

This was not a fault. The clock above the door showed the time outside. The one on Leena’s desk showed the time available for return. The third, a little travel clock with a cracked leather case, had belonged to her father and no longer moved at all. It displayed 4:17.

People came in because they had lost an hour.

They described it in different ways. A man would say he had sat down after lunch and looked up to find it dark. A woman would say the train journey home had vanished from her memory, although she had arrived with her bags and bought milk on the way. Children were more precise. They knew exactly when an hour had gone missing, and they were usually angry about it.

Leena asked for a date, an approximate time, and a description of the circumstances. Then she checked the ledger.

Most missing hours could be found. They gathered in the places where people stopped paying attention: hospital corridors, queues, airport lounges, kitchens during arguments. The office had been built to collect and hold them until their owners came looking.

On Tuesday morning, a man in a yellow raincoat asked for the hour he had spent waiting to learn whether his daughter had been born safely.

“She’s twenty-six now,” he said. “I don’t know why I thought of it today.”

“Is it lost?”

“I remember the chairs. The vending machine. I remember being frightened.” He folded his raincoat over one arm. “But when I try to remember what I did for that whole hour, there’s nothing.”

Leena found it under October, twenty-six years earlier. It had been stored in a small blue envelope, the kind used for airmail. She opened the flap and listened. Each hour made a sound if you held it close enough. This one contained shoes crossing a polished floor, a can falling into a vending-machine tray, and a young man whispering, “Come on,” to no one in particular.

“It’s here,” she said.

The man leaned toward the counter. “Can I have it back?”

“Of course. But I should tell you how it works.”

She had given the explanation thousands of times. An hour could be returned only once. It would not send him into the past or let him make a different choice. At some point in the next few days, he would find an ordinary hour of his life opening unexpectedly wide. Within it, he would remember what had been missing.

“That sounds all right,” he said.

“It can be difficult.”

He considered this. “She was born safely?”

“Yes.”

“I know. I called her last night.” He smiled with some embarrassment. “Go ahead.”

Leena gave him the envelope. He put it in his coat pocket with surprising care.

For most of her career, she had liked that part of the job. Someone arrived unsettled by a gap in their life, and she could tell them the hour had not been thrown away. It was still theirs.

The rest of the job was filing.

At noon she ate a pear over the sink in the back room. Then she opened a letter from the city council. Its language was plain. The office would close at the end of the month. Recent studies showed that recovered hours produced no measurable increase in wellbeing. Fewer people had applied each year. The building needed electrical work, and the shoe repair shop next door had asked about expanding.

Leena read the letter twice. There was a number to call if she had questions. She placed it beside the desk clock and served the next visitor, who wanted forty minutes from a school assembly in 1988.

By closing time she had decided not to call. She would begin with the storage cabinets. There were eleven of them, each as tall as the door, and an index that reached back eighty-three years. She did not know what the council intended to do with the hours, but she knew they would want a count.

The first cabinet held the oldest. Some of the envelopes had grown thin and soft. Their labels had been written by clerks who were long dead, in scripts Leena recognized as readily as faces. Mr. Vale pressed too hard with his pen. A woman named S. Rahman wrote her sevens with a line through them. The former chief clerk, whose name Leena had never learned, noted weather in the margins.

*October 3. Thick fog all morning.*

*June 18. Terrible heat.*

She counted until her eyes hurt. At the back of the third shelf, beneath a box of rubber bands, she found an envelope without a label. The paper was yellow and folded at one corner.

Leena held it to her ear. A screen door slammed. A spoon struck the rim of a cup. Someone was whistling badly, stopping and starting.

She knew the tune. Her father used to whistle it while he made tea. He never got past the first line.

She took the envelope to her desk and examined it under the lamp. In the lower right corner, almost erased by time, were her initials. She had written them at sixteen, when the office let children leave an hour for safekeeping.

She remembered the visit. Her father had brought her after school, telling her that the service was free and she might be glad of it one day. At the counter she had rolled her eyes. They had argued on the bus over whether she could travel alone to a concert in another city. At sixteen, she had thought he was keeping her life small on purpose. She had chosen an hour at random—or so she had believed—and made him wait outside while the clerk put it away.

Her father had died nine years ago. The hour had remained in the cabinet through the years Leena worked here, close enough to find whenever she had wanted to look for it.

She took it home.

Her apartment was on the fourth floor of a building with unreliable heating. The little travel clock stood on the kitchen shelf, still at 4:17. She did not remember when it had stopped. Her father had kept winding it long after he no longer traveled, and she had kept it without trying to make it run.

The envelope lay on the table while she cooked rice, washed the pan, and called her brother. She told him about the closure, but not about the hour.

“They’ll offer you something else,” he said.

“Maybe.”

“You could come here for a while.”

He lived by the sea, in a house full of children and wet shoes. Leena loved visiting him and was always relieved to leave. She said she would think about it.

After they hung up, she sat at the table and opened the envelope. There was nothing inside that she could see. The opening was enough; the hour knew where to go.

It arrived two days later while she was buying oranges.

She had gone to the market before work. Rain tapped on the canvas roofs. A seller was placing fruit into her bag when his spoon struck the rim of a cup, and she was suddenly aware of her father beside her. He was not there in the market. The hour had opened inside her, and she could remember the kitchen as clearly as she saw the seller’s hands.

She was sixteen again, sitting at the table in her school uniform. Her father had come home early to talk about the concert. She had prepared an argument, complete with train times and the address of the friend whose family would meet her at the station. But he had not begun with rules. He had set down his bag, filled the kettle, and asked her to show him the timetable.

She remembered doing so. She had forgotten what came next.

He studied the page as the kettle heated. He asked which train she would take home if the concert ran late, and she pointed to one marked in blue ink. He found a later train she had overlooked. He wrote its time on the back of an electricity bill, then checked whether there was enough money in the kitchen tin for both tickets.

“I don’t want you stranded,” he said.

She heard suspicion in his voice. When he asked for the friend’s telephone number, she snatched up the timetable and accused him of finding excuses to say no. He put the electricity bill down. They argued, as she had always remembered. What she had lost was the part before it: his patient work at the table, and the fact that he had been trying to find a way for her to go.

The market seller asked if she wanted a receipt. Leena said no. She carried the oranges home and stayed there until the desk clock would have shown her half an hour late.

She had gone to the concert. Her father had driven her to the station and waited while she bought her ticket. She remembered that part, too, once she let herself think about it.

For several days the office felt different to her, though none of the work had changed. She returned an hour to a retired bus driver who wanted to remember his first shift. She helped a boy find a summer afternoon at his grandmother’s house. She told a woman that the six hours she had spent asleep on a flight had never been lost; she had simply been asleep. Meanwhile, people from the council came to measure the rooms. They spoke courteously and wrote down the dimensions of each cabinet.

On the following Monday, the man in the yellow raincoat returned. This time he wore a dark sweater and carried no umbrella, though it was raining.

“I got it,” he said.

Leena invited him to sit. He remained standing.

“I remembered something while I was cleaning the bathroom. My daughter’s mother had been in labor for a long time, and they took her away. I was certain something was wrong. But what I’d forgotten was a nurse coming out to tell me she was doing well. The nurse stayed a minute because I couldn’t seem to understand her.” He looked at the floor. “I must have looked terrified.”

“Were you glad to remember?”

“Yes.” He nodded. “I was. I’d spent years thinking no one told me anything until it was over.”

After he left, Leena called the number on the council letter. She was transferred twice before reaching a woman who knew about the closure. The cabinets, she learned, would be collected by the municipal archive. Anyone could request an hour later, once the contents had been catalogued. The process might take some time.

“How much time?” Leena asked.

The woman could not say. The archive had a backlog.

That evening Leena wrote a notice for the office window. **If you have left an hour here, please come before the end of the month if you would like it returned.** Beneath it she put the address of the archive and the telephone number, though she could not promise either would help quickly.

For the first week, almost no one came. Then the local paper printed a photograph of the sign. A reporter called to ask what kind of hours people had left, and Leena refused to give examples. The next morning there was a queue past the lampshades.

She spent the day checking names and dates. The desk clock ran fast, as it often did when the room was crowded. Some visitors asked questions she could answer. Some were disappointed to learn that an hour would not bring back a person, or let them hear every word spoken long ago. A few left their envelopes in the cabinets.

One woman, looking at a small white envelope, said, “I don’t think I want this after all.”

Leena put it back without asking why.

Her brother arrived on the final Saturday with sandwiches, two of his children, and a cardboard box of pens. He had seen the notice online. While he and the children carried supplies, Leena worked through a line of people who had been waiting in the cold. By midafternoon the queue was gone.

“There are still thousands,” her brother said, looking at the cabinets.

“Yes.”

He helped her check the transfer list. Each shelf had a number; each box had to match it. The children drew pictures on scrap paper at the back table and asked if they could leave an hour from the afternoon.

“You haven’t lost it,” Leena told them.

“We might,” said the younger one.

“Then you can come and see me.”

She caught herself after she said it. Her brother looked up from the list, but neither of them corrected her.

On the last day, the clocks were as contrary as ever. Leena wrapped the travel clock in a scarf and took it home before the archive workers arrived. She checked every cabinet as they were emptied. When the shelves stood bare, she could see lighter rectangles on the walls where the boxes had shielded the paint.

The workers finished at 4:12 by the clock above the door. Leena waited while their van pulled away. Then she locked the front door and walked around the counter one last time, making sure the back window was shut and the sink tap had stopped dripping.

Outside, the shoe repairer was lowering his shutter. He asked what she would do now.

“I don’t know yet,” she said.

He nodded and wished her well. Across the street, a bus stopped. People stepped off into the evening, some hurrying toward home, others standing still for a moment to settle their bags and decide which way to go. Leena watched until the bus moved on.

Then she went home, where her father’s clock waited on the shelf. She took it down and wound it. The hands stayed at 4:17. She set it beside the bowl of oranges, put water on for tea, and called her brother to say she would visit.
