samples.result:
# The Things We Keep Running

On the hottest day of the summer, the sign outside the repair shop fell off the wall.

It had been hanging by one screw for months. The heat softened something—the paint, perhaps, or the old wood behind it—and by noon the sign was lying faceup on the pavement. **BELL & DAUGHTER: REPAIRS**, it said, though there had never been a Bell in the shop during any of the years I knew it. Beneath the name, in smaller letters, someone had once promised radios, lamps, small appliances, and clocks. A previous owner had crossed out *clocks* with a strip of black paint. You could still read it if you looked closely.

I was passing on my way to the hardware store when I saw Mara trying to lift the sign. It was heavier than it looked. We carried it inside together, each of us holding one end, and set it against a cabinet full of parts. The shop smelled of warm dust and metal. On the counter lay a fan with its grille removed, its blades motionless.

“Can you fix that?” I asked.

“Probably.”

I had meant the sign.

Mara followed my glance. “That too, probably. Different problem.”

I offered to hold it while she put in a new screw, but she said the wall needed work first. The wood was rotten around the hole. A bigger screw would hold for a while, then pull out a larger piece. She had a way of saying such things without making them sound like lessons, which meant I often noticed the lesson anyway.

I bought my lightbulbs and came back the next morning with a cassette recorder.

It had belonged to my mother. For years it had lived in the back of a closet, under a shoe box full of extension cords. When I found it, I remembered her pressing its red button to record messages for relatives overseas. She would begin formally, asking after everyone’s health, and then get distracted by ordinary details: a stubborn stain on the kitchen ceiling, a neighbor’s new dog, the price of peaches. She talked until the tape clicked off.

After she died, I kept the recorder but never tried it. Its plastic case was scratched, and one corner was held together with cloudy tape. I could have bought a working cassette player online. What I wanted, though, was to put the little machine she had held on a table and hear it play.

Mara made no promise. She opened the battery compartment, tilted it toward the light, and showed me the blue-green crust on the contacts.

“We can clean that,” she said. “Leave it here.”

The shop had been on Alder Street longer than I had lived in the city. Between a pharmacy and a store that sold phone cases, its narrow window displayed a rotating selection of things waiting for their owners: a desk lamp with a green shade, a kitchen scale, an electric train engine no longer than my hand. Mara wrote each customer’s name on a paper tag and tied it to the cord or handle. If an object had no place to tie a tag, she used blue painter’s tape.

I started stopping in on my walks home from work. At first I told myself I was checking on the recorder. Mara was usually busy, and I learned to ask only when she looked up. I watched her replace a plug, test a toaster’s heating elements, and search a drawer for a spring that seemed too small to matter. People came in carrying their broken things with an expression I recognized: a little embarrassed by the object, and a little hopeful on its behalf.

One afternoon, a man brought in a coffee grinder. He set it on the counter and explained that his wife used it every morning. Then he explained that she had died in February.

Mara turned the grinder over to inspect the base. “Does it still make any noise?”

“A hum,” he said. “No grinding.”

“Leave it with me.”

When he had gone, I asked whether she could repair it.

“I’ll find out.”

“You said it as if you already knew.”

“He didn’t need to stand here while I took it apart.”

That was how she worked. Some things she could fix quickly, while their owners waited. Others took weeks because a part was hard to find or she wanted to ask someone about a model she hadn’t seen before. A few could not be repaired safely. She called the owners herself when that happened. I heard her do it once, and heard her offer to give the appliance back assembled, though it would never run. The person on the other end wanted it returned.

In late August, the power went out across our part of the city. A transformer had failed during the evening rush, leaving the traffic lights dark and the apartments without air-conditioning. People stood on sidewalks holding their phones up, looking for news. In the upper floors, windows opened one after another. Our building’s hallway, usually cool and empty, filled with footsteps.

I went outside because it was cooler there. Mara was sitting on a folding chair in front of the shop, working on a battery-powered lantern. Several neighbors had gathered around her. She tightened a contact, switched it on, and handed it to the woman who had brought it. The small white light drew everyone’s faces toward it.

“The heat got us,” somebody said.

“The equipment was old,” somebody else replied.

Both were true, as far as I could tell. We stayed outside until long after dark, trading rumors about when the power would return. Someone brought out water. A boy rolled a basketball gently from one side of the street to the other. Without the shop lights, I could barely see through Mara’s window, but I knew what was inside: the crowded shelves, the paper tags, the sign propped against the cabinet because the wall still hadn’t been repaired.

The electricity came back a little after midnight. One by one, the windows shut. By morning the street looked ordinary, except for a row of water bottles people had left beside the shop door.

A week later Mara called to say the recorder was working. When I arrived, she placed it on the counter beside a pair of small speakers.

“The motor belt had gone loose,” she said. “The contacts cleaned up well.”

She pressed *play* without a cassette in it so I could hear the mechanism turn. It made a dry, steady sound. Then she stopped it and asked whether I had a tape to try.

I did. I had brought one in my pocket, wrapped in a handkerchief. There was no label on the cassette. I remembered finding it years earlier in the same box as the recorder, but I had no idea what was on it.

Mara put it in. For a moment there was only hiss. Then my mother’s voice came out of the speakers, distant and unmistakable. She was asking someone whether they had received the photographs. She mentioned my uncle, a birthday dinner, and a recipe she had promised to send. In the background I could hear dishes being moved. I was trying to place the year when she broke off to ask, “Is that rain?”

There was a pause. A younger voice answered her. It was mine.

I had forgotten how impatient I sounded at fifteen. I told her it was only the sprinkler next door and asked if I could use the phone. She told me to wait until she finished. I made a noise of protest. Then, with perfect composure, she returned to her message and described the weather.

Mara stood at the far end of the counter, giving me room. I listened to the tape click and hiss and continue. My mother was alive in its few minutes only in the plain sense that she had been alive when she spoke. The tape held her voice, not her thoughts. I could not tell her I was sorry for the things I had said at fifteen, or ask whether she had received an answer about the photographs. I could hear her take a breath before beginning her next sentence. That was more than I had expected to have.

At home I listened to the whole cassette. One side contained the message; the other held part of a radio program, recorded over by accident. Halfway through the message, my mother said the microphone was too close to the window and moved it. The sound of traffic grew faint. She finished with a request for news from everyone, however small, and said goodbye twice.

For several days I carried the recorder from room to room. I played the tape while I cooked and once while I folded laundry. Eventually I put it on a shelf. I still wanted to hear her voice, but listening required a decision. I found that I preferred knowing I could make one.

In September, a notice appeared in Mara’s window. The building had been sold. The new owner intended to renovate, and her lease would not be renewed in the spring. Someone had written **SAVE BELL & DAUGHTER** on a piece of cardboard and taped it beneath the notice. People began bringing Mara addresses for empty storefronts and names of friends who might know someone with space. She thanked them, filed the scraps of paper in a folder, and went on working.

One Saturday I helped her sort a shelf at the back of the shop. There were cracked cases she had saved for their screws, manuals for appliances no one had brought in for years, and three shoeboxes of power adapters. She tested each adapter before deciding where it belonged. I thought we were getting ready for a move, but Mara said she sorted that shelf every autumn. She had found two screws she’d been looking for since June.

We stopped for lunch on the shop steps. I asked about the name on the sign.

“Mr. Bell started the place,” she said. “His daughter ran it after him. I bought it from her.”

“Why keep their name?”

“People knew where to come.”

She told me she had learned repair work in her father’s garage. He fixed bicycles and lawn mowers for neighbors, and she liked opening things to see why they had stopped. Later she took a course in electronics, worked for a company that serviced office equipment, and, when that job disappeared, came to Alder Street. Mr. Bell’s daughter had stayed for a month to show her where everything was.

I asked if she planned to put the sign up again. She looked at its empty place on the wall.

“After I move,” she said. “No point fixing that wall for the landlord.”

Through the winter, customers kept arriving. Some came because they had always come. Others had seen the notice and seemed newly anxious to use the shop while it was there. Mara worked her usual hours and searched for a place when she could. A location she liked cost too much. Another had enough room but no safe way to vent her soldering station. For a while she considered sharing a workspace across town, though it would have been difficult for many of her customers to reach.

By February she had found a narrow ground-floor unit near the library, twelve blocks away. The rent was manageable, and its front room had a window wide enough for the workbench. She signed the lease, then worried aloud about moving the shelves.

On moving day, I arrived to find six people already carrying boxes. The man with the coffee grinder had borrowed a van. The woman whose lantern Mara had repaired brought a hand truck. Two teenagers who lived above the pharmacy took turns wrapping the desk lamps in blankets. The grinder worked again; its owner mentioned this while directing the van toward the curb, as though I had asked. Mara handed out coffee and assigned tasks. By afternoon the old shop was empty except for dust outlines on the walls and the sign.

We carried it out last. The paint had worn off its lower edge, and one of the letters in **DAUGHTER** was almost gone. It still weighed as much as it had in August. At the new place, Mara set it against the wall while she decided where it should hang. Someone offered to fetch a drill. She ran her hand over the plaster, found a sturdy place beside the door, and asked him to make the holes.

I have moved apartments twice since then. The cassette recorder sits in the living room of the second one, near the books. Once a year or so, I play the tape. I listen all the way through, including the stretch where my younger self interrupts. I used to wish I could cut that part out. Now I’m glad nobody did. My mother’s small pause and my own sharp voice put us back in the kitchen together, with dishes on the counter and a sprinkler running next door.

The repair shop is a little farther from my usual route, but I still go in. Last month I took Mara a desk fan that had begun to rattle. She took off the grille and found a blade loose on its shaft. I waited while she secured it and checked the cord. When she switched the fan on, it pushed a gentle current of air across the counter and stirred the paper tags hanging there.

I paid her, picked up the fan, and walked home past the library. The day was warm, though nowhere near as hot as the day the sign fell. At the crossing I stopped for the light and felt the fan’s handle settle against my fingers. At home, I would set it by the window, plug it in, and let it run.

# The Weather on Alder Street

When Mara came back to Alder Street, the rain gauge was full of leaves. It stood beside the back steps on a length of pipe her father had driven into the ground thirty years earlier. The clear plastic cylinder had gone cloudy, and a dandelion had rooted in the little mound of dirt beneath it. She nearly pulled the whole thing out. The estate agent was coming on Thursday, and there was no reason a buyer should have to imagine the yard without a piece of pipe in it.

Then she saw the pencil mark on the doorframe: **8:15**, written at the height of her shoulder. Below it, in smaller letters, her father had written **first frost**. She had grown up among such notes. They appeared on seed packets, grocery receipts, the margins of newspapers. As a child she had assumed all adults kept track of the world this way, the way they kept track of birthdays and how much milk was left.

Inside, the house smelled of dust, old wood, and the sharp lemon soap her father used until the week he died. Mara opened windows even though the air outside was damp. On the kitchen table sat three blue notebooks. Her father’s neighbor, Inez, had stacked them there after finding them in the garage, along with a note: **Thought you’d want these. There are more.**

There were twenty-eight more. They filled two shelves above the workbench, arranged by year. Each notebook began with the same heading, written in block capitals: **ALDER STREET WEATHER**. Underneath were columns for temperature, rain, wind, and remarks. At first the remarks were brief—*heavy fog*, *hail at noon*, *hot night*. Later they became less obedient. *Mrs. Vale’s pear tree blossomed six days early.* *Bus stuck by the pharmacy; water up to the second step.* *Mara says clouds look like bread dough.*

She found that last entry in a notebook from when she was seven. She remembered saying it. Her father had been making dinner, and she had come in wet from playing outside to tell him about the enormous gray sky. She did not remember him writing it down.

For three days Mara worked through the house. She made piles for donation, recycling, and the few things she would take back to her apartment. Decisions that should have been easy became strangely tiring. Her father owned seventeen mugs and no matching set of anything. He had saved instruction manuals for appliances he no longer possessed. In a drawer beside the stove, she found rubber bands wound around a paper towel tube, a flashlight that still worked, and six identical keys with labels too faded to read. The notebooks she left on the kitchen table, where she could see them without deciding anything about them.

Inez came over on Wednesday carrying a bag of tomatoes. She was a small woman with a broad face and the habit of looking past people toward the sky, as though expecting it to interrupt. She had lived next door since before Mara was born. As a child, Mara had been fed at her table often enough to know which chair wobbled.

“You’re moving fast,” Inez said, looking at the bare shelves in the sitting room.

“I only have the week.”

Inez put the tomatoes down. “Your father said you were busy.”

“He meant that kindly, I hope.”

“He did.”

They stood in the kitchen, where the open windows admitted the sound of a truck backing up somewhere nearby. Inez picked up the top notebook and turned a page with her thumb. “He used to call me when the wind changed,” she said. “Not every time. Just when he thought I should bring in the washing.”

Mara laughed. “Did you ask him to?”

“No. But I usually did.”

The next morning the estate agent arrived with a folder of comparable sales. He walked from room to room describing the house in terms that made it sound both attractive and insufficient: good bones, original floors, room for improvement. In the yard he paused beside the pipe.

“You’ll want to take that out,” he said.

“I know.”

He pointed beyond the back fence, toward a shallow strip of land thick with weeds. “Some buyers may ask about drainage. After the storms last spring, people are asking.”

“What about it?”

“There was water on the road. Nothing to do with this property, as far as I understand.”

That afternoon Mara went through the notebooks looking for last spring. Her father had recorded rain on nine days in May and eleven in June. Beside an entry for June 14, he had drawn a rough map of the neighborhood. The road dipped near the pharmacy, where a drainage ditch ran behind the houses on Alder Street. He had marked three places along the ditch with an X. In the margin he had written: **Water backed up before the road flooded. Noticed at 6:40. Tell council again.**

Mara remembered the photograph Inez had sent her: a brown sheet of water covering the pharmacy car park, a shopping trolley stranded against a fence. She had replied, *That looks awful. Are you all right?* Inez had been fine. Her father had said little about it when they spoke, beyond “A mess, but we managed.” She had taken him at his word.

When Inez came over for a second bag of donated books, Mara showed her the map. “What does ‘tell council again’ mean?”

“He’d been telling them for years. That ditch used to be kept clear. They stopped cutting it regularly, then somebody put a fence across part of it.”

“Whose fence?”

Inez hesitated. “The warehouse at the end of Mercer Lane. It’s a complicated property line.”

Mara looked at the notebooks spread across the table. “Did Dad think his records would help?”

“He thought facts ought to help.” Inez closed one of the books. “He was sometimes disappointed.”

After Inez left, Mara walked to the ditch. In her memory it had been an adventurous place, wide enough to feel secret, narrow enough for a child to jump across in summer. Now it was partly hidden by brambles. Plastic bags hung from the branches like pale, deflated fruit. Water stood in the lowest section though it had not rained since Tuesday. At the far end, a wire fence crossed the bank and disappeared into the growth. The ground beside it was littered with gravel, washed down from the warehouse lot.

A man walking a terrier stopped when he saw her looking. “Bad in June,” he said.

“I heard.”

“Pharmacy got it worst. They had to throw out half their stock.” He tugged gently at the lead. “You’re Ben’s daughter, aren’t you?”

She nodded.

“He came down here with a ruler,” the man said. “Stuck it in the mud and took a picture. I told him he’d lose his shoe.”

“He probably did.”

“He did,” the man said, delighted to have his memory confirmed.

Back at the house, Mara found the photographs on her father’s old computer. There were dozens: the ditch in rain, in sun, in winter when its edges were visible; water marks on a wall; a ruler held against a culvert opening. There were also pictures of things he must simply have liked—the first snow on Inez’s shed, a fox asleep under the hedge, Mara at eighteen, leaving for university with a suitcase too large to lift gracefully. He had photographed her from the front path. She was turning back toward him, smiling despite herself.

For years, Mara had thought of her father’s weather records as an affectionate oddity. It was easier to picture him measuring rainfall than making a complaint to the council. He disliked arguments. When a neighbor’s music kept him awake, he would go out and trim the hedge until it stopped. But his computer held copies of four letters about the ditch. They were courteous, precise, and increasingly difficult to ignore. One included a table comparing rain totals with the dates of standing water. Another asked who was responsible for keeping the culvert clear. The last, sent shortly before he became ill, had no reply that Mara could find.

She called the council office on Friday. A patient-sounding employee directed her to an online form. Mara explained that she was trying to follow up on an earlier report. The employee found its reference number and read the status aloud: closed. An inspection had been made after the June flood. Further work was pending review.

“What does that mean?”

“I’m afraid I can’t tell you until the review is complete.”

“When will that be?”

“I don’t have a date.”

Mara thanked her, then sat at the kitchen table feeling absurdly angry. She was not sure whether she was angry with the council, with her father for leaving a task unfinished, or with herself for discovering it only when she was preparing to leave. The agent had emailed two possible dates for photographs of the house. She chose the later one.

Over the weekend she made a spreadsheet from the last six years of notebooks. The work was slow because her father sometimes wrote numbers in the remarks column and remarks where the numbers belonged. He used a dash for no rain, a zero for a reading of no rain, and a question mark when he had been away and could not say. Mara, who worked with data for a living, found herself respecting the question marks. There were more of them in the final year. On one April page he had written, **Couldn’t get out early enough. Rain likely overnight.** She entered “unknown” and moved on.

On Monday she took the notebooks to the pharmacy. The owner, Mr. Desai, came out from behind the counter with reading glasses in his hand. He remembered her father at once.

“He checked our back step after every storm,” he said. “I thought he was worried about us.”

“He was.”

Mr. Desai turned the pages of the notebook Mara showed him. “He was worried about the water too. People think it comes straight off the road, but it arrives from behind first. We had sandbags at the door last time. It came through the wall.”

“Would you tell the council that?”

“I have. I’ll tell them again.”

By the end of the week, Inez had spoken to six neighbors, and Mr. Desai had found invoices from the flood damage. Mara had no plan for what to do with any of it. She had meant only to ask a few questions before returning to her life. Instead she found herself at Inez’s table on Saturday morning with a notebook, a map, and four people describing where water had gone during different storms. They disagreed about the hour it reached the road and whether the warehouse fence had made things worse. They agreed that the ditch no longer carried water away as it once had.

Mara drew a fresh map. She marked what they knew, wrote “uncertain” beside what they did not, and left room for more observations. It looked nothing like her father’s map, though she used the same kitchen ruler to make the lines straight.

The following Tuesday, rain began before dawn. Mara woke in her childhood bedroom to the steady tapping of drops on the sill. Downstairs, she emptied the leaves from the gauge and set it back on its pipe. By breakfast there were twelve millimeters in the cylinder. By noon there were twenty-three. She took an umbrella to the ditch and found water moving swiftly through the open section, then slowing where the brambles narrowed it. Gravel had gathered against the wire fence. She took photographs from the path and went home to change her soaked shoes.

At four, Inez knocked. She had been to the pharmacy and wanted to know whether Mara had seen the road. They walked together under a single umbrella, neither of them quite covered. Water was spreading across the lowest part of the pavement. Mr. Desai had already moved a shelf of goods away from the back wall. He came out to meet them and watched as a council van pulled up at the corner.

Two workers got out and went to the ditch with long-handled tools. Mara showed them the map and the photographs on her phone. One of them listened, then walked down the bank to inspect the culvert. It was clogged with branches and a surprising amount of gravel. They cleared what they could before dark. The water at the pharmacy stopped rising, though it took hours to drain.

The next morning the rain had ended. Mara emptied the gauge: thirty-eight millimeters in all. She wrote the number in a blank notebook she had bought for herself, then put it aside to make calls. The council had sent a crew back to the culvert. Inez reported that the road was open. Mr. Desai asked if Mara wanted tea when she came past.

The inspection report, when it arrived weeks later, did not settle every question. It recommended clearing the ditch and reviewing runoff from the warehouse lot. Responsibility for the fence still had to be established. Mara was back in her apartment by then, answering emails at her own kitchen table, where the view was mostly of brick and a narrow piece of sky. Inez called whenever she heard news. Sometimes she called with none.

Mara put the house on the market in autumn. She had the windows repaired and the back steps made safe. She left the rain gauge in place. When the buyers asked about it, she told them what it was and said she would take it if they preferred. They had a young son who immediately wanted to know how much rain had fallen that day. Mara showed him how to read the marks on the cloudy plastic. His mother said they might keep it.

On her last evening in the house, Mara walked through the empty rooms to check she had left nothing behind. The pale rectangles where pictures had hung made the walls look unfinished. At the kitchen door she found the pencil mark for the first frost. She had seen it all week without looking at the date beneath it. Now she noticed that her father had added one more line, lower down: **Mara home Saturday**.

She could not remember which Saturday he meant. It might have been a visit years ago, or the one she had promised shortly before he died and never got to make. Her hand rose to the mark, then fell. Outside, the evening was clear. She shut the windows, locked the door, and carried the notebooks to the car.

At her apartment, they took up an entire shelf. Mara intended to give most of them to the local history archive; the archivist had already said he would look at them. For now, she sometimes opened one at random while waiting for water to boil. A date would yield a temperature, a wind direction, a few words about the day. Once she found a pressed leaf. Once, beside a week of ordinary sunshine, her father had written, **Inez’s washing dry before lunch**.

Mara began checking the small gauge she had placed outside her own window. She missed days. A bird knocked it over once, and one morning she forgot to empty it before leaving for work. She wrote those things down too. When Inez phoned, Mara told her whether it had rained. Inez told her what was happening on Alder Street, and they compared notes before talking about everything else.

# The Shop That Fixed Small Things

On the morning I took the clock to be repaired, it began raining before I reached the end of our street. The clock was wrapped in a tea towel and tucked beneath my coat, where it knocked lightly against my ribs as I walked. Every few steps I put a hand over it, though there was no danger of its falling. It was a square kitchen clock with a yellow face, black numbers, and a red second hand that had stopped between seven and eight. It had hung above my mother’s stove for as long as I could remember.

The repair shop stood between a florist and a storefront that had been empty so long people still called it the shoe shop. Its window contained a silver toaster, three lamps, a sewing machine, and a cardboard sign that said, **BEFORE YOU THROW IT AWAY, ASK**. Below that, in smaller letters: **We might say no.** I had passed the place hundreds of times without going in. My mother had gone there regularly. After she died, I found six receipts in her kitchen drawer: a kettle, two radios, a vacuum cleaner, a table fan, and an item described only as “small thing with wheels.”

A bell rang when I opened the door. Inside, the shop smelled of dust, warm metal, and the sharp, clean scent of the florist’s cut stems next door. A woman at the counter was taking apart a desk lamp. She had a pencil behind each ear and a magnifying visor pushed up onto her forehead. At a workbench farther back, a young man was sorting screws into jars.

“Morning,” the woman said, without looking up. “Put it wherever there’s room.”

There wasn’t much room. I set the clock on a patch of counter between a blender and a ceramic dog with a missing tail.

She glanced at it. “That one’s familiar.”

“It was my mother’s.”

“Your mother was Mrs. Bell from Hawthorn Street?”

I said yes. For a moment the woman held the lamp’s plug in one hand and said nothing.

“I’m sorry,” she said at last. “She always asked how long a repair would take, then told me to take my time.”

My mother had never been patient with anyone at home. If I was late, she called twice. If I washed dishes while she cooked, she moved me aside so she could do them properly. Yet I could imagine her at this counter, giving a stranger all the time in the world.

The woman introduced herself as Len. She turned the clock over and loosened the back with a tiny screwdriver. Inside, the mechanism looked disappointingly ordinary. There were no delicate gears to admire, only a plastic box and a battery compartment dusted with pale blue corrosion.

“Can you fix it?” I asked.

“Probably. Though replacing the movement might cost more than buying another clock.”

“I don’t want another clock.”

Len nodded, as if she had expected that answer. She wrote my name on a paper tag and asked for my number. When I left, the tea towel was folded in my bag, and the space beneath my coat felt strangely exposed.

I had come back to town three weeks earlier to clear my mother’s house. I was living there while I worked, sleeping in my old room beneath a ceiling covered with faint stars that glowed after the lights went out. The stars had lasted longer than my first job, two apartments, and a marriage. Each morning I sat at the dining table with my laptop, answering messages from people in other cities. Each evening I chose one cupboard or drawer and emptied it onto the floor. I kept finding reasons to stop.

The clock had been one of them. For years, whenever I called, I could hear it ticking behind my mother’s voice. She had a habit of standing in the kitchen to talk, even if she was not cooking. During our last conversation, she told me the back gate was sticking and asked whether I still had the green scarf she made me. I said I did. I did not mention that I couldn’t remember where I had put it. We talked for twelve minutes. I know because I looked at the call record afterward, trying to find evidence of something I should have noticed.

A few days after I left the clock with Len, she called to say she had found the problem. The battery had leaked into the contacts, and one thin strip of metal had broken. She could replace the entire mechanism, or she could make a new contact.

“Which would your mother prefer?” she asked.

I looked around the kitchen. My mother had saved rubber bands in a jam jar and reused envelopes for shopping lists. On the other hand, she had bought a new electric kettle the moment the old one began switching itself off too early.

“I don’t know,” I said.

“Then come in and see.”

When I arrived, Len showed me the damaged piece through a magnifier. It looked like a bent scrap of foil. She explained how it carried power from the battery to the clock’s motor, then showed me a replacement she had cut from a sheet of spring metal. She held both pieces on her palm, one dull and eaten away, the other bright.

“Will the new one last?” I asked.

“It should. Something else might go wrong, of course.”

The young man at the back table laughed. “That should be on the sign.”

His name was Arun. He came in after school on Tuesdays and Thursdays and, according to Len, had repaired four lamps, a toy train, and one electric pencil sharpener. He looked pleased about the train and doubtful about the sharpener.

I left the clock there another day so Len could test it. The next afternoon, when I returned, its second hand was moving steadily around the yellow face. Len had cleaned the glass, too. It seemed brighter than it had in my mother’s kitchen.

“That’s fifteen pounds,” she said.

I paid, and she wrapped the clock in brown paper. Before handing it over, she made a note on the back: *new contact, cleaned, tested*. My mother’s receipts had looked the same. I wondered whether she had kept them because she liked records or because each one was proof that something had come home.

At the house, I carried the clock into the kitchen. A pale square marked its old place on the wall. I lifted it toward the nail, then set it on the counter instead. I told myself I wanted to wipe the wall first. For the rest of the week, the clock stayed beside the fruit bowl, ticking next to three oranges that slowly softened. I could hear it from the dining table when work was quiet. Sometimes I went into the kitchen merely to look at it, though its hands told me nothing my phone could not.

On Saturday, a storm moved across the town. Rain streamed down the windows and gathered at the corner where Hawthorn Street sloped toward the river. By afternoon, the water was over the curb. I went outside with the long broom from my mother’s shed and joined two neighbors trying to clear leaves from a drain. We pulled out handfuls of black, sodden clumps while the rain ran down our sleeves. When the grate opened, water began to circle above it and disappear. We stood watching until the puddle shrank enough to reveal the painted line along the road.

The florist’s van came past slowly, pushing a small wave ahead of it. I thought of the repair shop down near the river and walked there the next morning. Most of the street was dry, but water had got beneath the shop door. Len and Arun were carrying things onto the pavement: chairs, boxes, a low bookcase swollen at the bottom. The florist was there too, helping arrange rescued equipment on folding tables. She wore rubber boots and had a strip of silver tape stuck to her sleeve.

“Do you need help?” I asked.

Len handed me a crate of tangled cords. “Take these into the sun. No plugging anything in.”

We worked through the morning. I wiped mud from a row of table fans and set them where the breeze could reach them. Arun opened radios and held them at an angle so water ran out. Several customers arrived after seeing the open door. Some stayed to carry things; others went home and returned with towels, extension leads, or sandwiches. A man from the bakery brought coffee in a tray that was already softening with rain. By noon, the pavement looked like an untidy market.

Len was not cheerful about the flood. The bottom drawers of her parts cabinet had been soaked, and years of screws, washers, and switches were mixed with grit. She knelt beside one drawer and began picking through it.

“You could throw that lot out,” the florist said gently.

“I could,” Len answered.

She handed me a dry cloth and a tray. We laid out the pieces one by one. Some were rusted beyond use; some cleaned up easily. I learned that a screw which looked almost right could ruin a thread, and that Len remembered which appliance had supplied a particular black knob. Arun found a copper washer pressed flat beneath the drawer lining and held it up in triumph. By late afternoon our hands smelled of metal, and we had filled eleven labeled jars.

Before I went home, Len asked what I was going to do with my mother’s house. I told her I would probably sell it. I had a job elsewhere, and no plan to move back. She listened without trying to change my mind.

“I’ll miss her garden,” she said. “She gave me cuttings from that purple plant. Mine never took.”

“The one by the gate?”

“Yes. She said it could survive anything.”

I had spent three weeks walking past that plant without seeing it. Back at the house, I went to the gate. Its leaves were dark and wet, and small purple flowers hung beneath them. The latch stuck as it always had; I had to lift the gate before it would close. My mother had asked me about it on our last call. I fetched a screwdriver from the shed and tightened the loose hinge plate. Then I opened and shut the gate several times, enjoying the small, clean sound of the latch catching.

The next Tuesday, I returned to the shop with a cutting in a jar of water. Len put it on the windowsill. Much of the flood damage had been cleared, though the floor bore a faint brown line along one wall. A new cardboard sign stood on the counter: **REPAIR AFTER WATER DAMAGE TAKES TIME. PLEASE ASK FIRST.** Someone had written underneath: **We might say no.** The original window sign, I noticed, had curled at the corners.

Arun was trying to revive a music box shaped like a carousel. He wound its key, and a few notes came out before the horses stopped turning. Len leaned over it and showed him a tooth missing from a small gear. They discussed whether another gear could be cut to fit. I watched for a while, then asked if they ever needed extra hands.

Len looked at my neat work clothes, then at the jar of cuttings. “We need someone to sort what came out of the storeroom,” she said. “It’s mostly labels and old instruction manuals. You’re welcome to try.”

I came in on Thursday after work. The task was less useful than I had imagined. The manuals were damp, and many belonged to appliances no one had seen in decades. Still, there were pages worth saving. I spread them out, copied model numbers, and made piles while Len worked at the bench. Customers came and went. One woman collected a rice cooker and said she had bought it when her youngest son was born; he was now twenty-nine. A man brought in a torch he used for walking his dog. He wanted it back before the evenings grew darker.

Over the following weeks, I went to the shop whenever I could spare an hour. Sometimes I sorted parts. Once I washed the windows. I learned to test batteries and to check a plug for damage, and learned just as importantly when to leave something alone. The repairs themselves belonged to Len and Arun. There was plenty to do around them. People needed their names written clearly on tags, their screws kept together, their questions answered if Len was busy. They often wanted to explain where an object had come from. I got better at listening without promising it could be saved.

At home, I went on clearing cupboards. I gave away a set of heavy plates I had never liked, and kept the chipped bowl my mother used for lemons. I found the green scarf in a box with winter gloves. It was softer than I remembered. At the back of a drawer were the wheels from a child’s wooden pull-toy, each one newly attached to its axle. I turned them in my hands and thought of the receipt marked “small thing with wheels.” Then I packed the toy with a few other things I was taking with me.

Before I left town, I hung the clock back on its nail. It covered the pale square exactly. I stood beneath it for a minute, listening to the tick. In another month the house would belong to someone else, and they might take it down. For now it was where my mother had kept it. I locked the back door, lifted the gate so its latch caught, and carried my bags to the car. On the passenger seat was a small jar with a purple cutting from the plant by the gate. Len had shown me which stem to take and where to cut it.

The clock stayed with the house because I decided it should. I had photographs of the kitchen, and the green scarf folded in my bag. In the car, I set the jar in the cup holder, where it rattled gently as I drove. By the time I reached the edge of town, one leaf had turned toward the window.

# The Museum of Ordinary Sounds

When I came home, the town was quiet in a way I had never heard before. The bridge still carried cars across the river, and the bakery still ran its exhaust fan all night, but the bell at the textile mill was gone. It had marked the beginning and end of shifts for ninety-three years. Even after the mill closed, someone had kept it working. At seven each morning and five each evening, its blunt, unmusical note traveled through the streets. Now the mill was being taken apart, and the bell had been sent away with the rest of the salvage.

My mother had loved that bell. She said it was the sound of people knowing when to go home. As a child, I thought she meant that the bell told them. Much later, I understood that she meant it had made a promise on behalf of the town: there would be work, and then there would be an end to work.

She had been dead for four years when I returned to clear out her house. I lived three hours away. I had taken a week off, brought cardboard boxes, and made a list on the drive: kitchen on Monday, bedrooms on Tuesday, attic on Wednesday. I intended to sell the house by autumn.

In the pantry, behind jars of screws and a tin of birthday candles, I found a shoebox full of cassettes. Each had a date and a few words written on its label in my mother’s careful, compressed handwriting.

*Rain under the market awning, June 1998.*

*Mrs. Vale closing shop, 2003.*

*Mill bell, winter.*

There were dozens. I found an old player beneath them, put in fresh batteries, and chose the tape marked *Sunday washing up*.

At first I heard water running. Then plates touched plates, a drawer scraped open, and my father said, “The good knife goes on the left.” My mother told him that if it mattered so much, he was welcome to dry the cutlery himself. He laughed. He had been dead since I was sixteen, and I had forgotten that his laugh ended with a small, breathless cough.

I stopped the tape.

Outside the pantry window, a delivery van rolled over a loose drain cover. It made two knocks, one on each side of the wheel. I heard it clearly, as if my mother had turned up the volume on the street.

I sat on the kitchen floor for a long time. When I pressed play again, my parents discussed whether there was enough soap for another load of laundry. My father dropped something metal in the sink. The recording ended before either of them remembered to turn off the tap.

My mother had never mentioned the tapes. Perhaps she had planned to play them for me someday. Perhaps she knew I would find them when she was gone. I could ask neither question, so I carried the box into the sitting room and continued sorting.

By Wednesday I had made little progress. I had filled three bags for the charity shop, kept a chipped blue bowl I had no room for, and listened to eighteen tapes. My mother had recorded the river in flood, a marching band practicing the same eight bars for half an hour, the squeak of a gate someone had since replaced. She recorded voices too, but rarely when anyone was saying something important. On one tape, my aunt counted stitches while teaching me to knit. On another, two neighbors argued about the best way to grow beans.

That afternoon I walked to the library to ask whether they had equipment for copying cassettes. The library occupied the old post office, a building with a clock over the door that showed twenty past two no matter when you looked. The librarian, Leena, remembered my mother.

“She used to bring us recordings,” she said. “For the sound collection.”

I told her I had found a box. Leena led me downstairs, past local history shelves and a table stacked with jigsaw puzzles, to a room scarcely larger than a cupboard. A computer stood beside a turntable and a cassette deck. On the wall was a map of town dotted with colored pins.

“Your mother started this,” Leena said.

The collection was small: just over two hundred recordings. The council had funded the equipment, but most of the work had been done by volunteers. There were bird calls from the marsh, interviews with shopkeepers, traffic at the old crossroads before the bypass opened. My mother’s name appeared on record after record.

“She never told me,” I said.

Leena looked surprised, then apologetic. “Maybe it didn’t come up.”

That sounded exactly like my mother. She could spend six months organizing a community project and report only that the library’s basement was damp.

Leena showed me how to copy a tape and enter its details. She warned me that cassettes deteriorated and that we should handle the oldest ones first. We spent an hour transferring *Sunday washing up*. When the file was saved, the software displayed it as a band of blue peaks and valleys. My father’s laugh was somewhere in that shape. I knew because I had heard it, though I could not have pointed to the place.

Back at the house, I found more tapes in the attic. They were stored in biscuit tins among tax returns, instruction manuals, and a single roller skate. One tin held recordings from the year the mill closed. My mother had caught the bell on the last working day, first from our front garden and then from the footbridge half a mile away. The two versions sounded different. From the garden, the note rose over sparrows and a barking dog. From the bridge, it barely emerged from the steady rush of water.

I remembered that day. I was home from university, angry about something I can no longer recall. At five o’clock the bell rang, and my mother stood at the back door with a little silver recorder in her hand. I asked why she bothered. The bell would ring tomorrow. She said, “I want to hear what it sounded like today.”

She was right to make the recording. The bell did ring for another twenty years, but no other day sounded quite like that one.

On Friday, I brought the attic tins to the library. Leena found me an empty desk and a pair of headphones. A handwritten catalogue lay nearby. My mother had begun it in a ruled school notebook, then moved to a spreadsheet after someone taught her how. Her descriptions were precise without being grand.

*West Street, 6:15 a.m. One bus, light rain, unidentified bird repeating three notes. Driver waits while passenger runs from corner.*

*Market square at closing. Crates loaded into van. Recording interrupted by request for help lifting table.*

That last note made me smile. My mother had never been able to stand still while someone else carried a table.

For several hours, I worked through her tapes. It was absorbing, exacting work. Some labels had fallen off, and I had to listen for clues: the church clock before it was repaired, a shop sign rattling in the wind, my own voice at an age when I still called everyone by their full name. I learned to leave a few seconds of silence at the beginning and end of each file, and not to clean away every hiss. Leena said the hiss was part of the tape’s history.

Near closing time, I came across a cassette marked *Saturday, kitchen*. I recognized the date. It was the week before my father died.

I put it aside. Then I put away the other tapes, returned the desk to order, and went home.

The house seemed different after the library. Until then, I had treated its sounds as disturbances: the refrigerator’s uneven hum, rain ticking against the blocked gutter, the stair that complained under my left foot. Now I found myself wondering which of them my mother would have recorded. She would have fixed the gutter before doing anything else.

I stood in the kitchen that night and called the estate agent to postpone our meeting. I needed more time to clear the attic. This was true, though it was not the whole reason.

The next morning, I climbed a ladder and pulled leaves from the gutter. My neighbor Mr. Anwar called across the fence to ask whether I was staying. He had lived next door since before I was born. I told him no, not for long.

“Your mother said that too,” he replied.

I laughed, thinking he meant she had always been too busy to sit down. But he was looking at the little recorder on the windowsill. I had taken it from the attic and had not yet worked out how to use it.

“She said she was going to finish the collection and hand it over,” he said. “Every year.”

“Why didn’t she?”

He shrugged. “People kept asking her to record things.”

Mr. Anwar told me she had come over one summer to capture the noise made by his daughter’s wheelchair on the wooden ramp. His daughter, Farah, had asked her to. By then the ramp was old, and it gave a cheerful rattle every time she came home. Farah wanted the recording before they replaced it. She had moved away, Mr. Anwar said, but still lived where she could use it.

That afternoon I wrote to Farah. She replied within an hour. She was a designer, and she had helped my mother arrange a listening event years ago. People had been invited to bring sounds they wanted others to notice. Farah brought the ramp and a recording of her grandmother tapping a pattern on the table to get her attention. She asked whether the library was still collecting.

I wrote back that I thought so. Leena confirmed it on Monday.

Word traveled through town faster than I expected. A man from the bakery offered to record the mixer before they replaced it. A teenager wanted to capture the basketball court on a busy evening. Someone asked if we already had the train passing the allotments. I found a note from my mother saying we did, but the recording was fifteen years old. The trains might sound different now.

For the rest of my week off, I went out with the recorder. I began at the mill site, where workers sorted bricks into stacks. I asked permission before recording and stood well clear while a forklift reversed with a high, polite beep. Across the road, a woman paused to watch.

“Are you from the paper?” she asked.

I explained about the library collection.

“Get the bell?” she said.

“Yes. My mother did.”

The woman kept watching the mill. “I could hear it from my first flat. My husband worked nights, so it usually woke him. Drove him mad.” She considered this. “I miss it anyway.”

She told me her name and where the flat had been, and agreed to let me record her saying it again. When I listened later, I could hear bricks being set down behind her. I was glad I had not asked her to move somewhere quieter.

My mother had understood that a sound seldom arrived alone. The mill bell had traveled over traffic, through open windows, past children being called in for supper. In her tapes, people talked over one another, dogs interrupted interviews, and wind struck the microphone at inconvenient moments. She had kept many of those moments. Listening to them, I could tell where she had stood.

I stayed another week. Each morning I dealt with the house, and each afternoon I took tapes to the library or went out recording. The house slowly emptied. I gave the blue bowl to Mr. Anwar, who promised to use it rather than put it on a shelf. I kept my mother’s notebook and the player from the pantry. The original tapes went to the library in acid-free boxes that Leena ordered with unusual excitement.

All that time, *Saturday, kitchen* remained in my bag.

I knew why I was afraid of it. My father had been ill, and my last conversation with him was an argument about whether I should cancel a trip with my friends. I went. He told me to go. I came back two days later, and we never had another proper conversation. For years I had imagined that, if given one more ordinary afternoon, I would speak more kindly. The cassette might offer such an afternoon, but I could not change anything I said on it.

On my final evening in town, I sat at the desk downstairs in the library. Leena had left me a key to the room. Upstairs, chairs scraped across the floor as a reading group packed up. I put the cassette in the deck and pressed play.

Someone was chopping vegetables. A drawer opened and shut. My mother asked whether we needed bread. My father said yes, unless I had eaten it all. Then my own voice said I was going out.

I remembered the argument as loud, but it began quietly. My father asked when I would be back. I said Sunday. He asked who was driving. I answered him twice, growing impatient. There was a pause, filled by the soft, quick sound of the knife on the board.

Then my father said, “Take my coat. It’s meant to rain.”

I said I had one.

“It’s a better coat.”

“I’ll be fine.”

A little later, I heard myself leave. The back door shut, and my parents resumed discussing bread. My mother was going to the shop anyway, she said. My father asked her to buy oranges too.

I sat with the headphones on until the tape clicked off. I had hoped, without admitting it, that I would hear him say something I had forgotten: advice, forgiveness, a declaration that settled everything. Instead, he wanted me to take his coat. I remembered it hanging by the door. It was heavy and dark green, with one button he had sewn on in the wrong place.

I copied the tape. In the catalogue, under description, I wrote: *Family in kitchen preparing dinner. Conversation about bread, oranges, and a coat. Door closes at approximately four minutes.* I saved the file, then sat a while longer before turning out the light.

The following month, the library held a listening afternoon. I drove back for it. Leena had put headphones at several tables and set out cards so visitors could suggest recordings. Farah came home for the weekend and helped people use the equipment. Mr. Anwar arrived with a photograph of the old ramp. The bakery brought buns.

There was no speech. People listened, compared memories, and sometimes disagreed about what they heard. One woman said the mill bell had always sounded lower in winter. A former mill worker said it depended where you stood. They went to the map and pointed out their houses.

A little boy listened to my mother’s recording of the market square, then asked why everyone was laughing. I put on the headphones. At first I heard crates and a van door. Then, behind them, one person laughed and another joined in. I had missed it every previous time.

Before I left, I took the recorder outside. The clock above the library still showed twenty past two. A bus pulled up, waited, and pulled away. Someone across the street was sweeping a step with slow, deliberate strokes. From the open basement window came the faint sound of people talking about the bell.

I recorded for two minutes. Then I went inside, wrote down where I had stood, and added the date.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
Every morning, a man on my street opens the little cabinet beneath the free library outside his house. The cabinet holds things nobody came to borrow: a screwdriver, a roll of tape, a dry cloth, and a pencil sharpened down to a stub. He checks the roof for leaks, wipes yesterday’s rain from the shelf, and puts the books upright again. Once I watched him repair a torn page with a narrow strip of tape. He did it slowly, as if the page belonged to someone, though the book had no name written inside it.

I used to think the interesting part of the library was the exchange. A stranger leaves a mystery novel; another takes it home. A child discovers a book about whales. That is the story the painted sign seems to promise. But without the morning visits, the shelves would soon smell of damp paper. The door would stick. The books would curl, and people would stop opening it. The exchange depends on a less visible practice: someone noticing small problems before they become reasons to give up.

Maintenance rarely feels like an event. It has no satisfying moment when everything is finished. You wash the cup, and tomorrow there is another cup. You tighten a loose screw, knowing that elsewhere another one is working free. This repetition can seem bleak when compared with making something new. Yet there is a particular pleasure in it, too. The cup is ready for the next person. The door closes cleanly. A bicycle chain runs quietly after being cleaned, and the rider feels the difference all the way to work.

We are inclined to praise beginnings. We celebrate the opening of a garden, the launch of a website, the first day in a new apartment. Beginnings make good photographs: a ribbon, a key, fresh soil in neat rows. The following months are harder to picture. Someone must pull weeds, answer messages, clear the drain beside the steps. These acts do not diminish the original achievement. They allow it to keep meaning something. A garden is not a failed project because it needs water; needing water is part of being a garden.

The same is true of places we share with people we may never meet. A bus shelter with an intact light lets a tired passenger read the timetable. A sidewalk without broken glass lets a child walk home in thin shoes. When these things work, we pass through them without much thought. When they fail, the failure lands unevenly. Someone with a car can avoid a dark shelter. Someone who has no choice but to wait there cannot. Care for common places is often quiet, but its absence can be painfully loud.

Some kinds of maintenance are harder to see because nothing physical is being fixed. A friend remembers that you have an appointment you dread and asks how it went. Two colleagues explain a recurring task clearly enough that the next person will not have to guess. A family member notices that the conversation always turns away from one person’s worries and makes room to hear them. None of these gestures repairs a relationship once and for all. They make it possible for people to return to one another without stepping over the same unspoken obstacle every time.

Still, we should be careful about praising maintenance without asking who is doing it. Repetitive work is often assigned to people whose time is treated as endlessly available. The pleasant sight of a clean room can conceal a worker hurrying through too many rooms for too little pay. The ease of a holiday gathering can rest on one person’s exhausting preparation. Calling this work noble does not make that arrangement fair. If we value what is kept running, we ought to notice the labor, share it where we can, and pay for it properly where we cannot.

There are also things we cannot maintain forever. A beloved coat wears thin at the elbows. A tree comes down in a storm despite years of careful pruning. Friendships change as people move and grow. Maintenance is not a promise that nothing will end. Sometimes the most attentive choice is to mend a coat again; sometimes it is to thank it for its years and let it go. We need judgment alongside devotion, or else care can become a demand to preserve every object and arrangement exactly as it was.

Perhaps that is why the small library interests me. Its keeper does not decide which books must stay. People add and remove them, sometimes leaving odd combinations: a cookbook beside a detective story, a guide to birds beside a novel with its cover missing. He looks after the space that lets these choices happen. His work gives strangers a little room to surprise one another. On a rainy morning, that can feel like a generous idea: not to control what a place contains, but to keep it welcoming enough for something new to arrive.

Last week I stopped at the library on my way home. Its door swung open easily. Inside, the shelves were dry, and the books had shifted since my last visit. I took a collection of essays and left a paperback I had finished. Before closing the door, I noticed a small scrap of paper under one of the shelves. It had been folded to level a wobble. I had never noticed the wobble itself. I stood there for a moment with my hand on the latch, grateful for a repair so modest that it had almost disappeared.

At home, I put the essays on my desk and found that one leg of the desk was loose. For several days I had been bracing it with my knee while I wrote, irritated each time it moved. I got a screwdriver and turned the screw until the leg held firm. It took less than a minute. The desk was still old, the room was still untidy, and there were plenty of things I could not put right so easily. But when I sat down again, the surface stayed steady beneath my hands.

The town had a museum for things nobody thought to save. It occupied the old post office, between a bakery and a shop that sold batteries. There were no paintings on its walls. Instead, glass cases held a single blue button, a chipped teaspoon, a paper ticket to a cinema that had closed before I was born. Every object had a label explaining who had brought it and what they remembered. The museum charged no admission. Most days, nobody went in.

I started visiting during the summer I was meant to leave town. My train ticket was booked for September, and I had a list of practical things to do: sell my bicycle, pack my clothes, call the landlord about a leak. Instead, I spent afternoons reading labels. The button had come from a winter coat worn by three sisters in turn. The teaspoon had belonged to a man who stirred every cup of tea exactly seven times. Someone had kept the cinema ticket because it was the first time she had gone anywhere alone.

At the back of the museum, behind a curtain, was a room without cases. Shelves held hundreds of small cardboard boxes. A handwritten sign said **SOUNDS**, though the boxes appeared empty. I lifted the lid of one marked *Front gate, 1986* and heard a metal latch click, followed by footsteps hurrying across gravel. I nearly dropped it. When I opened it again, the same footsteps crossed the same gravel.

The curator found me standing there with the lid in my hands. Her name was Mrs. Vale, and she was old enough that people had begun describing her as if she were a historic building. She said the boxes worked only for sounds someone had loved enough to remember clearly. She did not know why. Her predecessor had discovered the first one decades ago, after placing an empty box beside his bed to catch a mouse. In the morning, it contained his mother singing while she washed dishes.

I asked whether anyone could make one. Mrs. Vale handed me a box and told me to try. I thought of the leak in my apartment, but all I heard was my own breathing. I thought of the bakery bell, which rang each time the door opened, and heard nothing. Then I remembered my father knocking twice on my bedroom door before entering. For a moment, two firm taps sounded inside the box. They were quieter than I expected, but unmistakable.

My father was alive, only three streets away. Still, I carried the box home in both hands. I had not lived with him for years, and I could no longer recall when his knock had stopped being part of my days. That evening I found him repairing a chair at his kitchen table. I told him about the museum. He laughed, asked whether Mrs. Vale had finally persuaded someone else to dust the shelves, and offered me the chair once its leg was sound.

Over the next few weeks, I helped at the museum. People arrived with memories they wanted to put in boxes: a dog’s paws crossing a wooden floor, rain on a particular roof, the uneven whistle of a kettle long since thrown away. Mrs. Vale showed them how to sit quietly and pay attention. Often they left disappointed. Remembering that a sound existed was not the same as hearing it again in your mind. Some returned the next day with better luck. Others brought photographs or stories instead.

One morning a little boy came in with his grandfather. They had spent the weekend trying to remember the grandmother’s laugh. Both knew it had been loud. The boy said she sometimes laughed so hard she covered her face; his grandfather said she never did. They went back and forth, correcting each other, until the boy grew upset. Mrs. Vale gave them tea and suggested they come back another time. As they were leaving, the grandfather remembered how she used to clear her throat before telling a joke. The boy remembered that too. They made a box for it together.

Near the end of August, I packed the last of my things. The bicycle went to a neighbor’s daughter. My father kept the chair and lent me a suitcase whose wheels pulled stubbornly to the left. On my final day, I returned the box with his knock to the museum. I had listened to it often enough to notice a faint sound after the second tap: my younger self calling, “Come in.” I had forgotten that part. I showed Mrs. Vale the label I had written, and she found it a place on the shelf.

The museum did not make leaving harder. If anything, those weeks had taught me that a town could remain itself without my standing in it. People would keep opening the bakery door and buying batteries. My father would find another chair to repair. Perhaps someone would come looking for the sound of the train as it left the station, though I doubted they would need a box to remember it while trains still ran every day.

On the platform, I heard my father call my name and turned. He had come to return a book I had left in his kitchen. I put it in the crooked suitcase. Then the train arrived, with brakes that squealed all along the platform, and we said goodbye over the noise. Once I had found my seat, I opened the book. Tucked between its pages was a note in his handwriting: *You can always come in.* I read it twice before the train pulled away.

The city had a department for things people could no longer hear.

It occupied the second floor of a narrow brick building between a locksmith and a shop that sold umbrellas. Most residents passed it without noticing the brass plaque beside the door: **OFFICE OF LOST SOUNDS**. Those who did notice assumed it concerned noise complaints. In a way, it did.

The office received its first case on a Tuesday in March. A woman named Irena climbed the stairs and told the clerk that the floorboard outside her son’s bedroom had stopped creaking. She had stepped on it every night for twelve years, trying not to wake him, and every night it had betrayed her. Now her son lived across the country. The board was silent.

The clerk, who was new, suggested a carpenter.

“I don’t want it repaired,” Irena said. “I want to hear it once more.”

The clerk was unsure what to do, so he wrote her name on a form. In the space marked *Description of sound*, he wrote: *A short, complaining note, like a violin tuning itself in another room.*

By Thursday, there were six more forms. Someone missed the rattle of a particular tram that had been retired. A baker missed the tiny crackle made by paper bags folded shut. A man wanted the sound of his old dog drinking water, though he admitted he had no idea what he would do if the office found it.

The department had been founded decades earlier for an entirely different purpose. Its cabinets held recordings of factory whistles, demolished train stations, and public bells removed because they rang at inconvenient hours. The collection was meant to preserve the city’s history. But the new clerk began to suspect that history had less to do with great events than with the sounds that happened while nobody was paying attention.

His name was Tomas. Each morning, before the streets filled, he carried a recorder through the neighborhoods. He captured shutters rising, delivery carts crossing cobblestones, spoons striking cups. He learned that the fountain in the square made three distinct sounds: a hiss where the water entered the basin, a hollow splash near the center, and a bright patter along the rim. He also learned that people became remarkably patient when asked to describe what they missed.

“A cough,” said one visitor. “My grandfather’s. He was always pretending he didn’t need a doctor.”

“The click of a lamp,” said another. “It took two tries to turn on.”

“The way my sister knocked,” said a third. “As if she were apologizing to the door.”

Tomas could not retrieve those sounds. Often he could find no recording, no surviving object, no willing imitator. He started keeping a second file, one containing descriptions alone. He arranged them alphabetically, then abandoned that system when he realized nobody came looking for *A cough* or *A click*. They came looking for a person, a room, a time in their life.

One afternoon, an elderly watchmaker visited with a small wooden box. Inside lay a clock with no hands.

“My father made this,” the watchmaker said. “It ran badly. Every seventh tick came late.” He wound the clock and set it on Tomas’s desk. For a moment nothing happened. Then it began: tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick—tick.

“There,” said the watchmaker, smiling. “It still remembers.”

Tomas recorded the clock. When the watchmaker returned the next day, he did not ask to hear the recording. He simply thanked Tomas for having listened.

That evening, Tomas stayed late. Rain moved over the roof in soft waves. Downstairs, the locksmith lowered his metal shutters with a long, familiar crash. Tomas sat at his desk wondering whether the office was collecting sounds at all. Perhaps it was collecting proof that ordinary days had occurred: that someone had climbed the stairs; that a dog had leaned over its bowl; that a child had slept behind a door while a parent paused outside it.

He thought of his mother’s kitchen. On winter mornings she used to open a tin of tea with the edge of a spoon because the lid was too tight. Metal scraped metal, then the lid came free with a pop. He had not heard it in years. His mother still lived, and the kitchen was still there, but she had replaced the tin with a glass jar. He could call her. He could visit. What he could not do was stand in that kitchen at the age of nine, waiting for the kettle to boil.

The next morning, Tomas changed the sign outside. Beneath **OFFICE OF LOST SOUNDS**, he added: **YOU MAY ALSO BRING ONE YOU STILL HAVE**.

At first, people brought predictable things: music boxes, squeaky toys, a bicycle bell. Then they brought stranger offerings. A woman recorded her husband laughing while he tried to tell a joke. Two brothers argued over the proper sound of their childhood gate and went home to record it together. A schoolteacher brought in her class to capture the noise of thirty children putting away their chairs. When Tomas played it back, the room sounded less like a classroom than a flock preparing to migrate.

In late summer, Irena returned. She carried a small recorder in her coat pocket. Her son was visiting, she explained, and she had asked him to walk down the hall while she stood in the kitchen. She pressed play. There were footsteps, a muffled conversation, the opening of a door. No creak.

“I thought you wanted the floorboard,” Tomas said.

“I did,” she answered. “But listen.”

He listened again. Just before the recording ended, her son called out, “I’m going to make tea. Do you want some?”

Tomas looked up. Irena was smiling.

Outside, a tram passed the office. It was not the old tram, and its rattle was wrong. Downstairs, the locksmith was speaking to a customer. Rainwater dripped from someone’s umbrella onto the wooden floor. None of these sounds would last forever.

Tomas took out a fresh form and began to write them down.

On the first Saturday of every month, a folding table appeared outside the old train station. It held a tin of mismatched screws, three screwdrivers, a sewing kit, electrical tape, and a sign written in blue marker: **BRING WHAT’S BROKEN. WE’LL SEE.** The station had not served a train in twenty years. Its clock had stopped at 4:17, its ticket window was boarded up, and weeds grew between the bricks. Still, people knew where it was. By nine o’clock, they would begin arriving with lamps, coat zippers, radios, and things they could not quite explain why they had kept.

The table belonged to Mara, who had retired from repairing laboratory equipment at the hospital. She had spent forty years working on machines that measured tiny, consequential things. Now she liked objects whose problems could be seen without a microscope. A loose chair leg. A kettle switch that refused to stay down. She never promised she could fix anything. The sign was honest about that. “We’ll see” made room for failure, and it also made room for surprise. Sometimes the remedy was a new wire. Sometimes it was showing someone how to turn a screw they had been afraid to touch.

At first, Mara worked alone. The station sat beside the Saturday market, and shoppers would pause to watch her examine a toaster or thread a needle. After a few weeks, a teenager named Luis asked if he could help. He knew how to replace phone screens, though Mara did not let him begin with anyone else’s phone. Instead, she handed him a desk fan and asked him to find out why it rattled. He removed the cover, discovered a pebble inside, and held it up between two fingers. The fan’s owner laughed so hard she had to sit down.

By autumn, the table had grown into three tables. Someone brought a box of donated tools. Someone else supplied coffee in a dented silver urn. A retired tailor named Mrs. Okafor took charge of fabric repairs and had firm opinions about which buttons belonged on which coats. People began to arrive without anything broken, just to talk while they waited for the market to open. Mara sometimes found this distracting, especially when she was trying to follow a thin copper wire into the dark heart of a radio. But she noticed that nobody seemed eager to leave.

One cold morning, a man carried in a wooden music box wrapped in a dish towel. It had belonged to his mother, he said, and had not played since the year she died. Its lid showed a painted landscape: two trees, a river, and a house no bigger than a thumbnail. Mara wound the key gently. Nothing happened. She opened the bottom panel and found a cracked gear. No spare in the toolboxes would fit it. The man nodded as if he had expected this. He reached for the dish towel, but Luis asked if they might keep the box for a week.

Luis had recently learned to use a small printer at the community center. He measured the broken gear, drew a replacement on a computer, and made three versions before one turned properly. The next Saturday, they fitted it into the music box. The tune came out slowly at first, a few bright notes separated by awkward pauses. Then the cylinder turned again, and the melody found its pace. The man closed his eyes. Nobody at the table said anything. Mrs. Okafor kept sewing, though she was watching over the rim of her glasses.

Word of the music box traveled faster than news of all the kettles and lamps. In November, a local reporter came to take photographs and asked Mara what the project was really about. Mara disliked that question. She glanced at a line of people waiting with their belongings: a child holding a stuffed rabbit by one ear, a cyclist with a bent wheel, a woman carrying a clock. “It’s about trying,” she said. The reporter looked disappointed. Perhaps she wanted a grander answer. Mara returned to the clock, which had a perfectly good spring and a great deal of dust.

Winter changed the work. Their fingers grew stiff, and the glue took longer to dry. When rain came sideways across the station steps, they crowded under the awning, passing tools carefully from hand to hand. Some Saturdays, they fixed almost nothing. But people still brought things in. They described where a lamp had stood, who had given them a scarf, how long a drawer had been stuck. These details were not always needed for the repair. Mara listened anyway. She had come to understand that asking someone to mend an object was also a way of asking them to look at it closely.

In February, the station clock began ticking again. No one had meant to repair it. Mara and Luis had gone inside looking for an outlet and found the clock mechanism behind an unlocked door. Over several afternoons, they cleaned it, replaced a worn bearing, and tested the hands. On the day they restarted it, Mara set the time by her watch. For a minute, the hands did not move. Then the long hand advanced, so slightly that Luis thought he had imagined it. Outside, people crossing the square looked up when the bell struck noon. A few checked their phones to see if it was right.

By spring, Mara had learned to arrive without knowing what the day would ask of her. That morning there was a broken umbrella, a lamp with a frayed cord, and a bicycle bell that rang only when turned upside down. The clock above them kept time, losing a minute now and then. Luis was teaching a younger child to hold a screwdriver straight. Mrs. Okafor called for more thread. Mara picked up the umbrella and opened it carefully, away from everyone’s faces. One spoke had slipped loose. She found the place where it belonged and asked its owner to hold the fabric steady.
