The first sound I recorded was a refrigerator trying to start. It belonged to my grandmother and made a low, stubborn hum before clicking into silence. A minute later it tried again. She called it “the old man clearing his throat” and said she could sleep through anything except the night it finally stopped. I was twelve, holding a cassette recorder borrowed from school, and I thought I was collecting interesting noises. Really, I was collecting evidence that her kitchen existed: the motor, the tap dripping into a steel sink, her slippers against the floor.

The assignment was to make an audio portrait of our neighborhood. Most of my classmates recorded traffic or interviews with shopkeepers. I recorded the little things people asked me to ignore. A gate squeaked outside the pharmacy. Rainwater gurgled through a pipe behind the laundromat. At the bus stop, a loose advertising panel knocked against its frame whenever the wind came from the west. These sounds were so familiar that I hardly heard them until I put on headphones. Then each one seemed to belong to a particular hour, place, and season.

My grandmother liked the tape. She listened with her eyes closed and named things before they happened. “Now the kettle,” she said, a second before its whistle began. “Now you’ll hear Mrs. Vale’s dog.” She was pleased with herself, but she was also paying attention in a way I had not expected. When the tape ended, she asked me to record the stairs in her building. Every step had a different creak. She could tell who was coming up long before anyone knocked.

I went back on a Saturday and spent an hour climbing and descending while she listened from her apartment. Later, playing the tape, we heard my footsteps, the dry protest of the wood, and, faintly, her laugh through the door. I had not known the recorder would catch it. For years that laugh was the part I replayed. It arrived without warning, tucked between the seventh step and the eighth, as if she were still waiting at the top.

The recorder eventually broke. The play button sank under my thumb and refused to come back up. I took it to a repair shop on a side street, where a man named Mr. Sen kept radios in the window and a bowl of screws on his counter. He opened the machine while I watched. Inside, a thin rubber belt had slipped from its wheel. He replaced it with one from a drawer, tested the tape, and handed the recorder back. I asked what I owed him. He said, “Next time, bring the tape you’re making.”

I did. Over the next few years, I brought him recordings of market stalls being folded at dusk, of basketballs hitting the wall behind the school, of the train passing slowly through the station during a snowfall. Mr. Sen rarely commented on the sounds themselves. He wanted to know how close I had stood, whether I had sheltered the microphone from the wind, and what I had meant to capture. He taught me that a recording always includes more than its subject. It holds the distance between the person listening and the thing they hoped to hear.

When I left for college, the recorder went into a box. I bought a small digital one that fit in my pocket and saved hundreds of files with names like “Tuesday walk” and “rain maybe.” They were sharper than the old tapes and easier to forget. Sometimes I played one and had no idea where I had been. A sound could be perfectly clear and still tell me almost nothing. I began speaking a few words at the start of each recording: where I was, who was there, why I had stopped.

On a visit home, I found Mr. Sen’s shop closed. The radios were gone from the window; a notice said the building would be renovated. My mother knew he had retired and moved closer to his daughter, but she did not know where. I felt foolishly disappointed. I had imagined that if I needed another belt, or an answer about a strange noise, I could simply push open his door. Instead I stood outside the empty shop while someone upstairs dragged furniture across a floor.

That evening I found the cassette of my grandmother’s building. She had died the previous winter. The tape hissed before my first footstep, and for a moment I worried that time had rubbed away the rest. Then the stairs began: one low creak, two quick ones, a pause where I must have looked up. Her laugh was quieter than I remembered. I listened to it twice, not because I thought it would bring her back, but because I could hear how amused she was with me, performing my slow climb for a machine.

I still record the neighborhood when I visit. The pharmacy gate is silent now, and the laundromat is a bakery. The bus stop has a new glass shelter that does not knock in the wind. Other sounds have taken their places: a coffee grinder, an electric delivery bike, children calling to each other from the basketball court. I no longer try to make a complete portrait. I record a minute or two, say where I am, and let people talk if they want to.

Last month I played the old cassette for my niece. She asked why the stairs were so loud and why my grandmother laughed. I could answer the first question: the recorder had a poor microphone, and I held it close to the banister. For the second, I could only tell her about the afternoon, how my grandmother sat just behind the door while I went up and down. My niece asked to hear it again. This time she counted the steps aloud, and at the seventh, she started laughing too.

### The Umbrella Shop

The shop appeared whenever it rained hard enough to make people stop pretending they were dry. On clear days, the narrow storefront between the bakery and the locksmith was a brick wall. On wet days, there was a green door, a window crowded with umbrellas, and a hand-painted sign: **REPAIRS WHILE YOU WAIT, IF YOU CAN WAIT**.

Mara discovered it on a Tuesday when her umbrella turned inside out at the busiest crossing in the city. A bus passed, sending a sheet of water over her shoes. One spoke of the umbrella caught in her hair. She freed herself, saw the green door, and went in.

The room smelled of wet wool and tea. Umbrellas hung from the ceiling like folded bats. Behind a counter sat an old man in a yellow waistcoat, fitting a tiny brass hinge to a red handle.

“Can you fix this?” Mara asked.

“Probably,” he said. “What happened to it?”

“The wind.”

He looked at the broken spokes. “That’s what happened outside. What happened to it before?”

Mara nearly left. She had a meeting in twenty minutes, and her socks were wet. But the man had already set a towel on the counter for the puddle dripping from her umbrella.

“It belonged to my mother,” she said. “I found it in a cupboard after she died.”

The man nodded, as if she had finally told him the part he needed to know. He opened the umbrella with care. Blue cloth stretched over the frame, patterned with small white squares. Mara had never liked it much. Her mother had bought it at a station because she was always forgetting hers, and then, somehow, she had kept this one for twenty years.

“Sit down,” the man said. “There’s tea.”

Mara checked her phone. The meeting had been cancelled. She sat on a low stool while he removed the bent spoke with a pair of pliers. Rain tapped steadily on the window. From the bakery next door came the smell of cinnamon. For the first time that morning, she noticed she was cold.

“Why only open when it rains?” she asked.

“Not much demand otherwise.”

“But where does the shop go?”

“Nowhere,” he said. “People just don’t look for it.”

He worked for several minutes without speaking. Then he drew a strip of paper from beneath the umbrella’s handle. Mara leaned forward. It was no longer than her thumb, curled tight as a spring.

“Things collect in old umbrellas,” he said.

On the paper, in her mother’s slanting handwriting, were four words: *Mara likes the rain.*

She laughed once, surprised. “I did. When I was little, she’d let me walk home without a hood. We counted how many people ran for cover.”

“Who won?”

“The people, usually. We were slow.”

The man placed the note beside her tea. Mara wondered when her mother had written it. She could picture her at the kitchen table, perhaps waiting for the kettle, turning the umbrella’s handle in her hands. The picture was so easy to make that Mara almost mistook it for a memory.

The old man replaced the spoke and stitched a small tear near the tip. When he opened the umbrella again, its blue canopy stood round and even.

“What do I owe you?” Mara asked.

“Whatever it’s worth to keep using it.”

She found a few coins in her bag. He accepted them solemnly, then gave one back because, he said, she would need it for the bus.

Outside, the rain had softened. Mara walked past the crossing and on toward the river instead. She held the umbrella high enough to see the sky ahead of her. Once, at a traffic light, she caught herself counting the people who ran.

Over the following months she passed the bakery often. Sometimes the green door was there. Sometimes there was only brick. She never tried to decide whether the weather made the difference, or whether the old man had been right about people not looking.

One afternoon in November, rain drove sideways through the streets, and she found the door again. The old man was at his counter, mending a black umbrella with a wooden handle. He seemed unsurprised to see her.

“This one’s fine,” Mara said, lifting her mother’s umbrella. “I wondered if you needed help.”

He gave her a needle, a spool of thread, and an umbrella whose torn edge had been pinned together. Her first stitches were uneven. He made her take them out and try again. By closing time, she could sew a straight seam, and she had learned that a broken rib was called a rib even though it was made of metal.

She returned the next rainy Saturday, and the one after that. Customers told her what had happened outside: a door had caught the canopy, a child had used it as a sword, a gust had pulled it from someone’s hand. Sometimes they told her what had happened before. Mara learned to listen while she worked.

In spring, the old man let her repair an umbrella by herself. Its owner, a woman with paint on her cuffs, waited by the window and watched the rain. Mara replaced two ribs and tightened the runner. There was no paper hidden in its handle, no story beyond the woman’s account of getting caught in a gate. When Mara handed it back, the woman opened and closed it twice.

“Perfect,” she said, and went out smiling.

After she left, Mara put the tools away. The old man made tea, though it was nearly time to close. Through the window she could see people passing beneath bright canopies, each carrying a little patch of shelter through the grey afternoon. Then she saw a boy stop in front of the shop. He held a green umbrella with its fabric dragging behind him.

Mara went to open the door.

**The Last Bus to Bellwether**

The last bus to Bellwether arrived at 11:47 every night, except when it didn’t. Mara knew this because she had been its driver for seventeen years. She knew which corners flooded after rain, which windows rattled above thirty miles an hour, and which passengers wanted conversation even when they said they didn’t. On Thursdays, a man boarded with a violin case but never a violin. On Fridays, two sisters carrying groceries argued about recipes in a language Mara did not know. Every night, the bus emptied gradually, until only the sound of the engine kept her company.

Bellwether was the final stop: a shelter beside a shuttered post office, three miles beyond the last streetlight. Years ago, there had been a factory nearby. Now its windows were boarded and weeds grew through the loading dock. Mara still drove there because the timetable said to. Occasionally someone waited beneath the shelter’s roof, hands deep in their pockets, looking relieved at the sight of her headlights. That seemed reason enough to keep going.

One November evening, rain blurred the windshield so badly that the road appeared to dissolve a few feet ahead. Mara leaned forward and drove slowly. At Bellwether, she found a boy standing in the shelter with a cardboard box. He could not have been more than twelve. Water dripped from his hair onto the box, which he held carefully against his coat.

“You missed the bus,” Mara told him through the open door. “This one’s going out of service.”

“I know,” he said. “I just need to get to my grandmother’s.”

“Where does she live?”

He gave an address on Willow Street, halfway back along the route. Mara looked at the dark road behind her. Company rules were plain: passengers could not ride on an out-of-service bus. They were less plain about leaving a child alone beside an abandoned factory in freezing rain.

“Get in,” she said. “Watch your step.”

The boy sat in the front seat. Inside the box, something rustled.

“What have you got there?”

“A clock.”

Most clocks, Mara thought, did not rustle. At a red light, the boy opened the top just enough for a small gray bird to peer out. It had one bright eye and a patch of yellow feathers on its throat.

“That’s not a clock,” Mara said.

“It’s my grandmother’s clock bird. It flew out when the cage broke. She says it sings at six every morning, even if you cover the cage. I caught it by the factory, but then I missed the bus.”

Mara considered asking why his grandmother needed a bird to tell her the time. Instead, she asked whether it had a name.

“Tuesday.”

“Today’s Thursday.”

“He doesn’t know that.”

By the time they reached Willow Street, the rain had softened. A porch light burned at the address the boy had given. Before he stepped off the bus, he turned back and said, “She’ll be glad I found him. She can’t see the clock anymore.”

Mara watched him hurry up the path. An older woman opened the door and took his wet face between her hands before she noticed the box. The boy lifted its lid. Mara could not hear what the woman said, but she saw her shoulders drop with relief. Then the porch door closed, and the two of them were inside.

At the depot, Mara filled out her paperwork. She left the space marked *Reason for delay* blank for a while, then wrote: “Weather.” It was true, though it did not account for all six extra minutes. She parked the bus, turned off the engine, and sat listening to the ticks and pops of its cooling metal. She thought about how carefully the boy had carried the box. She wondered whether Tuesday would sing in the morning.

The next Thursday, the man with the violin case boarded at his usual stop. As Mara drove, he told her that he carried tools inside it. He repaired accordions, and the case was the only one long enough for some of his equipment. She had imagined all sorts of reasons for the missing violin, none of them close to the truth. A few stops later, the sisters climbed aboard with their groceries. When one of their bags split, Mara gave them a spare paper sack she kept under her seat. Their argument paused long enough for both of them to thank her.

On Friday, Mara left the depot with an empty cardboard box on the seat beside her. She had picked it up outside the grocery store because she needed somewhere to put the loose papers in her kitchen. By the time she reached Bellwether, she had forgotten it was there. No one waited at the shelter. The factory stood dark, and rainwater gleamed in the cracks of the road. She checked the timetable, pulled away at 11:47, and drove back through the quiet town.

On Saturday mornings, the library basement fills with objects that have stopped doing what they were made to do. Lamps arrive with dark bulbs and loose switches. Toasters arrive carrying the faint smell of their last successful breakfast. A woman once brought a music box in a shoebox padded with towels, as carefully as if she were transporting a bird. Above us, people return novels and argue quietly with the printer. Down here, among folding tables and extension cords, we try to persuade things to work again.

Our repair group began when Mara, who knows more about sewing machines than anyone I have met, put up a handwritten sign: **BROKEN? BRING IT BY.** She expected a few neighbors. Twelve people came the first week, some carrying appliances, others carrying tools, and several just curious. Four years later, we still meet twice a month. Nobody is in charge, though Mara knows where everything is and can make the room fall silent by asking who took her small screwdriver.

I came because of a radio. It was a squat brown one with a cracked dial, inherited from my grandfather. As a child, I had watched him tune it at the kitchen table, easing the needle through a storm of static until a voice emerged. He listened to baseball games, weather reports, and late-night conversations with strangers. After he died, the radio sat on my shelf. One winter, I plugged it in and got nothing—not even the soft pop it used to make when it woke up.

I carried it to the library in a grocery bag. Mara looked at the cloth-covered cord and told me, kindly but firmly, not to plug it in again. She introduced me to Dev, a retired electrician who had brought his own meter and a sandwich wrapped in wax paper. He showed me how to remove the back without breaking the brittle case. Inside was a miniature city of wires and dusty components. I had expected a single loose connection, something we could find and fix before lunch. Instead, Dev taught me how to look.

That is most of what happens in the basement. People come in hoping for a quick answer, and someone invites them to hold a flashlight or turn a screw. The work slows down. We ask when an object last worked and whether anything unusual happened before it failed. We look for scorch marks, frayed cords, worn teeth, and the tiny springs that leap out when a casing opens. We take photographs so we can remember how the pieces fit together. Sometimes the answer is simple. Often we have to admit that we do not know yet.

The radio took three Saturdays. A damaged cord was easy to identify, but replacing it did not bring back the sound. Dev and I tested one component after another while other repairs rose and fell around us. A child learned to patch a bicycle tube. Mara freed a jammed sewing machine and then spent an hour helping its owner thread it. Someone brought in a kettle with a handle too broken to make it safe to carry hot water. We could not repair that one. Its owner stayed anyway and helped sweep the floor.

On the third Saturday, Dev found a failed capacitor. He had suspected it earlier but wanted to show me how to rule out other faults. We replaced it, set the radio on the table, and kept our hands clear while he switched it on. The speaker crackled. Then came a burst of music, loud enough to make everyone turn. Dev grinned, though he had been warning me all morning that the repair might not work. We listened for a minute, and then I turned the dial slowly, searching through static the way my grandfather had.

I used to think a repair was valuable only if the object lasted afterward. By that measure, some mornings in the basement are failures. We cannot get parts for everything. Some devices are sealed so tightly that opening them does more damage. Once, after two hours of work, a blender ran for six seconds and stopped again. Its owner laughed, then looked disappointed, then helped us pack away the tools. I remembered his face later when I was deciding whether to throw out a lamp at home. I brought it in instead.

There is an economy to this work, though it rarely saves anyone much money. A new lamp can cost less than the time spent repairing an old one. What people save is harder to put on a receipt: the trouble of throwing something away, the worry that they should have known how to fix it, the distance between wanting to try and knowing where to begin. When a person leaves carrying an object that works, they usually carry a little more knowledge as well. When they leave without a repair, at least they know what went wrong.

I keep coming back for the workbench more than for the finished objects. At home, I can put a broken thing aside and forget it. In the basement, someone will ask what I have tried. Someone else will remember a similar problem. We disagree, borrow each other’s tools, lose screws, find them under chair legs, and make room for whoever walks in next. The room has taught me practical skills, but it has also made me less embarrassed to be a beginner. There are plenty of beginners there, including people who have been fixing things for decades.

My grandfather’s radio now lives in my kitchen. I turn it on while I make breakfast, though I still have to be careful with the dial; a slight movement can send the station drifting away. Some mornings I listen to the news. Some mornings I leave it between stations and hear only static while the kettle heats. I know that one day the radio may fail again. If it does, I will carry it back to the library, find an empty space at the table, and take off the back.

The first tomato on the roof was an accident.

Someone had left a paper cup full of potting soil beside the old television antenna, and a seed from someone else’s lunch had found its way in. By August, a vine hung over the cup’s rim, its leaves dusty and determined. It produced one green tomato, then a second. Nobody knew who had brought the cup upstairs. Everybody who saw it watered it.

Our building was not the sort of place people called a community. It had six floors, a stubborn elevator, and a lobby noticeboard devoted mostly to warnings. *Please stop leaving bicycles by the mailboxes.* *The washing machine is not a storage shelf.* We knew one another by noises: the man on three who practiced trumpet scales, the twins on five who raced down the hallway, the woman whose shoes clicked home after midnight. In the elevator we studied the numbers above the door.

The roof changed slowly. In September, Mrs. Alvarez from the second floor carried up a rectangular planter that no longer fit her windowsill. She filled it with mint, which spread until its scent followed anyone who brushed past. The trumpet player brought two folding chairs. One had a cracked seat and tilted dangerously to the left, but people kept sitting in it, careful to put their weight on the right. A bag of soil appeared by the stairwell door. Then a watering can.

No one proposed a plan. That may have been why the garden survived. Plans in our building usually meant meetings, and meetings meant arguments about money, noise, and who would be responsible when something went wrong. A tomato plant required a smaller decision. If its soil was dry, you gave it water. If the wind had knocked it over, you stood it up. By spring there were four planters, a bucket of scallions, and a handwritten sign asking visitors to keep the door from slamming.

I started going up after work because my apartment was hot. On the roof, the sun stayed an extra twenty minutes, and a person could watch it travel across the windows of the buildings opposite ours. At first I took a book and read. Later I found myself looking down into the street instead. From six floors up, traffic lost its urgency. Delivery cyclists waited at the light. A dog refused to cross until its owner lifted it over a puddle. The man at the fruit stand packed away his oranges one neat row at a time.

One evening I found the twins kneeling beside the tomato plant. It had grown again from seeds that had fallen into the soil, though its fruit was still weeks away. They were arguing about whether a worm could hear.

“Ask him,” one of them said when she noticed me.

I admitted I didn’t know. We looked it up on my phone. Worms have no ears, but they can sense vibrations through the ground. The twins tested this by tapping the planter with their fingers. I suggested they leave the worm to its work. They stopped at once and watched it disappear beneath the soil.

After that, people began to linger when they met on the roof. Conversation was easier when there was something to do with your hands. Mrs. Alvarez showed me how to pinch the tops from a basil plant so it would grow fuller. I learned that the trumpet player’s name was Simon and that he worked nights cleaning trains. He learned that I could sew, and asked whether the torn strap on his instrument case could be mended. We talked while I stitched it. He held the case steady and told me which trains were quietest at dawn.

The garden was not a cure for anything. The elevator still broke down twice that summer. Someone stole the better folding chair, and the basil developed pale spots we could not identify. A letter arrived from the property manager reminding us that the roof was not designed for “unauthorized horticultural activity.” We moved the heaviest planters against a wall and promised one another we would ask permission. For several weeks, nobody did. Then Mrs. Alvarez went to the office with photographs, a list of the containers and the name of the tenant willing to move them if necessary. They allowed us to keep them.

By late August, the tomato plant was taller than the twins. Its branches needed string to hold them upright. On Saturday mornings someone would climb up with coffee and find two or three others already there, comparing the fruit for signs of red. When the first ripe tomato finally appeared, Simon spotted it before anyone else. It was small and oddly shaped, with a split near the stem. We decided to pick it before the birds did. Mrs. Alvarez took it downstairs, cut it into eight thin pieces, and brought it back on a plate with a little salt.

I remember that tomato mostly for the trouble we took over it. We passed the plate around carefully so nobody lost a slice to the wind. The twins each swallowed theirs whole. I ate mine slowly, tasting salt and warm skin and a little sweetness. Across the street, the fruit seller was putting out his crates for the afternoon. Simon asked whether anyone had seen his missing chair. Nobody had. Mrs. Alvarez said she had one in her kitchen that she could bring up next time. Then she asked who was going to water the plants on Sunday.

On the last Tuesday of every month, Mara opened the library after midnight.

The town knew about its books. Children borrowed atlases and returned them with pressed leaves inside. Retired teachers argued over the history shelves. In December, someone always tied a red scarf around the stone lion by the steps. What the town did not know was that the library also kept sounds, and that midnight was the only hour when they could be borrowed.

They lived in a cabinet behind the circulation desk, sealed in small glass jars. Each jar carried a handwritten label: **Rain on a tin roof, 1948.** **A brother laughing with his mouth full.** **The first note of a song forgotten by everyone who sang it.**

Mara had inherited the cabinet with the job. Her predecessor, Mr. Vale, had explained it on his final evening while showing her how to reset the alarm.

“People lose things,” he said. “Sometimes they don’t know what they’ve lost.”

He lifted a jar marked **Kitchen, before the fire** and loosened its lid. For an instant Mara heard cutlery touching plates, a woman asking someone to pass the salt, and a chair scraping across a floor. Then Mr. Vale sealed it. The fluorescent lights hummed back into place.

“Who brings them here?” Mara asked.

“Mostly,” he said, “they find their own way.”

For three years she told no one. She dusted the jars, copied fading labels, and opened the library once a month for whoever appeared at the door. There were never many visitors. A man came to hear the bark of a dog he had loved as a boy. A woman borrowed the sound of a train approaching her hometown, although the station had been demolished forty years earlier. They sat at the reading tables with their jars open before them, listening until the sounds faded. By morning, each jar was full again.

Mara did not ask why this was possible. She had asked enough questions of ordinary life to know that answers could make a thing smaller.

One Tuesday in October, a boy arrived carrying a bicycle helmet under his arm. He was perhaps twelve, with wet cuffs and a solemn expression.

“I’m looking for a sound,” he said.

“Do you know its name?”

“No.” He glanced toward the cabinet. “It happened when I was little. My dad used to make it.”

Mara brought out the drawer labeled **Homes**. The boy listened to a kettle coming to a boil, footsteps on a staircase, and someone humming tunelessly over a sink. He shook his head at each one. She opened **Voices**, then **Gardens and Streets**. The clock struck one, then two.

“Tell me what you remember,” Mara said.

The boy turned his helmet in his hands. “I remember sitting on the floor. There was light on the carpet, in squares. He’d come home, and then I’d hear it. I’d get up because I knew he was going to pick me up.”

“His voice?”

“I don’t think so.” The boy frowned. “Maybe keys?”

They found seventeen jars of keys. Keys dropped into bowls, keys rattled in locks, keys searched for at the bottoms of bags. None was right. At half past two, the boy looked embarrassed and said he should go.

Mara followed him to the door. As he pushed it open, the brass plate at its base gave a low, familiar shiver.

The boy stopped.

“That,” he said.

It was the sound of a door closing gently, not quite catching, then closing once more with a firmer push. His father must have entered their home that way every evening. The boy had remembered the squares of light and the promise of being lifted, but not the door between them.

They went back to the cabinet. Mara searched until she found a jar in the lowest drawer: **Someone coming home, several times**. Inside were doors of many kinds. The third was his. He held the jar close and listened to the soft double click again.

Before he left, he asked, “Will I remember it now?”

“For a while,” Mara said. “Come back if you need to hear it.”

After he rode away, she remained at the desk. Mr. Vale had said that the sounds found their own way to the library, but Mara knew each jar had once belonged somewhere else. She wondered whether the boy’s father could still make that sound, or whether the door itself was gone.

The next morning, while returning books to their shelves, she noticed a jar she had never seen before. It stood beside the dictionaries, small and cloudy, with no label. Mara carried it to the desk and waited until the last patron had left. Then she opened it.

At first she heard nothing. She leaned closer. A page turned. Somewhere nearby, a pencil tapped twice against wood. A woman drew a breath as if she meant to speak, changed her mind, and went on reading.

Mara knew the room. She knew the pencil, too; it was the one she kept beside the returns ledger. The sound was from this library, from some quiet afternoon she could not identify.

She listened until the jar emptied. There had been no visitor that day, no reunion or farewell. Someone had sat at a table and read. Mara had worked behind the desk. Neither of them had known the moment would be kept.

She found a pen and wrote on the label: **A person feeling at home in the library.**

That night she left the jar beside the returns ledger. In the morning it was full again.

### The Bench at the End of the Route

At the end of the number six bus route stood a bench painted the yellow of old butter. It faced an empty lot, a chain-link fence, and, beyond them, the backs of three warehouses. People waiting there had little to look at. This was why Mara liked it.

She drove the first bus of the morning. At 5:42, she pulled up beside the bench and opened the doors for whoever had been awake long enough to meet her. Usually it was Mr. Vale, who cleaned a bakery across town, and a nursing student named Imani, who slept through most of the ride with her head against the window. Sometimes there was nobody, and Mara waited anyway. The schedule allowed forty seconds.

One Tuesday in October, she found a paper cup on the bench. Inside it was a sunflower seedling, no taller than her thumb. Someone had filled the cup with soil and written, in careful block letters, **TAKE ME SOMEWHERE SUNNY**.

Mara could not take it. The dashboard was already crowded with the things drivers were permitted to keep: a route card, a radio, a flashlight, and a photograph of her brother. She left the seedling where it was and went to work.

The next morning, the cup was still there. Someone had moved it to the far end of the bench, where the first sunlight reached it. On Thursday there were two cups. By Monday, five.

At the depot, Mara mentioned them to another driver. “Sounds like a school project,” he said. “Or somebody clearing out a windowsill.”

Perhaps. But each morning the cups had changed places, following the narrow strip of sun that fell between the warehouses. By the second week, Mara began arriving a minute early to see where they had been put.

Then the weather turned. Wind came in hard from the river and knocked over the smallest cup. Mara stepped off the bus and set it upright. She pressed the loose soil back around its stem with one finger. Mr. Vale watched from the open door.

“They’ll need more than that,” he said.

“I know.”

He took a folded grocery bag from his coat and placed it around the cups as a windbreak. Mara thanked him, and they left the seedlings on the bench.

By November, people had begun adding things. There was a chipped blue saucer under one cup to catch water, a row of smooth stones to hold the bag down, and, once, a note offering extra gloves to anyone who needed them. Imani told Mara she had seen a woman watering the plants at night from a bottle carried in her bicycle basket. Neither of them knew who had brought the seedlings.

The city announced that the bench would be removed in December. A notice had been tied to one of its slats with orange string: the stop was being moved two blocks east to improve traffic flow. The new stop had a shelter and a digital sign. There was no reason to keep the old bench.

Mara read the notice during her forty seconds. The new stop would be better for her passengers in the rain. She could picture the empty lot after the bench was gone: five paper cups on the pavement, if they survived that long.

On her day off, she walked to the lot. In daylight, without the bus idling at the curb, it felt quieter and less remote. Someone had written names on the cups—*Sol*, *Big One*, *Maybe Marigold*—though they were all sunflowers. Mara carried them across the street to a patch of ground outside the fence, where weeds had found room to grow. She set the cups down and noticed that their roots had pushed through the paper.

A bicycle bell sounded behind her. A woman in a green raincoat stopped at the curb, one foot on the ground and a water bottle in her hand.

“I was wondering who kept moving them,” the woman said.

“I only righted one,” Mara replied. “And moved these just now.”

The woman looked at the cups. “I started with one. I had too many seeds.”

“You could have put it somewhere warmer.”

“I did.” She nodded toward the bench. “There’s a bakery cleaner who sits here. He told me he’d look after it until someone took it home.”

They stood for a moment, considering the evidence of everyone else who had done a little more than that.

The woman was called Elise. She lived above a laundromat on the other side of the lot. She knew the fence belonged to the city, but not whether the strip outside it belonged to the city too. Mara knew someone who might be able to find out: a dispatcher whose wife worked in the parks office. It was a small lead, and she offered it.

Over the following weeks, the stop moved, the shelter opened, and the old bench disappeared. The buses no longer came down that street. Mara passed it once in her car and saw that the cups had been replaced by a wooden box filled with soil. It stood on the strip outside the fence, with a laminated notice from the parks office attached to one side. Above the box, the warehouses blocked most of the winter sun.

In March, Elise sent Mara a photograph. Tiny green shoots had appeared in the box. Someone had set the chipped blue saucer beside it, filled with water for birds. Mara showed the picture to Mr. Vale when he boarded at the new stop. He studied it carefully before handing back her phone.

“Those weren’t all sunflowers,” he said, pointing to a corner of the box. “Somebody’s planted peas.”

When her shift ended, Mara took the number six home. She sat behind the driver and watched the familiar streets pass without having to turn onto any of them. At her stop, she thanked him, stepped down, and walked the remaining blocks in the afternoon sun.

At the bottom of some medieval manuscript pages, just outside the main text, you can find a word that seems to have wandered off on its own. It is often the first word of the next section.

This is a **catchword**. Manuscripts were made in small groups of folded leaves, called gatherings, which had to be assembled in the right order before binding. A scribe could write the next gathering’s opening word at the end of the current one, giving the binder a simple check: if the words matched, the sequence was right.

Catchwords are easy to overlook because they were never meant to be part of the text a reader followed. Some disappeared when a book was rebound and its pages trimmed. Others survived in the margins, occasionally decorated with a flourish.

I like them because they make a manuscript feel less like an ancient, finished object and more like a thing people were actively making. That stray word is a small message between workers, still sitting there centuries after its job was done.

No one knew what it opened.

Every few months, someone would find it and hold it up to the light. It was too small for the front door, too old for a bicycle lock. “We should throw this out,” they’d say, and then put it back, just in case.

On the morning the sea returned the doors, Mara was sweeping sand from the library steps.

There were seven of them, upright in the surf, turning gently as if deciding whether to come ashore. One was painted yellow. One had a brass knocker shaped like a fox. The others had swollen beyond recognition, their handles bitten dull by salt.

By noon, everyone in town had come to look. The mayor suggested a storm had torn them from houses farther down the coast. The fishermen said there had been no storm. Old Ivo, who remembered things no one else did, touched the yellow door and began to cry.

“It belonged to the bakery,” he said.

Mara knew the bakery. Or rather, she knew the empty lot beside the post office, which people still called the bakery though no building had stood there in her lifetime.

That evening, she went home and asked her mother about it.

“There was a bakery,” her mother said, peeling an orange in one long ribbon. “Ivo bought his bread there every morning.”

“Why did they knock it down?”

Her mother set the orange on the table. “They didn’t.”

This was the first strange thing about the doors: no one could agree on what had happened to the buildings they came from. Some remembered fires. Others recalled demolition, or a slow collapse into the sea. Mara’s mother insisted the bakery had simply been gone one morning, leaving flour on the pavement and a warm smell in the air.

The second strange thing was that each door, when placed in a wall, opened somewhere.

The town learned this by accident. Someone leaned the fox-knocker door against the harbor warehouse. At dusk, the warehouse owner pulled it aside to make room for a cart, and the door swung inward. Behind it was a narrow staircase carpeted in blue. His daughter climbed three steps before he caught her sleeve.

She said she could hear music above them.

By morning, a crowd had gathered. The mayor ordered the door nailed shut, but the nails bent. He ordered it burned, but the wood would not catch. Finally he appointed a committee, and the committee asked Mara to keep the doors in the library, where there were locks, dry floors, and a person accustomed to telling people not to touch things.

For six days she refused to open one.

She listened instead. Through the yellow door came the faint clatter of pans. Through the fox-knocker door, a violin played the same four notes, stopped, and began again. A white door with three panels gave off the scent of rain on hot stone.

On the seventh day, Mara found a note slipped beneath the smallest door. It was no bigger than a cupboard, painted green, and had no handle.

The note read: **You can ask.**

She sat on the library floor for a long time. Then she said, “What’s behind you?”

The green door swung open.

Beyond it was a kitchen Mara had not seen since she was nine. A blue cup stood upside down beside the sink. There were lemon seeds drying on a windowsill. Her father sat at the table, bent over a radio with its back removed.

He looked up.

Mara shut the door so hard the glass in the library windows trembled.

For the rest of the day, she checked books out with shaking hands. Her father had died twenty-three years earlier. She remembered the hospital, the breath that seemed to leave him without sound, the way her mother had washed the blue cup when they came home because washing something was possible.

After closing, Mara returned to the green door.

“You can ask,” she read aloud.

She thought of asking whether he was real. She thought of asking if he had waited there all those years. Instead she asked, “What are you?”

From the other side came a click. The radio had found a station. Her father’s voice, younger than she remembered, said, “I don’t know how to fix this.”

Mara put her palm against the wood.

By winter, the town had learned to live with the doors. The mayor forbade anyone from going through them, a rule most people obeyed for reasons of their own. Ivo visited the yellow one every Thursday and sat outside it with a paper bag in his lap. The warehouse owner’s daughter practiced her violin by the fox-knocker door until, one afternoon, the unseen player followed her into a new tune.

People brought chairs. They brought questions. Sometimes a door opened. More often it remained closed, offering only a sound or a smell, a draft of air from a room that could not be there.

Mara stopped trying to decide what any of it meant.

In spring, her mother came to the library carrying a small jar of orange marmalade.

“I made too much,” she said.

They sat beside the green door. Mara told her what she had seen, and her mother did not interrupt. When Mara finished, her mother looked at the jar in her hands.

“He never could fix that radio,” she said. “He took it apart every Sunday. I think he liked seeing what was inside.”

“Do you want me to ask it to open?”

Her mother considered this. From behind the door came the scrape of a chair. For one breath, Mara was nine again, waiting for her father to call her into the kitchen and show her a screw so small it could vanish in the lines of her hand.

“No,” her mother said at last. She unscrewed the jar and offered Mara a spoonful.

It ran in a neat blue line behind the library, past the school, and out through the fields to the east. On the ground, that route held a parking lot, three streets, and the back wall of a supermarket.

When I was little, I asked my father where the river had gone.

“Under us,” he said. “They put it in a pipe.”

“Why?”

He considered this. “It was in the way.”

Years later, when I came home to clear out his house, I found a hand-drawn map folded into the back of his desk. He had marked the river’s course in pencil. Alongside it were dates and brief notes:

*April 6: Heard it beneath the library steps.*

*June 18: Rain. Water over the curb at Willow Street.*

*October 2: Sounded strong today.*

On the last page, in writing shakier than the rest, he had drawn an X behind the supermarket. Beside it he wrote: *Best place to listen.*

I had never known him to go behind the supermarket. I had barely known him to make notes about anything.

That evening I walked there. Delivery doors lined the wall, and a security light clicked on as I approached. Between two dumpsters, a drain sat low in the pavement.

At first I heard traffic and a refrigerator motor. Then, underneath both, water.

It wasn’t loud. I had to crouch to hear it properly. It rushed and caught against something, then rushed on. I stayed until my legs cramped.

The next morning I took my father’s map to the library. The woman at the desk remembered him.

“He used to come in when it rained,” she said. “He’d stand on the steps for a while.”

I told her about the drain. She came with me on her lunch break. On the way, she pointed to a dip in the road where water collected after storms. We stopped there and heard the river through a manhole cover.

People began taking walks with the map. Most places were too noisy, or the river was too deep to hear. Behind the supermarket, you could usually catch it.

“Can you hear it?” he asked.

She nodded. Then she moved aside so he could listen too.

The first key arrived on a Tuesday, tucked inside a mussel shell.

Mara found it while collecting driftwood below the seawall. It was brass, green around the teeth, with a paper label tied to it in ordinary kitchen string. The label said **NUMBER 14**.

There had not been a Number 14 on Gull Street since the storm of ’83. Mara knew because she lived at Number 12, and because her mother had told the story so often: how the house next door had gone into the water whole, curtains in the windows, yellow kettle still on the stove.

By Thursday, the beach was covered in keys.

They lay among the bladderwrack and bottle caps, silver and brass and black iron. Some had labels. **BACK DOOR.** **SHED.** **DON’T LOSE THIS ONE.** Some were attached to rings with faded plastic dolphins. Others had no markings at all.

People came down with buckets. The mayor asked everyone to take only keys they recognized, which was a sensible request for about an hour. Then Mr. Vale found the key to his first car, sold forty years earlier, and opened its door on an empty patch of road.

The car was there. It smelled of hot vinyl and the peppermint sweets his wife used to keep in the glove box. He sat inside until evening. When he got out, there was only road again.

After that, nobody listened to the mayor.

Mara didn’t go back to the beach. She kept Number 14 on the kitchen table, where she could see it while she washed dishes. Her mother had lived long enough to forget the storm but not long enough to forget the house. In her final year she would sometimes ask Mara to go next door and fetch the yellow kettle.

On Saturday morning, Mara put the key in her coat pocket and walked down Gull Street.

Between Number 12 and Number 16 stood the familiar narrow strip of grass. She had crossed it thousands of times to cut through to the harbor. Now there was a gate.

It was plain wood, painted blue. Beyond it stood a house with lace curtains and a front step worn hollow in the middle. Mara could see the kitchen through the window. The kettle was on the stove.

She fitted the key into the front door. Inside, the air was cold and smelled faintly of damp plaster. A child’s red mitten lay on the stairs.

Mara stopped. She had expected the house to be empty, or to contain a younger version of her mother folding towels. Instead she heard footsteps overhead.

“Hello?” she called.

The footsteps stopped.

A woman came down the stairs carrying a laundry basket. She was about Mara’s age, with wet hair and a pencil behind one ear. She looked at Mara, then at the open door.

“You found the key,” she said.

Mara gripped the knob. “Who are you?”

“Anwen. I live here.”

“The house washed away.”

“I know.” Anwen set down the basket. “I was in it.”

Neither of them spoke for a moment. Outside, a gull cried over the harbor.

Anwen told Mara what she could remember. On the night of the storm she had been eight. Her father woke her and her brother and told them to get their shoes. Water was coming under the front door. He went upstairs for their mother. Then the house lurched, and Anwen found herself in the hallway alone. The water had gone. So had everyone else.

She had grown up in the house, though she couldn’t say how. Food appeared in the pantry; the seasons changed beyond the windows. She could see Gull Street, but until this morning, whenever she opened the front door, she found only the kitchen on the other side.

“My brother’s mitten,” she said, noticing Mara glance at the stairs. “I keep meaning to put it away.”

Mara thought of the people digging through the sand with buckets. She thought of Mr. Vale in his car.

“Do you want to come out?” she asked.

Anwen looked past her at the strip of sun on the road. “Yes.”

They walked to the gate together. Anwen put one hand on it, then let go. She went back inside for her coat, leaving Mara to wait on the step.

By the time she returned, the house had begun to make small settling noises. A crack ran down the kitchen window. Mara held the gate while Anwen crossed the grass. Behind them came a long, low sound, like a boat scraping over stones.

When they turned, there was no house. The gate stood by itself between Numbers 12 and 16.

Anwen stared at the empty space. Mara didn’t know what to say to her. She took off her own coat and offered it; Anwen was shivering despite the sun.

They went to Mara’s kitchen. Anwen sat at the table and held the brass key while Mara made tea. She asked what year it was, and whether there was a telephone she could use.

On Monday, Mara went back to the beach. Most of the keys were gone. People had taken them home in jars and pockets, and the tide had covered the rest. Near the seawall she found one small iron key with no label. She left it where it lay.

At Number 12, Anwen was waiting by the window. She had borrowed Mara’s pencil to write down the names she still remembered. There were six on the page so far. Mara put the kettle on, and they went through the telephone book together.

The last public phone in Bellwether stood outside the closed pharmacy, under a green metal hood. It took coins, though nobody knew where the coins went. The pharmacy had become a place to store broken chairs, and the town council had voted twice to remove the phone. Both times, the contractor arrived to find a car parked across the pavement.

“I can smell it from upstairs,” the woman said. “Would you check?”

Then the line went dead.

Mara put down the receiver. Across the road, the former boardinghouse had been empty for years. Its windows were boarded and its front steps buried in weeds. A notice on the fence said it would be pulled down that Friday.

She told herself the call was a prank. Still, she crossed the road and stood by the fence. At the back of the building, a narrow window had been left uncovered. Through it she could see a kitchen full of dust. In the corner sat an old gas stove.

The fire crew found a leaking pipe beneath the floor. They shut off the gas and thanked Mara for calling. When she told the captain about the woman, he asked whether she had seen anyone enter the building.

“No,” Mara said. “She was on the phone.”

The captain glanced toward the pavement. Mara let him think she meant a mobile.

After that, she took the long way home each evening.

For a week the phone was silent. Then it rang while she was passing with a bag of oranges.

A man asked if the ferry had come in. Mara told him there had been no ferry since the new bridge opened. He said, “Ah,” with such disappointment that she wished she had lied.

A child called from the cinema on Quarry Street and asked when the lights would come back. The cinema had burned down before Mara was born. She found a photograph of it at the library: red seats, a painted ceiling, a sign outside advertising a film nobody remembered.

Every caller seemed to be in a place that was gone, or nearly gone. Mara wrote their words in a notebook. She tried asking their names, but most spoke as if she should already know them. Sometimes the line broke before she could say anything at all.

In November, the council announced that the library would close for repairs. Rain had got into the roof. The upper floor smelled of wet plaster, and a section of ceiling had bowed above the local-history shelves. Mara spent her days moving books into boxes and her evenings under the green hood, hoping the phone would ring.

It did, three nights before the closure.

She heard water first, then a scraping noise.

“Which part of the library are you in?” she asked.

Someone breathed close to the mouthpiece.

“The door won’t open,” a boy said.

Mara gripped the receiver. “What door?”

“The little one behind the map.”

There was only one large map in the library, fixed to the wall of the upstairs reading room. Mara had worked there for eleven years and had never known of a door behind it. She asked the boy his name, but the water grew louder and the call ended.

At opening time the next morning, Mara went upstairs with a screwdriver. The map showed Bellwether as it had been seventy years ago, when the river still bent around the old market. Its wooden frame was screwed into the wall. She removed it and found a narrow door, painted over so many times its edges had nearly disappeared.

Inside was a cupboard containing three rolled banners, a broken globe and a stack of newspapers. There was no boy. Water ran down the back wall in a thin, steady line.

Mara called the building manager. By noon, a plumber had found a split pipe above the cupboard. He said it was lucky she had noticed: another day or two, and the ceiling below might have come down. Then he looked at the open cupboard.

“What were you after in there?”

Mara considered telling him. “Old newspapers,” she said.

The council closed the library early and moved the repairs forward. No one was hurt. Mara checked the cupboard before she left. She could hear the plumber working overhead, but there was no water on the floor.

That evening she waited by the phone until the streetlights came on. When it finally rang, she answered before the second bell.

For a moment there was only static. Then the boy said, “It’s open.”

“Are you all right?”

“I think so.” He sounded out of breath. Behind him, Mara heard footsteps and a grown-up calling for someone named Daniel.

“Go to them,” she said.

He did not answer. The receiver filled with a dull hum, and Mara hung it up.

She never found a record of Daniel in the library files. Perhaps he had been there during another leak, years before. Perhaps the phone had reached a day that would no longer happen. Mara kept both possibilities in her notebook without choosing between them.

Winter came. The contractor removed the pharmacy sign and cleared the broken chairs. One morning he put orange cones around the public phone.

Mara asked when it was going.

“Thursday,” he said. “If the truck can get near it.”

On Thursday, she walked to work before dawn. The street was empty, and the hood shone with frost. She stood beside it for a while, listening. Then she took her keys from her pocket, crossed to the library and brought back the small sign she had made the night before.

She tied it to the phone with string.

**If it rings, please answer.**

By nine o’clock, a car was parked across the pavement. Mara did not recognize it.

The first thing the rain returned was a brass key.

It landed in Mara’s coffee with a small, decisive plink. She fished it out, wiped it on her sleeve, and recognized the green thread tied through its bow. It was the key to her childhood bicycle, lost twenty-three years ago somewhere between her parents’ house and the quarry.

Outside, the gutters were filling with teaspoons.

By noon, the city had stopped pretending this was normal. People stood under awnings holding up earrings, chess pieces, foreign coins. A dentist found a patient’s gold crown in his sleeve. Someone’s wedding ring struck a bus windshield hard enough to crack it.

The mayor asked everyone to stay indoors. Nobody listened.

Mara worked at the municipal lost property office. She had spent eleven years telling people that a blue scarf, a blue umbrella, or a blue backpack was not distinctive enough to locate without further information. Now she watched her desk disappear beneath the contents of a thousand forgotten pockets.

On the second day, the rain brought paper. Ticket stubs stuck to windows. Grocery lists washed along the curbs. A little boy arrived carrying a drawing of a yellow dog and announced that he had made it when he was four, before he knew dogs could be brown.

“Are you giving it to us?” Mara asked.

“No,” he said. “I’m showing you.”

He held it up once more, then tucked it safely inside his coat.

Mara began looking for her father’s notebook.

He had carried a small red notebook everywhere, filling it with things he intended to remember: the name of a waitress who had been kind, which stair on the porch creaked, how long to boil an egg for Mara, who liked the yolk almost set. He lost it during the last summer of his life. By then, forgetting frightened him. They searched the house together, opening drawers he had already opened and checking the pockets of coats he had not worn in years.

“It will turn up,” Mara had told him.

He had looked at her with the patient skepticism of someone who had heard that too often.

Now she searched the streets after work. She wore a helmet against falling cutlery and carried a laundry basket lined with towels. She found three notebooks, none red. She returned a photograph to a woman who pressed it to her chest without looking at it. She found the clasp from a necklace she had broken as a girl, and could not remember the necklace.

By the fourth day, the city smelled of wet cardboard and old pennies. Volunteers sorted the heavier objects beneath tarpaulins. The lost property office extended its hours. People who had not spoken in years met over shared claims: a kite made by two brothers, a set of keys from an apartment neither lived in anymore.

Then the rain began to thin.

Mara stood beneath the awning of the closed bakery, watching it fall. A man beside her held a single leather glove. He kept turning it over.

“Yours?” she asked.

“My wife’s.” He smiled, though his eyes were red. “She hated these gloves. I bought them for her.”

“Will you keep it?”

“I haven’t decided.”

Mara looked out at the street. A bottle cap rolled slowly toward the drain. Somewhere, beneath all this weather, her father’s notebook might be lying open to a page about eggs. Or it might not be there at all. He had lost other things that summer: the way home from the shops, the word for kettle, eventually the knowledge that she was his daughter. None of those had fallen from the sky.

She thought of their last search for the notebook. He had sat on the porch while she checked the kitchen again. When she came out empty-handed, he had moved over to make room for her. They had watched a blackbird pull a worm from the lawn, both of them hoping it would get away.

The man stepped into the rain. Mara waited until he had crossed, then went back to work.

At closing time, a woman brought in a child’s rubber boot. She had found it in the road and thought its owner might come looking. Mara set it on the shelf beside the umbrellas. It was yellow, with a faded blue whale on the heel. She wrote down where it had been found.

In the morning, the rain had stopped. People came to collect what they could. A few stayed to help sort the rest. By evening, Mara could see her desk again, though the shelves behind it were full.

Before locking up, she took the brass key from her drawer. The bicycle was long gone. She slipped the key onto her own keyring anyway, then turned out the light.

On the morning the ocean disappeared, Mara was late for work.

She noticed the absence from the bus window. Beyond the row of beachfront hotels lay a wide basin of dark sand, crossed by tire tracks, littered with shells. At the far edge, where the horizon should have been, stood a wall of fog.

The other passengers had their phones out. Mara took a picture too, then remembered that her mother would not be able to see it.

At the aquarium, the seals were barking. Their pool was full; the pumps worked; all the small captive seas remained where they belonged. Mara changed into her blue shirt and began her rounds, feeding the fish that needed feeding and writing down the temperature of each tank.

At eleven, her supervisor gathered everyone in the break room. Nobody knew where the ocean had gone. The coast guard had sent boats across the sand and lost radio contact. For now, the aquarium would stay open. Admission was free.

By noon, people were lined up around the block. They came to look at water, Mara supposed. She found them standing in front of the biggest tank, watching a shark turn slowly through its accustomed blue. Nobody pointed at it. A little boy pressed his palm to the glass and kept it there until his father pulled him away.

Mara’s mother called during lunch.

“Have you seen it?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“What does the bottom look like?”

“Like a beach that forgot where to stop.”

Her mother laughed, then coughed. Mara listened to her catch her breath. Since the diagnosis, she had grown skilled at listening without asking if everything was all right.

“I wish I could get down there,” her mother said.

“You’re not missing much.”

“That’s never stopped me.”

After work, Mara drove to her mother’s apartment. She found her sitting by the window in her coat, shoes tied, handbag on her lap.

“I could have picked you up tomorrow,” Mara said.

“I know.”

The traffic toward the shore was motionless, so Mara took the back streets. Her mother supplied directions to a beach Mara had never heard of, one where she had gone as a girl. The road ended at a chain-link fence, and beyond it the ocean floor sloped away into fog.

People had brought flashlights. Their beams searched the sand and lit up bottles, a bicycle frame, the white ribs of a small wreck. Farther out, people wandered where no one had ever walked. A man was calling for everyone to turn back. He sounded far away.

Mara helped her mother through a gap in the fence. They crossed the hard, rippled ground slowly. After a while her mother stopped and bent to pick something up: a green glass marble, cloudy with scratches.

“I lost one here,” she said.

“You did?”

“Probably not this one.”

She put it in her pocket anyway. They stood together while the sky darkened. Without the water, the shore had lost its familiar edge. Mara could not tell how far they had come or where it would be safe to stop.

Her mother slipped her hand into Mara’s. “We should go back,” she said.

Mara turned on her flashlight. As they made their way toward the fence, she kept looking over her shoulder, expecting the fog to move. It did not. The sand held the marks of their shoes all the way home.

The city kept its lost minutes in a basement beneath the public library.

This was not advertised. The library’s signs directed visitors to Fiction, Local History, and the restrooms. To find the basement, you had to ask the woman at the returns desk what time it was. If she told you the time, you were not ready. If she said, “Which time?” she would hand you a brass key.

I found out on a Tuesday after missing a train.

The train had pulled away while I stood on the platform reading a message from my mother. It said, *Call when you have a minute.* I had not called her in eleven months. I read the message twice, put my phone away, and looked up at the empty tracks.

At the library, the woman at the desk said, “Which time?” before I had asked anything.

Downstairs, the room was bright and crowded with filing cabinets. A man in a green cardigan sat behind a counter, polishing a teaspoon.

“I lost seven minutes,” I told him.

“People usually start with a story.”

“I missed a train.”

He set down the spoon. “You can look for them, if you like.”

He gave me a drawer number. Inside were hundreds of narrow envelopes, each labeled with a date and a location: a grocery queue, a stairwell, the kitchen of an apartment I had left years ago. I opened the envelope marked *Tuesday, station platform*. It held a strip of pale paper. On it was written: *Seven minutes spent imagining the phone call instead of making it.*

“That doesn’t seem lost,” I said.

The man looked up from his spoon. “No?”

I went back to the drawer. I had been late for work because I could not decide which shirt to wear. I had stood beside my father’s hospital bed, trying to remember the name of a bird outside the window. I had sat in my car after a party until the streetlights went off. Each envelope held a minute I could describe but had never quite occupied.

At the bottom was one labeled *Sunday, my mother’s house*. I knew the date. I had gone to tell her I was moving across the country. She was making soup, cutting carrots into coins. We spoke about boxes and rent and the weather there. I stayed for an hour, then left.

The envelope was heavy. I slid out the paper.

*Fourteen minutes available while the soup simmered. Neither person mentioned the move.*

“I want those back,” I said.

The man folded his hands. “What would you do with them?”

“I’d tell her why I was going.”

He waited.

“I’d ask her if she was angry.”

He waited a little longer, but I had no more words.

From somewhere among the cabinets came the ticking of many small clocks, each one a little out of step with the others. The man placed the teaspoon in a drawer.

“Can I have them?” I asked.

“You can take the envelope.”

I put it in my coat pocket. By then I had missed the next train, too.

Outside, rain had begun in the uncertain way it sometimes does, a few drops spaced so far apart they seemed unrelated. I walked to the station slowly. At a crossing, I took out my phone and called my mother.

She answered on the fourth ring. There were voices behind her and the clatter of dishes.

“Hello,” I said.

“Oh,” she said, with a pleased surprise she made no effort to hide. “Is everything all right?”

“Yes. I missed my train.”

“Where are you?”

“Still here.”

A bus went by, throwing water over the curb. I moved back under the awning of a closed shop. My mother asked when the next train was. I said I didn’t know. She told me she had bought a little lamp for the table by her bed. She had seen it in a window for weeks and gone in for it that morning.

“What color?” I asked.

“Yellow glass. It makes the room look warm even when it’s cold.”

We spoke until I reached the station. I told her about the rain. She told me the soup she was making had too much salt. When she asked if I remembered the old kitchen, I said yes, and told her about the day I left.

“I remember,” she said.

“I wanted to say more.”

“I thought you might.”

The announcement for my train sounded overhead. I could hear her washing something at the sink.

“Were you angry with me?” I asked.

“For moving? No.” She paused. “I was angry that you thought you had to give me good reasons. I knew you wanted to go.”

I had not known she knew. I stood against a pillar while people moved around me.

“I was afraid you’d ask me to stay,” I said.

“I nearly did.”

We heard the train arrive through the phone, brakes squealing on the rails. My mother said, “You’ll miss that one as well.”

“I might.”

“Get on it,” she said. “Call me when you’re home.”

I boarded just before the doors closed. From my pocket I took the envelope, softened now by the rain. The paper inside still described fourteen minutes in her kitchen. Nothing had been crossed out or corrected. I put it away and found a seat by the window.

We passed the library as the train left the station. Its upstairs windows were lit; from here, the basement was invisible. I could see the returns desk for a moment, and a woman leaning across it to speak to the librarian. Then the train curved, and the building disappeared behind the others.

My phone was still warm in my hand.

The streetlamp outside our building went dark every night at 2:17.

It stayed dark for forty-three seconds. I knew because I had counted, once, during a winter when sleep seemed like something other people had invented. The light would vanish, and the room would become a room again instead of a pale copy of the street. Then it would return with a small electrical click.

I thought I was the only person awake for it until Mrs. Alvarez from the third floor mentioned it in the lift.

“That’s when I turn my bread,” she said.

I asked what she meant.

“The lamp goes out. I turn the dough. It comes back on, I cover the bowl.”

Mrs. Alvarez used to run a bakery. Now she baked for her grandchildren and, occasionally, for people who looked as if they had forgotten to eat.

After that, I began noticing things. At 2:17, a window across the courtyard opened and a man leaned out to water the basil on his sill. On Thursdays, someone in the building opposite carried a cello case down the stairs just as the light returned. Sometimes I saw a little square of blue from the top-floor kitchen, where a teenager apparently studied by the glow of a laptop until the lamp blinked her into darkness.

We were not keeping the same hours. We were only passing through one another’s nights.

In March, a notice appeared on the lamp post. The council would be replacing faulty equipment along the entire road. New lamps, brighter and more efficient, would be installed by the end of the month.

I read the notice on my way to work and forgot about it until Mrs. Alvarez stopped me that evening.

“They’re fixing it,” she said.

“It is broken.”

“I know.”

She held a paper bag against her coat. Inside were two rolls, still warm. She gave me one and went upstairs.

The replacement crew arrived on a Monday. They wore orange jackets and had a truck with a lift on the back. By noon the old lamp was gone. The new one was slim and white, with a flat head that looked down at the pavement as if it disapproved of it.

That night I woke at 2:14. I watched the clock on my phone change to 2:17. The light stayed on.

I turned over. Then I turned back.

The man across the courtyard opened his window with a watering can in his hand. He stood there a moment, looking at the basil. Without the dark interval, I could see him clearly for the first time: middle-aged, barefoot, wearing a red dressing gown. He watered the plants and shut the window.

I had an early meeting. I ought to have gone back to sleep. Instead I lay awake until I heard footsteps on the stairs, then the front door opening for the cellist.

Over the next few weeks, I tried to stop waking at 2:17. Some nights I managed it. On others I made tea or read, enjoying the privacy of knowing that most of the building was asleep. Yet I missed the little click that had told me where I was in the night.

One afternoon, I met the cellist outside our door. I recognised the case before I recognised him.

“Did you used to leave for work at two in the morning?” I asked.

“Two twenty,” he said. “I play at a hotel. Why?”

I told him about the lamp. He laughed, then shifted the case higher on his shoulder.

“I wondered why you were always at your window,” he said.

“I thought you couldn’t see me.”

“I could when the light came back.”

We stood there, considering the odd fact of having watched each other for months without ever waving. His name was Tomas. He told me the hotel wanted a cellist in its restaurant because it sounded elegant, but they asked him to play quietly enough that no one had to stop talking. I told him I worked at a claims office and liked it more than I admitted at parties.

A few days later, Mrs. Alvarez put a handwritten note beside the letterboxes: *Extra bread Saturday. Take some.*

By Saturday afternoon, Tomas had added: *Does anyone know how to fix a sticking cello-case latch?*

Under that, in small blue writing, the teenager from the top floor offered to help. She was learning to repair bicycles and thought she might have the right tools.

The notes stayed up. Someone asked to borrow a ladder. Someone else returned it. Mrs. Alvarez began leaving bread in the foyer every other weekend, with a clean tea towel over the basket. One evening I found the man with the basil carrying an enormous bag of compost upstairs and held the door for him. His name was Martin. He grew herbs because the plants in his kitchen never got enough sun.

In June, the new streetlamp failed. It went out at 11:36 on a warm Friday night and did not come back on.

I was awake, though I no longer watched the road from my bedroom. I went downstairs to see whether someone had reported it. Martin was already outside with his phone. Tomas came around the corner carrying his cello. A little later Mrs. Alvarez opened the building door, worried that the dark steps might catch someone out.

We stood beneath the unlit lamp while Martin reported the fault. It was hot even at that hour. Somewhere nearby, people were laughing in an open-windowed kitchen.

When the call was done, no one moved straight away. Tomas set down his case. Mrs. Alvarez said she had rolls rising and invited us up for tea while they baked. We went with her, leaving the streetlamp to the council.

The first thing the river returned was a shoe.

It appeared on the mudbank one April morning, upright and polished, though it had gone into the water thirteen years before. Mr. Vale recognized it by the crooked heel. His wife had lost it while crossing the bridge on their wedding day, and they had spent the rest of that day laughing about how she’d arrived at the reception with one bare foot.

By noon, everyone in town had come to see.

The river had always taken things. Umbrellas, fishing rods, a red bicycle, a whole section of fence during the flood of ’82. It had taken people, too, but nobody said that while they stood on the bank looking at the shoe.

The next April it returned a teaspoon. After that, a set of house keys, a child’s mitten, and a photograph so faded that no one could agree who was in it. One thing each year, on no particular day. The town learned to watch the mudbank when the water ran high.

My father kept a notebook of the returns. He measured the objects, made drawings, and wrote down every account of how they’d been lost. When I was small, I went with him to ask questions. He let me carry the notebook because he knew I liked being taken for his assistant.

“Why does it bring them back?” I asked once.

He was drawing the teaspoon. “I don’t know.”

“You know everything about the river.”

“I know where it’s shallow,” he said. “That’s different.”

He died in November, when I was thirty-six. That winter, I found the notebook among his things and brought it home. I meant to read it. Instead, I left it on the kitchen table under a stack of bills.

In April, the river returned a blue glass marble.

I found it before anyone else. Rain had made the bank slippery, and I had gone down there to clear my head after a difficult phone call. The marble was lying beside a clump of reeds, bright against the silt.

I knew it at once.

When I was nine, I had owned six marbles in a velvet pouch. Five were plain. This one had a twist of yellow through the middle. I carried it everywhere, until I dropped it from the bridge while trying to show my father how the yellow looked in sunlight. He had climbed down to search the shallows. I stood above him, angry that he couldn’t find it, and angrier still when he said it was time to go home.

I picked up the marble and wiped it on my coat. It was smooth and cold and no different from any marble you could buy for a few coins.

Mr. Vale saw me coming up the path. He was old by then and walked to the river most mornings.

“What’s it brought us?” he called.

I opened my hand. He leaned close, then gave a disappointed little smile.

“Do you know whose it is?”

“Mine.”

“Well,” he said. “That’s a bit of luck.”

News traveled anyway. By lunchtime three people had asked to see the marble, and the woman at the post office told me I must be glad to have something back from my father. I said yes because she meant well.

At home, I put the marble beside the notebook. For weeks I had been trying to remember the sound of my father’s laugh. I thought an object from our childhood might help, but all I could remember was him standing knee-deep in the river, looking down through the moving water. When I showed him the marble at nine, I had expected him to know exactly where it would land. I had expected him to bring it back.

That evening I opened his notebook. The first pages were careful: dates, dimensions, names. Over the years his handwriting loosened. He had begun adding details that had nothing to do with the returns. Beside the mitten, he had written that its owner was now grown and worked at the bakery. Beside the fence, he had noted that the flood had left three trout in the school playground.

On the last filled page was a drawing of the bridge. Under it he had written, *Went looking again. Too much water to see the bottom.*

There was no date. I read the line several times. Then I turned back through the notebook, looking for the marble, but found no mention of it.

The following morning, I went to the bridge. I had the marble in my pocket and the notebook under my arm. From the middle of the bridge, I could see Mr. Vale making his slow way along the bank. He raised a hand to me. I raised mine back.

I took out the marble. Its yellow twist caught the light, just as I remembered. For a moment I thought of dropping it in. My father had spent an afternoon searching for it and, perhaps, another morning many years later. I could leave it where he had wanted to find it.

Instead, I put it back in my pocket. I went down to the bank and walked with Mr. Vale until he needed to sit. He asked whether I’d found the marble a place to keep it.

“Not yet,” I said.

He pointed to the notebook. “Will you write it down?”

I opened to a clean page and wrote the date. Then I drew the marble, badly. Mr. Vale watched the river while I worked, and when I finished, he told me what he remembered about the shoe.
