On Thursday morning, nobody in Bellwether woke up.

They woke on Friday instead.

At first, the town blamed its clocks. The one above the bakery had been unreliable since a pigeon made a nest behind its hands. But phones said Friday too, and newspapers arrived with Friday printed at the top. At school, the children insisted they had skipped spelling tests. Their teachers insisted the tests were still due.

By noon, the missing day had become a practical problem. Thursday’s bread dough had risen and collapsed. A wedding florist had a church full of flowers and no wedding. Mara Bell, who repaired watches in a shop between the florist and the bakery, discovered that her father had missed his seventy-third birthday.

“I was coming over,” she told him on the phone.

“I know,” he said. “You always do.”

Mara closed her shop early and went looking for Thursday.

She began at the town hall, where the mayor was holding an emergency meeting about whether parking restrictions still applied. From there she walked to the railway station. The departures board showed no trains cancelled, but the station clock had acquired a thin scratch across its face, just past midnight.

Mara found the same scratch on the clock at the bank. And on the bakery clock, beneath the pigeon nest. Each mark pointed toward the old cinema at the end of Mercer Street.

The cinema had been closed for twelve years. Its sign still advertised a film nobody remembered seeing. Through the glass doors, Mara could make out a glow from the projection booth.

Inside, Thursday was playing on the screen.

Not all at once. The screen showed small, ordinary scenes: a woman finding the earring she thought she had lost; a boy eating an apple down to the seeds; Mara’s father setting out two cups for tea. Mara watched herself appear at her workbench, repairing a watch that was already finished. She would have stayed late on Thursday, she realized, then arrived at her father’s house after he had put the kettle away.

In the projection booth sat Mr. Vale, the former cinema manager. He had grown thinner since Mara had last seen him, but he still wore a bow tie.

“You can’t keep a whole day,” Mara said.

“I thought I could borrow it.”

He showed her the projector. Its reels were wound with narrow strips of paper covered in handwriting. They were appointment reminders, receipts, lists left on kitchen tables. Mr. Vale had been collecting them for months. On Wednesday night, he fed them into the machine. He hadn’t known it would work until Thursday appeared on the screen.

“Why?” Mara asked.

“My wife died on a Thursday,” he said. “Tomorrow makes ten years.”

Mara waited. The projector rattled steadily behind him.

“We used to come here,” he said. “Even after I stopped showing films, we’d bring our supper and sit in the back row. I wanted one more Thursday before that date came around.”

He had spent the stolen day in the cinema, watching the town live it without him. He could not find his wife on the screen. Mara looked down at the piles of paper by his chair. For years, Mrs. Vale had kept the cinema’s accounts; her handwriting was on half the labels still fixed to the shelves. None of those had gone into the projector.

Outside, people had begun to gather. News traveled quickly in Bellwether, especially when no one had a day to lose. The florist stood in the aisle holding a box of bruised peonies. Behind her came the baker, two teachers, the mayor, and Mara’s father, who waved when he saw her.

Mr. Vale tried to turn off the projector. Mara stopped him. “If you do that, I don’t think we get it back.”

“Then what?”

She had no answer. She climbed down from the booth and stood in front of the screen. Her father was there again, turning over a teacup to drain it. She wanted to reach into the light and tell him to leave it out.

Instead, she moved aside so he could see.

For an hour, the people of Bellwether watched their Thursday. The baker learned exactly when his dough had gone wrong. One teacher saw that a child had been sick during the missed spelling test. The florist found her bride in the church doorway, laughing as she took off her shoes. People called out to one another across the seats, pointing out things the camera had caught.

Then the film reached midnight. The screen went white, and every clock in the cinema struck twelve.

It was Thursday morning.

There was some argument about what to do next. The baker had to start his dough again. The wedding flowers would need trimming. At the school, the spelling tests were postponed, though the teachers refused to say it was because the children had been right.

Mara went home, slept badly, and opened her shop at nine. She finished the watch from the screen, then left a note on the door: *Back at four.*

Her father answered on the third knock. He had already made tea.

“You’re early,” he said.

“I know.”

They sat at his kitchen table. For a while he told her about the plants on his windowsill, and she told him which watches she had managed to fix. When he got up to fetch a small cake from the cupboard, Mara turned over the second cup and put the kettle on again.

The library opened at nine, but the rain was already waiting outside.

It stood beneath the awning in a neat gray column, dripping on the steps. I unlocked the door and held it open. The rain passed through me without getting me wet, which meant it belonged to someone else.

On the returns desk, I found its card.

**ONE AFTERNOON OF STEADY RAIN.**  
**Borrower: Mr. Vale.**  
**Due: Yesterday.**

Mr. Vale was usually punctual. He came every Thursday to borrow weather for his garden: two hours of sun in April, a gentle frost in November. Once, he checked out a thunderstorm because his youngest daughter had never seen lightning. He brought it back early, saying she had seen enough.

I shelved the rain between a cool breeze and a cloudless Tuesday. Then I went to find him.

The weather library occupied the old train station. People had once stood on its platform hoping to be taken somewhere else; now they came hoping tomorrow might feel different. We could not change a season or stop a flood. The collection held only small things: a fog for an anniversary, a patch of shade for a parade, snow that would melt before anyone had to shovel it.

On my way through town, I passed Mrs. Anwar carrying an armful of paper plates.

“Are you going to the orchard?” she asked.

“I’m looking for Mr. Vale.”

“That’s where he’ll be. Tell him six o’clock, not seven.” She stopped. “Does the library have a clear evening?”

I said I would check.

At the orchard, a ladder leaned against a tree. Mr. Vale sat on its lowest rung, turning an apple in his hands. The ground smelled of damp soil, although the sky was bright.

“You returned the rain without its card,” I said.

“I left it there.”

“I know. That’s why I came.”

He set the apple down. Across the road, a truck waited with its engine off. A man beside it was rolling up a measuring tape.

“They’re taking the trees tomorrow,” Mr. Vale said. “I wanted one more day to water them.”

I looked along the rows. Some trees were old and crooked; others were hardly taller than I was. Red fruit lay in the grass. I had lived in town all my life and could not remember an autumn when Mr. Vale had not told me to take an apple.

“Mrs. Anwar says six,” I told him.

He nodded. “The neighbors are coming to pick what’s left.”

He had sold the land. I knew that much. His wife needed care in a place closer to her sister, and the orchard had been losing money for years. None of that told me what to say while he sat among the trees.

“The rain was good,” he said. “It fell all afternoon. I sat here and listened.”

I told him I was glad he’d borrowed it.

We walked back together. At the library I found a clear evening on the top shelf, then asked if he wanted to take it home.

He glanced at the card. “That one belongs to you.”

It did. I had donated it years earlier, after my father died. We had spent our last ordinary evening together fixing a loose board on his porch. I remembered the bent nails, the warm wood under my hands, his voice calling from the kitchen to ask whether I wanted tea. I had kept the weather from that day because, for a long time, it was easier to visit the evening than the house.

“Will it work over the whole orchard?” Mr. Vale asked.

“I think so.”

At six, people arrived with baskets, crates, and bags that would split before they got home. Children ran between the rows. Someone brought a long pole to shake fruit from the highest branches. Mrs. Anwar set out her paper plates and a pie still warm enough to steam.

I opened the borrowed evening just as the sun reached the fence. Its light spread over the orchard, catching in the leaves and on the faces of people looking up. Mr. Vale stood beside me for a moment, then went to show a child which apples could be reached from the ground.

I picked until my bag was full. Now and then I thought about the porch and my father, but I also had to watch where I put my feet. There were fallen apples everywhere, and people kept calling me over to help.

By dusk, the crates were stacked along the fence. Mr. Vale thanked each person as they left. When he came to me, I handed him an apple I had saved from the first row.

“You can keep the evening,” I said.

He looked out at the nearly bare trees. “I think we used it.”

The next morning, I returned to the library with the empty weather box. Its card required a note about the conditions in which it had been used. I wrote: *Clear throughout. Good light for picking. Lasted until everyone was done.*

Then I put the box on the shelf.

The city hired Mara to record buildings before they came down.

At first she thought they wanted interviews: the grocer who’d sold peaches beneath the railway arches, the families from the apartment block on Venn Street. Instead, her supervisor handed her a recorder and a list of addresses.

“People are already telling their stories,” he said. “Get the buildings.”

She learned that an empty apartment block was never silent. Pipes ticked as they cooled. A lift cable knocked softly inside its shaft. Wind entered through a cracked window on the fifth floor and made the mailboxes downstairs tremble.

She recorded each place from the doorway, then from the center, then from wherever the sound seemed to gather. At the old cinema, that was the last row of the balcony, where rain tapped on the roof in a rhythm so regular she mistook it for a projector.

After six months, she could recognize a building with her eyes closed. The shoe warehouse breathed through its vents. The public baths whistled when the boiler shut off. In the library scheduled for demolition, a loose pane gave a brief, offended rattle whenever a bus passed.

The library was her last job of the year. She arrived early, before the crew, and found the doors unlocked. Shelves stood bare except for a single atlas, too water-damaged to move. Its pages had swollen into a landscape of pale hills.

Mara set her recorder on a table and waited.

Across the room, something clicked. Then clicked again.

She followed the sound to the children’s section, where a small clock still hung above the doorway. Its hands had stopped at 4:17, but its mechanism was struggling on. Every few seconds it made a noise like a person trying a key in the wrong lock.

A man in a hard hat appeared behind her.

“Sorry,” he said. “Didn’t know anyone was here.”

“I’m nearly done.”

He looked up at the clock. “My mother brought me here on Thursdays.”

Mara checked the recorder’s red light. She wasn’t supposed to interview people, but she let it run.

“She’d pick books for herself,” he said. “I’d pick the same one every week. Book about a boat. She got so tired of it.”

“Do you remember what it was called?”

“No.” He smiled. “Not even what kind of boat.”

Outside, a truck reversed, beeping steadily. The man said he had to go. Mara stayed until the truck went quiet and the little clock could be heard again.

Back at the office, she labeled the file *North Branch Library, interior, 8:42 a.m.* She listened to it once through headphones. The clock clicked seven times. The man spoke. At the end, a door closed somewhere far away.

Her supervisor would cut the conversation from the archive. It wasn’t what the city had asked for. She saved a copy anyway.

That evening, on her way home, Mara stopped at the temporary library in a former bank. She asked the woman at the desk whether they had any old children’s books about boats.

“Thousands,” the woman said.

“The same one a child might borrow every Thursday.”

The woman considered this without laughing. “Try the returns cart.”

Mara spent half an hour turning over books. There were boats with sails, boats with motors, a boat captained by a mouse. She couldn’t know which one he’d meant. She took the mouse to the desk and borrowed it.

At home, she opened it on the kitchen table. Inside the front cover, a previous reader had written a name in uneven pencil, then crossed it out. The boat in the story got lost in a fog. By morning, it had found its way to a shore full of trees.

Mara read it through, though no one had asked her to. Then she placed it by the door so she would remember to return it on Thursday.

On Tuesday morning, the shadows stopped following us.

Mine stayed on the kitchen wall when I left for work. I tried stepping back into it, but it held its shape: a dark woman with one hand raised toward the light switch. I had not raised my hand. At least, I didn’t think I had.

Outside, the street was full of people walking carefully around their shadows. A cyclist had abandoned his beside the bakery and gone on without it. Two children were trying to coax theirs home with pieces of toast.

By nine, the mayor had called an emergency meeting. I attended because I worked in the Department of Streetlights, and nobody knew which department handled shadows.

“We could turn all the lights off,” suggested the chief electrician.

“It’s daytime,” I said.

He wrote *daytime* on the whiteboard and underlined it twice.

At noon, the shadows began to move.

Not far. They slid across floors, climbed walls, gathered beneath tables. From my office window, I watched them collect in the square until the paving stones were almost black. Then they arranged themselves into letters.

The mayor read the message aloud.

**WE WOULD LIKE A DAY OFF.**

No one spoke for a moment.

Then the chief electrician said, “From what?”

The answer appeared slowly, as if the shadows were considering how much to explain.

**FROM GOING WHERE YOU GO.**

By evening, negotiations had begun. The mayor offered Sundays. The shadows asked for Tuesdays. A business owner objected that customers might find an unshadowed shop suspicious. A shadow shaped like a woman carrying grocery bags climbed onto his shoes and refused to move until he withdrew the objection.

I was sent home to draft a schedule. The mayor liked my handwriting.

My shadow was still in the kitchen. In the late light, it stretched across the wall and onto the ceiling. I made tea. It did not come over to the kettle as it usually would have.

I sat at the table, looking at the raised hand.

“That’s what I was doing when you stopped,” I said.

I remembered reaching for the switch. The morning had been bright enough without it, but I had reached anyway. It was something my father used to do: turn on the kitchen light even in summer, then apologize to the electricity bill. He had died in February. Since then, I had kept forgetting which small habits were his and which were mine.

“I’m sorry,” I told the shadow. “I’ve hardly looked at you.”

It remained on the wall. I didn’t know whether shadows could hear.

The next morning, I took the schedule to the square. It gave them every Tuesday off, with an exemption for anyone crossing a road after dark. The shadows considered this. Then they formed another message.

**YOU MAY NEED US AT OTHER TIMES TOO.**

The mayor called that thoughtful of them. I thought it sounded tired.

We agreed that shadows could leave whenever they wanted, provided they came back when someone called for one. We had no way to enforce the agreement. Neither, apparently, did they.

For the next few weeks, the town looked untidier. Shadows rested on park benches while their people queued for coffee. They lay in patches of sunlight, which seemed to do them no harm. Sometimes they chose to follow someone other than the person who had cast them. People pointed this out to one another, at first with alarm and then with curiosity.

Mine began leaving the kitchen. It spent a whole afternoon under the table at work. Another day I found it waiting at the bus stop, though I had walked there by a different route.

On the first Tuesday in April, I came home and found it on the kitchen wall again, one hand raised.

“I know,” I said, setting down my bag. “I keep meaning to change that bulb.”

The shadow lowered its hand.

The bulb had not worked since February. I had been using the kitchen light without noticing how dim it was, reaching for the switch each morning out of habit. I stood on a chair and changed it.

When I climbed down, my shadow was at my feet. I moved one hand; it moved one hand. Then I turned off the light, and we both disappeared.

On the hottest day of the year, Mara began mapping the shadows.

Her mother had to walk six blocks to the pharmacy. Six blocks was nothing in October. In July, with the sun reflecting off the shop windows and the bus shelter missing its roof, it was a journey her mother planned around a glass of water at each end.

Mara set out at eight with a notebook. She marked the shadow of the laundromat awning, then the thin shelter of a telephone pole. At nine, she went again. By eleven, the pole’s shadow had crossed the sidewalk and disappeared beneath a parked van. She drew an arrow beside it: **unreliable**.

That evening she made a map. It wasn’t very good. She had to draw three versions, one for morning, one for noon, one for late afternoon. Still, her mother took the morning map and came home with her prescription and a paper bag of peaches.

“Mrs. Alvarez wants one,” she said.

Mrs. Alvarez’s knees were worse than her mother’s. Mara made another copy. Then the man at the pharmacy asked for one for the noticeboard. By Friday, people were sending corrections.

*The bakery brings out its umbrellas at ten.*

*Don’t count on the maple outside number 14. They’re cutting it down.*

*There’s water at the hardware store. Ask for Dev.*

Mara walked the route again. The maple was already gone; its stump looked shockingly pale. She crossed out the green circle she had drawn around it.

A week later, someone sent her a photograph of a blue bedsheet stretched between the barber shop and the florist’s. Beneath it stood three people waiting for the light to change. The florist called to ask whether blue counted as shade.

“It counts,” Mara said.

The next edition of the map had a blue stripe.

Soon she needed symbols: a cup for free water, a chair for somewhere to rest, a dotted line for shade that appeared only after two. Dev at the hardware store laminated copies because sweaty hands were ruining the paper ones. Someone taped a map inside the bus shelter, where the roof should have been.

Under it sat her mother and Mrs. Alvarez, sharing a peach. They had walked to the pharmacy together and were taking their time coming back.

Mara added the umbrella to the map when she got home. Beside it, in the margin, she wrote: **Room for two chairs.**

The first shadow went missing on a Thursday.

It belonged to the butcher, who noticed its absence while sweeping sawdust from his doorway. The sun was behind him. His boots were on the pavement. Between them and the street there was nothing at all.

By noon, the school secretary had lost hers, as had a dog named Pickles and nearly everyone waiting outside the post office. The mayor called an emergency meeting. He held it indoors, where nobody could tell whether his shadow had stayed.

There was no panic at first. People checked one another’s feet and made jokes about getting lighter. Then the butcher’s shadow was seen crossing the square alone. It slipped between market stalls, climbed the steps of the public library, and settled on the patch of carpet where the children listened to stories.

The butcher stood at the window, watching it.

“I haven’t been in there since I was little,” he said.

Over the next week, other shadows were found. The school secretary’s lay under a tree in the park each afternoon. Pickles’s raced up and down the canal path, where Pickles himself was forbidden to go. The mayor’s stood outside the hospital, motionless, while he attended meetings and issued notices asking residents to remain calm.

Ada still had hers. She worked in the cinema, selling tickets on weekends and running the projector every evening. She’d become used to seeing her shadow travel ahead of her up the narrow stairs to the booth. Each night, when the film was over, she locked the front doors and made sure it followed her home.

On the second Tuesday, it didn’t.

Ada had stopped to buy milk. She came out of the shop carrying the carton and found herself alone under the streetlamp. She put down the milk and walked around the pool of light twice. Her shadow was nowhere on the pavement or on the shop wall.

She found it the following morning at the old railway station.

The station had been closed for twenty-three years. Weeds grew between the tracks, and the departure board still announced a train that would never arrive. Ada’s shadow sat on a bench beneath it. As she approached, it rose and moved to the platform’s edge.

Ada knew the bench. She and her younger sister, Ruth, had waited there one summer morning with two suitcases and enough money for a single ticket. Their father was ill. Ruth had found work in the city; Ada had meant to go too, once they knew he would recover. Instead, the train came, Ruth got on, and Ada carried her suitcase home. Over the years that followed, each sister said things the other remembered. They sent birthday cards for a while, then stopped.

Ada sat on the bench. Her shadow waited at the edge of the platform until the sun moved behind the station roof and she could no longer see it.

She returned the next morning, before work. It was there again. She tried calling to it, though she felt foolish the moment she spoke. She tried standing where it stood. Their outlines overlapped on the concrete, but when she stepped away, hers remained behind.

Throughout town, people had begun visiting the places where their shadows went. The butcher took his lunch to the library and came back with a stack of books. The school secretary carried a folding chair to the park. The mayor visited the hospital and stayed until the friend he had been avoiding woke up.

Ada went to the station every day. Sometimes she brought coffee. Once she brought the small blue suitcase she had kept under her bed, though she took it home unopened. She was uncertain what her shadow wanted, and more uncertain what she wanted herself. There were mornings when she was glad the trains no longer ran.

At last she wrote Ruth a letter. It took her three evenings. She told Ruth about the cinema, the leak in the kitchen ceiling, and how their father had liked having the window open even in winter. She described the shadows. She apologised for two things and decided not to explain a third. Then she put the letter in an envelope and walked to the post box before she could change it.

A reply came nine days later. Ruth lived in a town on the coast. She had a husband and a daughter Ada had never met. She wrote that she had kept their childhood photographs in a drawer by her bed. At the bottom of the page she wrote, *There’s a train from your town now. They reopened the line last spring.*

Ada read the letter twice, then looked up the timetable.

On Saturday morning she stood at the restored end of the station with her blue suitcase. The train was due in twelve minutes. She could see her shadow on the old platform, past the fence the railway had put up during construction. It had not come any closer.

She waited until the train arrived. Passengers got off, and someone bumped her suitcase with a bicycle. As she stepped aboard, she looked back. Her shadow crossed the old platform, passed through the fence, and reached her just as the doors began to close.

Ada found a seat by the window. She had not yet thought of what she would say when Ruth opened the door, or whether she would like the town where Ruth lived. She set the suitcase at her feet. Outside, the station slid slowly past, and her shadow went with her.

The first thing Mara lost was the sound of her father clearing his throat.

Not her father. He was still alive then, living three streets away and calling every Sunday to ask whether she’d checked the oil in her car. But one afternoon she tried to remember that small, familiar noise he made before offering advice, and found a blank space where it should have been.

She went to see him.

He opened the door in his slippers. The kettle was on; a newspaper lay folded beside his chair. She waited through tea, through a discussion of the damp patch under his kitchen window, through a story about a neighbour’s ridiculous new fence. Finally, just before he told her to have the car serviced, he cleared his throat.

“There,” she said.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

On the walk home she repeated the sound to herself, badly, like a person learning a word in a foreign language.

Years later, after he died, she could remember the newspaper and the slippers and the exact amber ring the tea had left on his table. She could no longer remember his voice. This seemed like a terrible exchange, though no one had offered her a choice.

One Saturday, Mara bought a small recorder at a second-hand shop. She carried it everywhere. She recorded the squeak of her front gate, rain ticking against the fire escape, the uneven applause at her niece’s school concert. She recorded her husband laughing with his mouth full of toast. He protested, so she recorded that too.

The files accumulated. Most were labelled carelessly: *Tuesday*, *Kitchen*, *Maybe birds*. Sometimes she listened to one and had no idea why she’d pressed the button. In a recording made outside a pharmacy, traffic rushed past for forty seconds before a woman said, quite faintly, “Wait for me.” Mara couldn’t place her. Perhaps the woman had been speaking to a child.

One winter evening, while sorting the files, Mara found a recording called *Dad*. Her hands went cold. She had bought the recorder long after his death, but she put on her headphones anyway.

At first there was only the hiss of wind. Then came the click of a gate and Mara’s own voice: “Careful. The step’s icy.”

Her niece, much younger, answered, “I know.”

They were at the cemetery. Mara remembered the day: frozen grass, a plastic bag of bulbs they had meant to plant and couldn’t because the ground was too hard. She had forgotten bringing the recorder.

For nearly a minute, neither of them spoke. Somewhere beyond the cemetery wall, a car struggled to start. Then her niece asked, “What was he like when you were little?”

Mara heard herself breathe in. She had no memory of what she’d said.

“He used to pretend he couldn’t find me,” the recording continued. “Even when I was standing right in front of him. He’d open the cupboards and look under the rug.”

Her niece laughed. “Under the rug?”

“He was very thorough.”

There was more wind. Mara’s voice, when it came again, was quieter.

“I wish I’d asked him what he remembered.”

The recording ended there.

Mara removed the headphones. Outside, a bus sighed to a stop. Someone was dragging their bins across the pavement. Her husband called from the other room to ask where they kept the batteries.

“In the drawer beside you,” she said.

Then she got up to show him.

The first time the sea came to Bellwether, it arrived in a teacup.

Mrs. Vale found it on her kitchen table one Tuesday morning: a little blue water, a little white foam, and a wave that rose against the porcelain and fell again. She lived three hundred miles from the coast. She called her son, who thought she was being poetic, and then the plumber, who thought she was being lonely. By noon, she had carried the cup to the town hall, where everyone agreed it was seawater and no one could agree what to do.

The mayor suggested a lid. The science teacher suggested a sample. Mrs. Vale suggested they let it be. In the end, they put the cup on a windowsill in the records office, between the deeds to an abandoned orchard and a photograph of the old bus depot. Every morning, the clerk checked it. Every morning, the wave arrived and broke without spilling a drop.

After a week, other things began turning up. Mr. Iqbal opened his tool shed to find a wind strong enough to rattle every hammer on the wall. At the school, a first grader’s mittens filled with snow that never melted. The pharmacist discovered a patch of afternoon sunlight in the back room, though the room had no windows. People brought these things to town hall in jars and boxes when they could. The wind would not fit in a box, so Mr. Iqbal brought the shed key.

Bellwether had plenty of theories. The science teacher measured temperatures and weights. The minister asked whether anyone had been praying for a change in the weather. A reporter came from the city and wrote that the town had “grown accustomed to miracles,” which irritated Mrs. Vale. She still stopped at the records office every morning to make sure the cup had not been knocked over. Miracles, she told the reporter, were the sort of thing people stopped looking after.

In October, the clerk found rain falling under his desk. It was gentle rain, falling through the closed drawers and onto a square of carpet that was always dry when he touched it. He moved his chair to the other side of the room. He had spent thirty-four years working at that desk, and it took him until lunchtime to admit that he missed it.

Winter arrived in the ordinary way. The pipes froze. The mayor lost an election. Mrs. Vale’s son came home for Christmas with his two children, who wanted to see the sea in the teacup. He had expected, perhaps, to find that the story had improved in the telling. Instead, there it was: the cup he remembered from childhood, and a wave no higher than his thumb.

His daughter watched it for a long time. Then she asked where it went when it went out.

Nobody had asked that. The adults leaned over the cup. The wave gathered, curled, broke, and drew back toward the painted flowers at the bottom. It looked as if it had somewhere to go. Mrs. Vale’s granddaughter put her ear close to the rim and said she could hear people. Her father heard nothing, but Mrs. Vale heard something like dishes being washed in a distant kitchen.

That night, she dreamed of her husband standing ankle-deep in water, trying to remember where he had put his shoes. He had been dead for eleven years. In the dream, she knew better than to tell him. She helped him look.

By spring, most of the strange weather had faded. The snow in the mittens turned to damp wool. The pharmacist’s sunlight slipped across the floor and disappeared beneath the door. Mr. Iqbal opened his shed one morning and found all the hammers hanging still. He was relieved, then disappointed, then relieved again.

The wave remained. Mrs. Vale continued to visit it, though some mornings her knees made the walk difficult. She never found out where it came from. She learned, instead, which windowsill warmed first, how dust gathered behind the cup, and the small sound the wave made just before it fell. When the clerk retired, she showed his replacement where to set the photograph of the bus depot so it would not cast a shadow over the water.

Years later, her granddaughter would remember the cup more clearly than she remembered Mrs. Vale’s face. She would remember being lifted high enough to see inside it, and her grandmother’s hand steady beneath her feet. Once, on a trip to the coast, she would wait at the edge of the surf and listen for dishes. What she heard was a wave drawing pebbles back through the sand. She stayed until her shoes were wet, then went to find her family.

On the morning the sea returned the piano, Mara was putting the kettle on.

It came in with the tide, upright and astonishingly intact, bumping gently against the stone steps below the harbor wall. A few people gathered to watch. The fishmonger guessed it had fallen off a ship. A boy suggested the sea had learned to play.

Mara knew whose it was.

Her father had owned a piano like that, though he had never learned to play more than the first eight notes of a song he refused to name. Every Sunday after lunch he would sit down, pick out those notes with one finger, and stop. When Mara was small, she thought the rest of the song must be terribly difficult.

The piano had gone missing twenty years ago, after he died. Her mother said she’d sold it, but Mara never found out to whom. Now here it was, a little swollen, its black paint dulled by salt, one brass wheel missing from its foot.

The harbor master arranged for two men to haul it onto the quay. Mara waited until the crowd had thinned before lifting the lid. Inside, the keys were yellow but clean.

She pressed one. It made no sound.

“Of course,” she said, and shut it again.

For a week the piano stood beneath a tarpaulin in her kitchen. It was too large for the room; she had to turn sideways to reach the sink. Neighbors came by with suggestions. Someone knew a restorer. Someone else thought it ought to go to the school, provided the school could find a place for it. Her friend Dev brought a screwdriver and offered to look inside, but Mara asked him not to.

She could not have said why. She made tea. She climbed around the piano. At night, coming down for water, she sometimes saw its shape in the dark and startled as if another person had arrived.

On Saturday she took the tarpaulin off.

There were scratches on the wood near the pedals. Her father had kept a stool with a loose hinge, and she remembered how he would slide his feet beneath it, careful not to catch his trousers. For a long time she stood there trying to remember whether he had sung as he played. She could picture his hands and the back of his head, but she couldn’t hear his voice.

That afternoon Dev returned. He brought lunch and, without asking, moved the piano a few inches so Mara could open the cupboard behind it. After they ate, she let him remove the front panel.

He worked slowly. A little sand fell out, then a coin, a hairpin, and a folded piece of paper wedged deep between two boards. Dev handed it to her.

It was a shopping list in her father’s handwriting: onions, matches, tea, blue thread. On the other side was a phone number Mara did not recognize.

She laughed. She had been braced for a message. Her father had left her errands.

“Blue thread,” Dev said. “That’s hard to find.”

“My mother was mending a coat.”

“You remember?”

“No. I remember the coat.”

Dev went on examining the piano. Several strings had snapped, and others had rusted through. The soundboard had split. He explained what could be replaced and what could not. Mara listened. She had spent the week afraid someone would tell her to get rid of it; now she found herself wanting to know what had happened to every part.

When Dev left, she put the list on the mantelpiece and called her mother.

“The piano washed up,” Mara said.

There was silence. Then her mother said, “Well, that’s a nuisance for whoever had it.”

“Did you sell it?”

“I gave it to your uncle Tom. His boy wanted to learn. They moved away, remember?”

“I’d forgotten.”

“Can it still play?”

“No.”

Her mother thought about this. “Your father would have tried anyway.”

That evening Mara sat on the floor and searched for the song. She played the eight notes on her phone, moving back and forth through recordings until she found them in an old dance tune. She listened to the whole thing. It was cheerful and quick, with a middle that rose far above the beginning and a final phrase that came tumbling down.

She tried to imagine her father hearing it. Perhaps he had meant to learn the rest. Perhaps he liked only the beginning. There was no one left to ask, and she was surprised to find that this did not spoil the song.

In the spring, a piano restorer came from the next town. Mara held one end of a board while he worked. He showed her how the keys lifted, how the hammers struck, and how long the salt had sat inside before the sea gave the instrument back. When he was finished, some notes were still uneven. He left her a receipt, a tuning date, and instructions to keep the kitchen window closed in wet weather.

On Sunday, her mother came for lunch. Afterwards she sat at the piano and played the tune almost to the end. She missed a note, swore, and started again.

Mara pulled up a chair beside her. “You know it?”

“Your father used to put the record on while we cooked,” her mother said. “He could never catch up with it.”

Outside, the tide was going out. Mara listened to her mother play, and when the tune came around again, she asked to try.

It had been installed beside the bus stop sometime in the nineties, though no one remembered by whom. Its buttons were labeled SUN, RAIN, FOG, WIND, and OTHER. For two coins, it dispensed a small paper ticket. The weather printed on the ticket arrived within the hour and lasted until sundown.

Naturally, the machine caused arguments.

Gardeners bought rain. Brides bought sun. Teenagers bought fog because it made the town look like a place where interesting things might happen. The town council tried to regulate it, but each proposed rule favored someone’s plans over someone else’s. In the end they put up a sign asking people to be considerate.

This worked about as well as signs usually do.

Nell used to pass the machine on her walk to the bakery. She had never bought anything from it. Most mornings, she could afford bread or weather, not both, and bread was more reliable. She knew the machine worked because she had watched a man feed it two coins, press WIND, and lose his hat before his ticket finished printing.

One November morning, Nell found the machine blinking. A ticket hung from its slot, unclaimed.

OTHER, it said.

Below that, in smaller letters: SOMEONE HAS ALREADY PAID.

Nell took the ticket. Nothing happened. She bought her loaf and went home.

By noon, everybody in town had begun remembering things differently.

The postmaster remembered learning to swim from his older brother, though his brother had died before he was born. A woman on Orchard Street remembered a dog she had never owned. Children recalled the endings of stories nobody had told them. At the bakery, Nell’s friend Ivo insisted that the shop had once been a cinema and described, in convincing detail, the red velvet seats.

There had never been a cinema in town.

Nell knew this because she had lived there all her life, as had her mother and her mother’s mother. Still, when Ivo spoke, she could almost smell the velvet after a wet coat had dried against it.

By evening, people were comparing their new memories in the square. Some were marvelous. Some were painful. The postmaster cried over his brother, then grew angry with anyone who pointed out that their afternoons at the river had never occurred.

Nell went to the vending machine. On its side, beneath years of scratched initials, she found a small brass plate she had never noticed before.

WEATHER IS WHAT HAPPENS TO THE SKY, it read. OTHER IS WHAT HAPPENS TO EVERYTHING ELSE.

The next morning, the memories remained. The postmaster could recall two childhoods equally well. Ivo opened the bakery and set out the bread where he said the cinema’s ticket counter had been. Customers came in to ask what was fresh, then stayed to describe films they had never seen.

Nell returned to the square with a notebook. She thought that if she wrote down what people remembered, she might discover who had paid for OTHER, or what it was meant to do. She spent the day listening. The mayor remembered a sister; his wife remembered no such person. Two children remembered the same dog, but disagreed on its color. An old man remembered planting the great oak by the church, although the oak had stood there when he was young.

At home, Nell read through her notes. Each account was detailed, but none told her where the memories had come from. She turned to the last page and found an entry in her own handwriting that she did not remember writing:

*Ask Ivo about the last show.*

She walked to the bakery after closing. Ivo was sweeping flour from the floor.

“What was the last film?” she asked.

He leaned on the broom. “I don’t know its name. I remember the audience leaving, though. It was raining outside. Someone had brought an umbrella for me.”

“Who?”

He thought for a long time. “You.”

Nell tried to remember it. She could picture Ivo at the cinema door and herself across the street, holding an umbrella with a bent spoke. Then the picture slipped away. She looked at her dry shoes, at the flour on his apron, and felt troubled by how much she wanted it back.

“I can’t tell whether it happened,” she said.

“Neither can I.”

They stood there while he finished sweeping. Before she left, Ivo offered her a loaf for the morning. Nell paid him for it.

A week later, the postmaster stopped telling people about his brother. He had not forgotten the river, but he had grown tired of being corrected. The children found a real dog wandering near the school and argued about its name instead of its color. Nell kept taking her notebook to the square. When someone wanted to talk, she listened and wrote down what she could.

In December, a hard frost sealed the machine’s coin slot. A council worker came to clear it and found a second ticket tucked behind the first. Its edges had gone soft in the damp. He brought it to Nell because her name was printed at the top.

On the back, there was a date: the November morning she had found the machine blinking. Nell turned it over.

OTHER, it said.

Below that: **THANK YOU FOR YOUR PURCHASE.**

Nell counted the coins in her coat pocket. There was no reason to think they were the same coins she had carried that morning. She stood for a while beside the bus stop, holding the ticket in her cold hands, until the bus arrived and blocked her view of the machine.

On the morning the clocks stopped, nobody noticed at first.

The baker pulled six loaves from the oven and found them pale. He put them back for five minutes, then ten, then stood with the oven door open until the heat stung his face. The loaves stayed pale. Across the street, a woman waited for the kettle to boil. Her tea went cold around the leaves.

By noon, people had begun to gather in the square. Every clock showed 8:17. Watches, phones, the brass face above the bank: all of them. The sun had moved, and the shadows had moved with it. Children had grown hungry. Whatever was wrong, it wasn't time itself.

Mrs. Vale arrived carrying her grandfather's pocket watch. It had no hands. Her grandfather had taken them out years ago, she said, after the watch began losing minutes that never turned up again.

“That doesn't help us,” said the mayor.

“It might,” said Mrs. Vale. “He's still alive.”

They found him at home, asleep in an armchair beside a cold fireplace. Mr. Vale was ninety-six and disliked visitors, but he listened while the mayor explained. Then he asked for his coat.

“There used to be someone who looked after the clocks,” he said as they walked. “His name was Harlan. He could hear a bad gear from the street. After he died, I tried to keep them running. They're old, most of them.”

At the square, he opened the bank clock with a key he had kept for forty years. Inside, the pendulum hung motionless. He gave it a push. It swung once, then stopped.

Mr. Vale lowered himself onto the steps and examined the works laid out beside him. A few people stayed to watch. Others went home to make supper without knowing when supper ought to be. The baker brought out the pale loaves. They were cooked through and tasted fine.

Toward evening, Mr. Vale found a broken tooth on a gear no bigger than a coin. The mayor sent someone for the clockmaker in the next town, but it was too late for him to come that night. Mr. Vale set the gear on a handkerchief and said there was nothing more to do until morning.

The sun went down. People lit lamps and went to bed. Some slept badly; others slept better than they had in years.

The clockmaker arrived the next day with a box of parts. By lunchtime the bank clock was ticking again. Its hands still pointed to 8:17, so the mayor asked what time they should set it to. No one was quite sure. They settled on twelve, because the sun was high and everyone was ready to eat.

For a while, the town was half a day out of step with everywhere else. Deliveries came unexpectedly. Calls were missed. The mayor bought a radio, and within a week all the clocks agreed with it.

But the baker kept one of the pale loaves on a shelf behind his counter. It hardened there, slowly, while customers came in to buy bread. When anyone asked about it, he told them how he had stood at the oven waiting for five minutes to pass, and how long it had taken him to open the door and look.

The first thing I found in the attic was a blue mitten, stiff with dust. The second was a cassette tape labeled **RAIN, 1987** in my mother’s handwriting.

I no longer had a player. I kept the tape anyway, tucked in my coat pocket while I sorted through boxes of tax returns, Christmas decorations, and appliance manuals for appliances that had long since died.

By afternoon, I had made three piles on the landing: keep, donate, and ask my sister. Every object seemed to belong in two of them. My mother had saved birthday cards from people she disliked. She had thrown out nearly all the photographs of herself.

At the bottom of a box of sewing supplies, I found a cassette player wrapped in a tea towel. The batteries were dead, but the cord was still there. I plugged it in beside the attic window and pressed play.

At first I heard only hiss. Then rain, close and heavy, striking what sounded like a metal roof. A chair scraped. Someone coughed.

“Is it working?” my father asked.

He had been dead for eleven years.

“You’ll use up the tape,” my mother said. She sounded young enough to surprise me.

“That’s what it’s for.”

For a while, neither of them spoke. The rain filled the attic, ordinary and insistent. In the background came the faint clink of dishes. I tried to work out where they had recorded it. We lived in a flat in 1987, and its roof was several floors above us.

Then I heard a smaller voice. “Do the thunder again.”

It was mine.

My father made a terrible thunder noise with his mouth. I laughed so hard I squeaked. My mother laughed too, a sound I knew well but had not heard in years without grief attached to it.

I sat on the floor among the boxes until the tape clicked off.

That evening, my sister came by for the things I had put aside for her. I played the tape again. She remembered the rain immediately: a week at a rented cottage, the roof over the kitchen, our father making thunder whenever the weather went quiet. I remembered none of it.

We listened without talking. When it ended, my sister turned the cassette over, but the other side was blank.

She took the blue mitten. I kept the tape.

The first thing Mara repaired was a blue umbrella with one bent rib. The second was a red one whose handle had fallen off. By the end of the week, the hallway outside her apartment was full of umbrellas belonging to people she had never met.

She had not advertised. She had only fixed the blue umbrella for Mr. Vale upstairs, who told his sister, who told a bus driver. The bus driver brought three umbrellas and a bag of oranges. After that, people began leaving things by her door with notes tucked under the straps.

Mara had learned the work from her grandfather. He had kept a shop between a locksmith and a bakery, and every afternoon the three proprietors stood outside together, arguing about whether the next cloud would bring rain. Her grandfather was usually wrong. He carried an umbrella anyway.

“It isn’t the weather I’m prepared for,” he once told her. “It’s the walk home.”

That sounded wise when she was twelve. At thirty-seven, she suspected he had simply disliked getting wet.

One Friday, a woman brought in a black umbrella that looked beyond help. The fabric was split at four seams. Its spokes were twisted together, and the little metal tip was missing entirely.

“You can throw it away,” the woman said. “I just thought I’d ask.”

Mara opened it carefully. A tag had been sewn inside: *E. Okafor, Room 14.*

“Was this yours?”

“My mother’s. She worked at the hospital.” The woman touched the strap, then let it go. “She died in February.”

Mara looked at the umbrella again. She could replace the spokes and sew new fabric over the old, but it would no longer be the thing the woman had carried in. She said so.

“I know.” The woman gave a brief, embarrassed smile. “I’ve been carrying it around in my car for months. I thought you might tell me what to do with it.”

Mara set the umbrella on her worktable. She had scissors, pliers, needles, and wire. None of them seemed useful for that question.

“Come back tomorrow,” she said.

After the woman left, Mara tried to open the umbrella fully. It caught halfway. She worked one spoke free, then another. Rain began tapping at the window, lightly at first, then hard enough to blur the building across the street. By evening, she had made no repair worth showing anyone. She closed the umbrella and noticed how smooth the wooden handle was in one place, where a thumb must have rested year after year.

On Saturday morning, the woman returned with two paper cups of coffee.

“I couldn’t fix it,” Mara told her.

The woman nodded, though she looked disappointed. Mara wished she had better news to offer. Instead, she showed her the worn place on the handle.

“That’s where my mother held it,” the woman said. She took the umbrella and fitted her hand around the wood. After a moment, she asked whether Mara had a small screwdriver.

They sat together at the table and removed the handle. The screw resisted them; the woman held the shaft steady while Mara turned it. When it came loose, they both laughed at how much effort it had taken. Mara found a short length of cord, threaded it through the handle, and made a loop so it could hang by the woman’s front door. The rest of the umbrella went back into her car. She said she might decide later what to do with it.

Soon the hallway filled again. Mara mended Mr. Vale’s blue umbrella for a second time and returned the bus driver’s three with the oranges still sitting on her counter. People collected their umbrellas, left new ones, stayed to talk while she worked. She liked hearing where they had been caught in the rain.

One evening, she finished a small yellow umbrella just as a storm broke over the neighborhood. Its owner, a boy of about eight, had come with his father. He opened it indoors despite being told not to, and a drop of old rainwater fell from the canopy onto his nose.

Outside, the pavement shone under the streetlights. Mara watched the boy and his father set off beneath the yellow circle, stepping around puddles until the boy began stepping into them instead. His father let him. At the corner, the wind pushed the umbrella inside out.

The boy stopped. Even through the rain, Mara could see him studying the exposed ribs, deciding whether to be upset. Then his father reached over, popped the umbrella back into shape, and they went on.

Mara turned off her work lamp and went downstairs. There was rain in the gutter and rain blowing under the awning. She had spent the whole day surrounded by umbrellas, but she had forgotten to bring one for herself. She waited a minute for the shower to ease. When it didn’t, she stepped out and started home.

The first time the town went quiet, people assumed the power had failed.

The traffic lights still worked. Refrigerators hummed. The church clock struck noon, though nobody heard it. For one hour, sound simply stopped traveling between people.

Mara was standing at the butcher’s counter when it happened. She saw the butcher’s mouth form *Anything else?* and answered with a shake of her head. Behind her, a child dropped a coin. It bounced twice on the tile, silently, and rolled beneath the door.

At one o’clock, the butcher’s knife struck its block with a crack. Everyone in the shop flinched.

By evening there were explanations. A factory experiment. A trick of the weather. A punishment, according to the man who always stood outside the pharmacy holding a cardboard sign. The next day, at noon, it happened again.

The council called it the Quiet Hour. It was inconvenient, but inconvenience is something a town can organize. Meetings ended at eleven fifty. The school printed cards saying FIRE and HELP. The butcher put a small bell on his counter and laughed, when sound returned, at the uselessness of it.

Mara worked in the public library. During the Quiet Hour she found that the building changed. Without voices to measure it against, the room seemed enormous. She could see the click of a keyboard in a patron’s fingers. She could watch dust turn in a shaft of light without waiting for someone to apologize for disturbing her.

One Thursday, an old man came in at eleven fifty-eight carrying a blue umbrella.

He set it beside the returns desk and handed Mara a book. Inside its cover he had tucked a note: *My wife borrowed this in 1997. I found it yesterday.*

Mara opened the book. It was a field guide to local birds, stamped overdue twenty-six years earlier. On page forty-three, someone had circled a drawing of a heron and written, *The one by the bridge.*

The old man looked at the note, then at her. The minute hand reached twelve. Mara pointed to the fine. He smiled, uncertainly, and reached for his wallet.

She shook her head. She crossed out the amount and stamped the book RETURNED.

He watched the stamp descend. Then he placed two fingers against the circled heron, as if keeping the page from blowing away. For a while neither of them moved.

After one o’clock, he thanked her. His wife had died in the spring, he said. She had marked birds all through the book, and he’d meant to find the bridge before bringing it back. Each time he set out, he forgot which bridge she meant.

“There are three,” Mara said.

“I know. I’ve been to all three.”

“Did you see one?”

“Not yet.”

He took the umbrella and left. Mara checked the field guide back out in his name.

That evening she walked home by the eastern bridge. The river below it was shallow and brown. Two boys were throwing stones at a bottle caught in the reeds. Mara stood there until they ran out of stones and went home. No heron appeared.

For the next week she tried a different bridge after work. At the railway bridge, she met a woman who fished with a little red chair. At the stone bridge, the path had nearly disappeared beneath nettles. Mara had lived in town for nineteen years and had never taken it.

On Tuesday, just before noon, she saw the old man ahead of her on that path. His umbrella was open against the sun. She hurried to catch up, but when she reached the riverbank the Quiet Hour began.

He was standing in the grass, looking toward the far shore. Mara followed his gaze.

A heron stood among the reeds. It was smaller than she had expected, and so still that she might have mistaken it for a branch. When it stepped into the water, it lifted each foot carefully, then set it down.

Mara touched the old man’s sleeve and pointed. He nodded. Perhaps he had seen it first.

They stayed until one o’clock. A train crossed the railway bridge upstream; its sound arrived halfway across, wheels clattering suddenly into the afternoon. The heron rose at once and flew around the bend.

“I think this was her bridge,” the old man said.

Mara looked at the place where it had stood. “I think so too.”

He closed his umbrella. They walked back through the nettles, keeping their eyes on the narrow path.

The first summer day I remember arrived in February, carried in a biscuit tin.

My father brought it home from the town hall with both hands around the tin, though it was no bigger than a loaf of bread. The lid was tied down with string. He set it on the kitchen table and told me not to touch it until morning.

“What’s inside?” I asked.

“Tomorrow.”

I was seven. This seemed a perfectly reasonable answer.

The town had borrowed a day from August every February for as long as anyone could remember. At midnight, the mayor opened the tin on the hall steps. Warm air rolled down Market Street, the snow retreated into gutters, and the dark winter trees cast leafy shadows despite having no leaves. We wore sandals and ate peaches that appeared, for one day only, in the grocer’s crates.

In August, the borrowed day had to be returned. Frost settled on the football pitch. The swimming pool filmed over with ice. My father said this was fair, although it annoyed the tomatoes.

He kept the tin because he was the town clerk. He could make the correct form of almost any sentence, even a sentence about the weather. On the morning of the borrowed day, he would count the string marks around the lid to make sure no one had tried to open it early. Once, when I was eleven, I asked what would happen if they did.

“I don’t know,” he said. “That’s why we count.”

For years, the custom seemed to make everyone happy. People came out of their houses blinking and bare-armed. Old neighbours sat together on walls and complained that they could not remember where they had put their sunglasses. Children chased one another through the square. Even those who had spent the winter quarrelling would meet outside and talk about how good the sun felt.

Then my father retired, and I took his job.

I counted the string marks. I wrote the date on the label. I carried the tin to the mayor, who was younger than I was and afraid of dropping it. By then I had my own house, a small one with an apple tree beside the back door.

The first year, the tree put out three blossoms on the borrowed day. I noticed them while I was washing lunch dishes: pale petals against the February sky. By evening there were twelve. The next morning, when winter returned, they had turned brown.

That August, the tree produced no apples.

I mentioned it to the mayor. She said her mother’s lilacs had done the same thing. We asked around. In the allotments, beans had pushed up through cold soil and died. A pair of swallows had arrived early and spent a week hunting insects that weren’t there. Mr. Vale, who ran the grocer’s, said the peaches had been getting smaller each February. We all studied the fruit when it appeared the following year, but none of us could say for certain.

The old records were no help. My father had written down the day, the hour, and the condition of the string, but never what happened afterward. When I asked him about the tree, he looked out of his window for a long time.

“We always liked having that day,” he said.

“So did I.”

He nodded. Neither of us knew what else to say.

In February, I carried the tin to the town hall as usual. People were already gathering in the square. Someone had brought a folding chair for Mrs. Anwar. Two boys had cricket bats tucked under their coats. I could see the mayor on the steps, waiting for me.

On my way past the bakery, I met Mr. Vale’s granddaughter, Elsie. She was six and wore a red wool hat with a pom-pom.

“Will it be warm soon?” she asked.

“I think so.”

She considered this. “If my grandad plants his peas today, will they grow?”

I looked at the tin in my hands. The string was still tied, its three marks where they ought to be.

“I don’t know,” I said.

She seemed satisfied. Children are used to adults not knowing things.

At the hall, I gave the tin to the mayor but asked her to wait. Then I told everyone about the blossoms and the beans and the swallows. I told them we could open it, if that was what they wanted. The tin belonged to the town.

For a while, nobody spoke. It was cold enough that I could hear people stamping their feet.

Mrs. Anwar said her grandchildren were visiting and she had promised them a summer day. Mr. Vale said he had seen what happened to the peas. Someone asked whether we might borrow the day later in the month, when spring was nearer. Nobody knew if that would help.

In the end, the mayor held up the tin and asked for a vote. More hands stayed down than went up. She took it inside.

We were all still standing there. I felt foolish for not having thought of what people would do next. Then Mrs. Anwar asked her grandchildren to bring her chair into the bakery, where it was warm. The boys went home to fetch a board game. Mr. Vale brought over a crate of oranges, which he said weren’t peaches but were good ones.

By noon, the bakery windows had steamed up. People came and went, carrying soup or asking for a seat. My father arrived in his thick coat and sat beside me. We shared an orange. He peeled it in one long piece, as he used to when I was little, and handed me half.

In August, we opened the tin. The mayor stood on the hall steps while everyone who wanted to watch crowded into the square. When she lifted the lid, warm air came out smelling of dust and cut grass. It was a lovely day. The apple tree had fruit on it, small and green, and I went home afterward to see it in the sun.
